old: Adam also knew his wife again, and she gave birth to a son and called his name Seth, saying, "God has appointed another offspring for me instead of Abel, whom Cain killed."
new: Adam also knew his wife again, and she gave birth to a son and called his name Seth, saying, "God has appointed another seed for me instead of Abel, whom Cain killed."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: In the Vulgate verse numbering, Genesis 5 ends at verse 31, incorporating the notice of Noah's age and his three sons that Hebrew and most modern English Bibles place in a separate verse 32.
new: In this text's verse numbering, Genesis 5 ends at verse 31, which includes the notice of Noah's age and his three sons that the Hebrew places in a separate verse 32.
reason: Removes the claim about what English Bibles do and ties the numbering statement to the critical text as given.

old: Vulgate reads "God" (Deus) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has YHWH, and renders the debated Hebrew verb yadon as permanebit ("will remain"), agreeing with the Septuagint.
new: Vulgate reads "God" (Deus) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the divine name, and renders the debated Hebrew verb yadon as permanebit ("will remain"), agreeing with the Septuagint.
reason: Avoids transliterating the divine name in notes (house rule against Yahweh/Jehovah forms; cf. the 16:2 note's "the divine name").

old: Then God blessed Noah and his sons. And He said to them, "Grow and multiply, and fill the earth.
new: Then God blessed Noah and his sons. And He said to them, "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.
reason: Crescite et multiplicamini is rendered "Increase and multiply" in 1:22, 1:28 and 8:17; same formula, same sense.

old: As for you, grow and multiply, and go forth upon the earth, and fill it."
new: As for you, increase and multiply, and go forth upon the earth, and fill it."
reason: crescite et multiplicamini is rendered "increase and multiply" in 1:22, 1:28, 8:17 (and 9:1).

old: "Look, I will establish My pact with you, and with your offspring after you,
new: "Look, I will establish My covenant with you, and with your offspring after you,
reason: pactum is rendered "covenant" in this edition (17:4-21; and fœdus "covenant" in the same speech, 9:12-17); "pact" breaks the established rendering.

old: "Look, I will establish My covenant with you, and with your offspring after you,
new: "Look, I will establish My covenant with you, and with your seed after you,
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: and to every living soul that is with you, both among the birds and among the livestock and all the creatures of the earth that came out of the ark, and all the wild beasts of the earth.
new: and to every living soul that is with you, both among the birds and among the livestock and all the cattle of the earth that came out of the ark, and all the wild beasts of the earth.
reason: pecudibus terræ means "cattle/flock animals of the earth"; "creatures" generalizes it, and wild beasts are listed separately (bestiis).

old: I will establish My pact with you, and never again will all flesh be killed by the waters of a flood, nor will there be from now on a flood devastating the earth."
new: I will establish My covenant with you, and never again will all flesh be killed by the waters of a flood, nor will there be from now on a flood devastating the earth."
reason: pactum is rendered "covenant" in this edition (cf. 9:9, 17:4-21).

old: Latin filii Adam preserves "the sons of Adam" literally, whereas the Hebrew phrase bene ha-adam is commonly rendered "the children of men" or "humankind."
new: Latin filii Adam ("the sons of Adam") renders the Hebrew bene ha-adam ("sons of man") with the name Adam.
reason: Removes the claim about how English versions commonly render the Hebrew; keeps the neutral Latin/Hebrew comparison.

old: Come therefore, let Us go down, and let Us confuse their tongues there, so that no one may understand the voice of his neighbor."
new: Come therefore, let Us go down, and let Us confuse their tongues there, so that no one may hear the voice of his neighbor."
reason: ut non audiat is "may not hear"; "understand" follows familiar English renderings of the Hebrew rather than the Latin verb, and the literal idiom stays clear.

old: And the Lord appeared to Abram and said to him, "To your offspring I will give this land." And he built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him.
new: And the Lord appeared to Abram and said to him, "To your seed I will give this land." And he built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin ab oriente ("from the east") reflects a literal rendering of the preposition, whereas many Hebrew-based translations render the phrase "eastward."
new: Latin ab oriente ("from the east") renders the Hebrew miqqedem, which can also mean "eastward."
reason: Removes the claim about what other translations do; states the neutral Latin/Hebrew point.

old: All the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
new: All the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed forever.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth: if any man can count the dust, he will also be able to count your offspring.
new: And I will make your seed like the dust of the earth: if any man can count the dust, he will also be able to count your seed.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And Abram added, "Yet to me You have not given offspring, and look, my household-born servant will be my heir."
new: And Abram added, "Yet to me You have not given seed, and look, my household-born servant will be my heir."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And He led him outside and said to him, "Look up at heaven and count the stars, if you can." And He said to him, "So will your offspring be."
new: And He led him outside and said to him, "Look up at heaven and count the stars, if you can." And He said to him, "So will your seed be."

old: And it was said to him, "Know beforehand for certain that your offspring will be a stranger in a land not its own, and they will subject them to servitude and afflict them for four hundred years.
new: And it was said to him, "Know beforehand for certain that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own, and they will subject them to servitude and afflict them for four hundred years.

old: On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt as far as the great river, the river Euphrates,
new: On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your seed I will give this land, from the river of Egypt as far as the great river, the river Euphrates,
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And again he said, "Multiplying, I will multiply your offspring, and it will not be counted because of the multitude."
new: And again he said, "Multiplying, I will multiply your seed, and it will not be counted because of the multitude."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin "Ego sum" ("I am") renders the emphatic Hebrew pronoun ("As for Me, behold") as a divine self-declaration of being.
new: Latin "Ego sum" ("I am") renders the emphatic Hebrew pronoun phrase ("As for Me, look").
reason: "a divine self-declaration of being" is theological interpretation, not a statement about the Latin; also drops the banned "behold."

old: And I will establish My covenant between Me and you, and between your offspring after you throughout their generations, by an everlasting covenant, so that I may be your God and the God of your offspring after you.
new: And I will establish My covenant between Me and you, and between your seed after you throughout their generations, by an everlasting covenant, so that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you.

old: And I will give to you and to your offspring the land of your sojourning, all the land of Canaan, for an eternal possession, and I will be their God."
new: And I will give to you and to your seed the land of your sojourning, all the land of Canaan, for an eternal possession, and I will be their God."
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: God said again to Abraham, "And you therefore shall keep My covenant, and your offspring after you throughout their generations.
new: God said again to Abraham, "And you therefore shall keep My covenant, and your seed after you throughout their generations.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: This is the covenant that you shall observe between Me and you, and your offspring after you: every male among you shall be circumcised,
new: This is the covenant that you shall observe between Me and you, and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised,
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And God said to Abraham, "Sarah your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I will establish My covenant for him as an everlasting covenant, and for his offspring after him.
new: And God said to Abraham, "Sarah your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I will establish My covenant for him as an everlasting covenant, and for his seed after him.

old: And he said, "Lord, if I have found favor in Your eyes, do not pass by Your servant;
new: And he said, "Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant;
reason: Domine, said to one of three visiting men whom Abraham then offers water and food (18:4-5), is ambiguous (human "lord" or the Lord); capital "Your" settles a disputed referent, while sentence-initial "Lord" stays open (flagged for the lead).

old: Now after God brought me out from my father's house, I said to her, 'You will show this kindness to me: in every place that we enter, you will say that I am your brother.'"
new: Now after God brought me out from my father's house, I said to her, 'You will show this mercy to me: in every place that we enter, you will say that I am your brother.'"
reason: misericordia is rendered "mercy" elsewhere in this edition, also between persons (19:19, 21:23, 24:49); "kindness" breaks consistency.

old: Distinctively in the Vulgate, Abimelech's closing words read "et quocumque perrexeris: mementoque te deprehensam" ("and wherever you go; and remember that you were caught"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered "and before all you are vindicated."
new: Distinctively in the Vulgate, Abimelech's closing words read "et quocumque perrexeris: mementoque te deprehensam" ("and wherever you go; and remember that you were caught"), whereas the Hebrew reads "and before all you are vindicated."
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: God said to him, "Do not let it seem harsh to you concerning the boy and concerning your servant woman; in all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac offspring will be named for you.
new: God said to him, "Do not let it seem harsh to you concerning the boy and concerning your servant woman; in all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac your seed will be called.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular. Wording matches the same Latin (vocabitur tibi semen) as quoted at Romans 9:7.

old: But I will also make the son of the servant woman into a great nation, because he is your offspring."
new: But I will also make the son of the servant woman into a great nation, because he is your seed."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin Dominus videt ("The Lord sees") and In monte Dominus videbit ("On the mountain the Lord will see") render the place-name and proverb literally with "see," echoing "the land of vision" in verse 2 rather than "provide."
new: Latin Dominus videt ("The Lord sees") and In monte Dominus videbit ("On the mountain the Lord will see") render the place-name and proverb literally with "see," echoing "the land of vision" in verse 2.
reason: "rather than 'provide'" alludes to how English versions render the verse; the note should describe only the Latin.

old: I will bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore; your offspring will possess the gates of their enemies,
new: I will bless you and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore; your seed will possess the gates of their enemies,
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: and in your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice."
new: and in your seed all the nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice."
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: The Lord God of heaven, who took me from the house of my father and from the land of my birth, who spoke to me and swore, saying, 'I will give this land to your offspring,' He Himself will send His angel before you, and from there you will take a wife for my son.
new: The Lord God of heaven, who took me from the house of my father and from the land of my birth, who spoke to me and swore, saying, 'I will give this land to your seed,' He Himself will send His angel before you, and from there you will take a wife for my son.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: The Vulgate explicitly reads plural golden earrings weighing two shekels ("inaures aureas, appendentes siclos duos"; cf. v. 30), whereas the Hebrew and Septuagint describe a single gold ring weighing half a shekel.
new: The Vulgate explicitly reads plural golden earrings weighing two shekels ("inaures aureas, appendentes siclos duos"; cf. v. 30), whereas the Hebrew describes a single gold ring weighing half a shekel.
reason: The Septuagint also has plural earrings (enotia, a drachma each), so the note's claim about the Septuagint is inaccurate.

old: invoking prosperity upon their sister and saying, "You are our sister; may you grow into a thousand thousands, and may your offspring possess the gates of their enemies."
new: invoking prosperity upon their sister and saying, "You are our sister; may you grow into a thousand thousands, and may your seed possess the gates of their enemies."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Now Isaac grew old, and his eyes grew dim, and he could not see. And he called Esau, his older son, and said to him, "My son?" And he answered, "I am here."
new: Now Isaac grew old, and his eyes grew dim, and he could not see. And he called Esau, his older son, and said to him, "My son?" And he answered, "Here I am."
reason: Adsum is rendered "Here I am" at 22:1, 22:11 and 31:11.

old: And I will be your guardian wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land; nor will I leave you until I have fulfilled everything that I have spoken."
new: And I will be your guardian wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land; nor will I leave you unless I have fulfilled everything that I have spoken."
reason: nec dimittam nisi complevero: nisi is "unless"; "until" follows the Hebrew rather than this Latin.

old: Vulgate "experimento didici" ("I have learned by experience") renders the Hebrew verb often translated "learned by divination" in terms of practical observation. Here the Vulgate also reads "Deus" ("God") where the Hebrew has YHWH (compare 30:6 and 30:22, where the Vulgate reads "Dominus" for Hebrew Elohim).
new: Vulgate "experimento didici" ("I have learned by experience") renders a Hebrew verb meaning "learned by divination" in terms of practical observation. Here the Vulgate also reads "Deus" ("God") where the Hebrew has the divine name (compare 30:6 and 30:22, where the Vulgate reads "Dominus" for Hebrew Elohim).
reason: Removes the claim about how the verb is "often translated" and the transliterated divine name (YHWH), which the house style excludes from notes.

old: Clementine Vulgate "furtim me arguent" preserves the form "furtim" (literally "by stealth") in place of the genitive "furti" ("of theft") found in earlier manuscripts, conveying the sense "convict me of theft."
new: The Latin text here reads "furtim" ("by stealth") where other Vulgate editions read the genitive "furti" ("of theft"); "convict me of theft" gives the evident sense of "furtim me arguent."
reason: The Clementine Vulgate itself reads "furti me arguent"; the note wrongly attributes "furtim" to the Clementine and makes an unsupported manuscript claim.

old: and he commanded them, saying, "Speak in this way to my lord Esau: 'Your brother Jacob says this: I have lived as a foreigner with Laban and have remained until the present day.
new: and he commanded them, saying, "Speak in this way to my lord Esau: 'This is what your brother Jacob says: I have lived as a foreigner with Laban and have remained until the present day.
reason: Latin "Hæc dicit frater tuus Jacob" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads vadum Jacob ("the ford of Jacob") where the Hebrew text has the stream name Jabbok.
new: The Latin text here reads vadum Jacob ("the ford of Jacob") where the Hebrew text has the stream name Jabbok.
reason: The claim is true of the Latin in this text, not of Clementine editions generally (which read Jaboc); attribute it to the Latin text here.

old: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate treats Salem as a proper place name ("Salem, the city of the Shechemites") rather than the adverb "safely" as in most translations from the Hebrew, and renders Hebrew Paddan-aram as "Mesopotamia of Syria."
new: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate treats Salem as a proper place name ("Salem, the city of the Shechemites"), where the Hebrew word can also be read as the adverb "safely," and renders Hebrew Paddan-aram as "Mesopotamia of Syria."
reason: Removes the claim about what "most translations" do; keeps a neutral comparison with the Hebrew.

old: and the land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I will give to you and to your offspring after you."
new: and the land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I will give to you and to your seed after you."
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin in infernum (literally "into the lower realm / underworld," traditionally rendered "into hell") translates Hebrew Sheol, the abode of the dead, rather than the place of eternal punishment.
new: Latin in infernum ("into the underworld," literally "into the lower regions") here renders Hebrew Sheol, the abode of the dead.
reason: Removes the claim about traditional English renderings ("into hell") and the doctrinal contrast with eternal punishment; keeps the lexical point.

old: The Vulgate names the sellers Madianei ("Midianites," matching Mazianitis, a Clementine spelling for Midianite, in 37:28; cf. Hebrew Medanim), and describes Potiphar specifically as eunucho ("eunuch") and magistro militiae ("commander of the army," a Roman military title).
new: The Vulgate names the sellers Madianei ("Midianites," matching Mazianitis, the Latin text's spelling of Midianite, in 37:28; cf. Hebrew Medanim), and describes Potiphar specifically as eunucho ("eunuch") and magistro militiae ("commander of the army").
reason: Mazianitis is this Latin text's spelling, not a general Clementine one; the unsupported "Roman military title" aside is dropped.

old: and he spoke to them, "Will we be able to find such a man, who is full of the Spirit of God?"
new: and he spoke to them, "Will we be able to find such a man, who is full of the spirit of God?"
reason: spiritu Dei is spoken by Pharaoh, where the referent is genuinely disputed; a capital "Spirit" settles it, so lowercase keeps the Latin's ambiguity (edition capitalizes elsewhere where God or the narrator speaks).

old: The Clementine Vulgate distinctively reads "non erat panis" ("there was no bread") in Egypt, contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text and the Septuagint, which read that "there was bread."
new: The Latin text here reads "non erat panis" ("there was no bread") in Egypt, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and the Septuagint read that "there was bread."
reason: non erat panis is the reading of this Latin text, not of Clementine editions generally (which read erat panis); attribute it to the Latin text here.

old: Clementine Vulgate reads first-person plural "ut possimus vestros probare sermones" ("so that we may be able to test your words"), rather than a passive clause ("so that your words may be verified") as in the Hebrew text.
new: The Latin text here reads first-person plural "ut possimus vestros probare sermones" ("so that we may be able to test your words"), rather than a passive clause ("so that your words may be verified") as in the Hebrew text.
reason: possimus is the reading of this Latin text rather than of Clementine editions generally (possim); attribute it to the Latin text here.

old: Vulgate lists "resinae, et mellis, et storacis, et stactis, et terebinthi, et amygdalarum" ("resin, honey, storax, stacte, terebinth, and almonds"), reflecting Jerome's identifications of rare Hebrew plant products often translated elsewhere as gum, myrrh, and pistachio nuts.
new: Vulgate lists "resinae, et mellis, et storacis, et stactis, et terebinthi, et amygdalarum" ("resin, honey, storax, stacte, terebinth, and almonds"), reflecting Jerome's identifications of several rare Hebrew plant products.
reason: Removes the claim about how the words are "often translated elsewhere".

old: The Vulgate reads "his mother has him alone" (ipsum solum habet mater sua), translated strictly from the Latin rather than harmonized to the Hebrew "he alone is left of his mother."
new: The Vulgate reads "his mother has him alone" (ipsum solum habet mater sua), where the Hebrew has "he alone is left of his mother."
reason: Removes commentary about this translation's method ("translated strictly ... rather than harmonized"); keeps the neutral Latin/Hebrew comparison.

old: and all that he possessed in the land of Canaan; and he came into Egypt with all his offspring,
new: and all that he possessed in the land of Canaan; and he came into Egypt with all his seed,
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: and said, 'I will increase and multiply you, and make you into companies of peoples; and I will give this land to you and to your offspring after you as an everlasting possession.'
new: and said, 'I will increase and multiply you, and make you into companies of peoples; and I will give this land to you and to your seed after you as an everlasting possession.'
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: he said to his son, "I have not been deprived of the sight of you; furthermore, God has shown me your offspring."
new: he said to his son, "I have not been deprived of the sight of you; furthermore, God has shown me your seed."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: But he, refusing, said, "I know, my son, I know; this one too will indeed become peoples and will be multiplied, but his younger brother will be greater than he, and his offspring will grow into nations."
new: But he, refusing, said, "I know, my son, I know; this one too will indeed become peoples and will be multiplied, but his younger brother will be greater than he, and his seed will grow into nations."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin "et partus tempus advenerit" ("and the time of birth has come") renders functionally the difficult Hebrew phrase usually translated "upon the birthstool."
new: Latin "et partus tempus advenerit" ("and the time of birth has come") renders by sense the difficult Hebrew phrase "upon the two stones" (apparently a birthstool).
reason: Removes a claim about how translations usually render the Hebrew; keeps a neutral factual comparison.

old: Latin "ipsae enim obstetricandi habent scientiam" ("for they themselves have the knowledge of midwifery") is a notable Vulgate reading following ancient interpretive traditions, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly rendered "for they are vigorous."
new: Latin "ipsae enim obstetricandi habent scientiam" ("for they themselves have the knowledge of midwifery") is a distinctive Vulgate reading, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text says that they are "lively" (vigorous).
reason: Removes an unsupported claim about 'ancient interpretive traditions' and a claim about how the Hebrew is 'commonly rendered'.

old: Latin "Qui est" ("He Who Is") uses a third-person ontological formulation shared with the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text repeats the first-person form ("I AM").
new: Latin "Qui est" ("He Who Is") is a third-person formulation shared with the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text repeats the first-person form ("I am").
reason: "Ontological" is a theological characterization, not a description of the Latin; the capitalized "I AM" is a confessional typographic convention.

old: Latin "vocavit nos" ("has called us") agrees with the Septuagint against the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which is commonly rendered "has met with us."
new: Latin "vocavit nos" ("has called us") agrees with the Septuagint against the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "has met with us."
reason: Removes a claim about how the Hebrew is 'commonly rendered'; states the Hebrew reading directly (as the 5:3 note does).

old: Latin mitte quem missurus es ("send the one whom You are going to send") uses the future active participle, retaining the ambiguity between asking God to send someone else and, in traditional Christian exegesis, pointing toward the coming Messiah.
new: Latin mitte quem missurus es ("send the one whom You are going to send") uses the future active participle; the Hebrew reads "send by the hand of whom You will send."
reason: Messianic exegesis is doctrinal comment; the note now only describes the Latin construction and the Hebrew wording.

old: Therefore the Lord says this: "By this you will know that I am the Lord: look, I will strike the water of the river with the staff that is in My hand, and it will be turned into blood.
new: Therefore this is what the Lord says: "By this you will know that I am the Lord: look, I will strike the water of the river with the staff that is in My hand, and it will be turned into blood.
reason: Latin "Hæc igitur dicit Dominus" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: The Lord also said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, and you will say to him, 'The Lord says this: "Let My people go, so that they may sacrifice to Me;
new: The Lord also said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, and you will say to him, 'This is what the Lord says: "Let My people go, so that they may sacrifice to Me;
reason: Latin "Hæc dicit" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: The Vulgate translates "into the remains of your food" (in reliquias ciborum tuorum) where the Hebrew has "into your kneading bowls." Following the Hebrew chapter division, vv. 26-29 conclude chapter 7 in the Vulgate (corresponding to 8:1-4 in many English versions).
new: The Vulgate translates "into the remains of your food" (in reliquias ciborum tuorum) where the Hebrew has "into your kneading bowls." Following the Hebrew chapter division, vv. 26-29 conclude chapter 7 in this Latin text (8:1-4 in the alternative numbering).
reason: Removes a claim about what English versions do; the numbering statement is now limited to this Latin text.

old: In the Clementine Vulgate, Exodus 8 begins at the command to stretch out Aaron's hand (corresponding to 8:5 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most modern English Bibles), because the preceding warning about frogs appears at 7:26-29; thus chapter 8 has 28 verses rather than 32.
new: As in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, chapter 8 of this Latin text begins at the command to stretch out Aaron's hand, because the preceding warning about frogs appears at 7:26-29; thus chapter 8 has 28 verses rather than the 32 of the alternative numbering, in which this verse is 8:5.
reason: The note wrongly made this verse 8:5 in the Masoretic Text (whose chapter 8 also begins here, after 7:26-29), and it made a claim about English Bibles.

old: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses direct future indicatives (percutiam ... peribisque, "I will strike ... and you will perish") rather than the counterfactual past sense common in translations from the Hebrew ("I could have struck ... and you would have been cut off").
new: As in the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses future indicatives (percutiam ... peribisque, "I will strike ... and you will perish"), whereas the Hebrew uses past forms, generally understood as counterfactual ("I could have struck ... and you would have been cut off").
reason: Removes a claim about what translations from the Hebrew do; states the Hebrew grammar neutrally.

old: The Vulgate reads in limine ("on the threshold"), reflecting one meaning of the ambiguous Hebrew noun saph, which many other versions render "basin."
new: The Vulgate reads in limine ("on the threshold"), reflecting one meaning of the ambiguous Hebrew noun saph, which can also mean "basin."
reason: Notes should not make claims about what other versions do; restated as a neutral fact about the Hebrew word.

old: For the Hebrew term often rendered "frontlets," the Vulgate reads quasi appensum quid, ob recordationem ("like something hung, for remembrance").
new: For the Hebrew totaphot ("frontlets"), the Vulgate reads quasi appensum quid, ob recordationem ("like something hung, for remembrance").
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: Latin Dominus exaltatio mea ("The Lord Is My Exaltation") interprets the altar's name distinctively, where the Hebrew reads YHWH-Nissi ("the Lord is my banner").
new: Latin Dominus exaltatio mea ("The Lord Is My Exaltation") interprets the altar's name distinctively, where the Hebrew name means "the Lord is my banner."
reason: Notes avoid the transliterated divine name; "the divine name" is used instead.

old: Latin regnum sacerdotale ("a priestly kingdom") translates the Hebrew "kingdom of priests" with an adjective modifying "kingdom," paralleling the Greek Septuagint.
new: Latin regnum sacerdotale ("a priestly kingdom") translates the Hebrew "kingdom of priests" with an adjective modifying "kingdom."
reason: The Septuagint has basileion hierateuma ("royal priesthood"), where the adjective modifies "priesthood", so "paralleling the Greek Septuagint" is inaccurate and is removed.

old: The Vulgate explicitly reads "suffers a miscarriage, yet she herself lives" (and "if her death follows" in v. 23), whereas the Hebrew reads "her children come out, yet there is no harm." Note also that Vulgate 21:37 corresponds to Exodus 22:1 in the Hebrew numbering.
new: The Vulgate explicitly reads "suffers a miscarriage, yet she herself lives" (and "if her death follows" in v. 23), whereas the Hebrew reads "her children come out, yet there is no harm."
reason: The numbering sentence is false: this text's 21:37 is also 21:37 in the Hebrew numbering (it is 22:1 only in common English numbering), and it has nothing to do with this verse.

old: Whoever has sexual relations with an animal must certainly die.
new: Whoever has sexual relations with an animal must surely die.
reason: morte moriatur is rendered "must surely die" everywhere else in this section (21:12, 15, 16, 17).

old: hyacinth-blue and purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen, goat hair,
new: violet-blue and purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen, goat hair,
reason: hyacinthus is rendered "violet-blue" elsewhere in the edition (e.g. 26:1, 26:4, 26:31, 26:36); this is the only "hyacinth-blue".

old: Vulgate "thuribula" ("censers") is a distinctive Latin rendering for one of the golden table vessels (Hebrew "menaqiyyot," usually "bowls" or "jars").
new: Vulgate "thuribula" ("censers") is a distinctive Latin rendering for one of the golden table vessels.
reason: In the Hebrew list (qe'arot, kappot, qesot, menaqqiyot) the last term lines up with cyathos, not thuribula, so the Hebrew identification is inaccurate and is removed.

old: Latin de janthinis pellibus ('of violet-colored skins') follows the Septuagint rendering of the obscure Hebrew term tahash, which modern translations often render as fine leather or the skins of marine animals.
new: Latin de janthinis pellibus ('of violet-colored skins') follows the Septuagint rendering of the obscure Hebrew term tahash, whose meaning is uncertain.
reason: Notes should not make claims about what modern translations do; the clause is replaced with a neutral statement.

old: You shall also gild the boards themselves, and you shall cast golden rings on them through which the bars may hold the boarding together; and you shall cover the bars with golden plates.
new: You shall also gild the boards themselves, and you shall cast golden rings on them through which the bars may hold the boarding together; and these you shall cover with golden plates.
reason: Latin has only the relative quos ('which/these'), which may refer to the rings or the bars; supplying 'the bars' decides the antecedent (cf. the edition's 'these' for the same construction at 38:18).

old: Latin capita ('capitals' or 'heads') describes the tops of the pillars (as also in 26:37 and 27:10, 11, 17), where the Hebrew refers to 'hooks'; similarly, 'propitiatory' in 26:34 directly translates Latin propitiatorium, the golden atonement cover traditionally called the mercy seat.
new: Latin capita ('capitals' or 'heads') describes the tops of the pillars (as also in 26:37 and 27:10, 11, 17), where the Hebrew refers to 'hooks'.
reason: 26:34 now renders propitiatorium with the edition's standard 'mercy seat', so the clause about 'propitiatory' is obsolete; 'golden atonement cover' was also interpretive.

old: You shall also place the propitiatory upon the ark of the testimony in the Holy of Holies,
new: You shall also place the mercy seat upon the ark of the testimony in the Holy of Holies,
reason: propitiatorium is rendered 'mercy seat' throughout the edition (30:6, 31:7, 35:12, 38:5, 38:8, 39:14).

old: And they will receive gold, violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed crimson, and fine linen.
new: And they will receive gold, violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen.
reason: coccum bis tinctum is 'twice-dyed scarlet' in 26:31, 26:36, 27:16, 35:6, 35:23, 36:9, 36:15; 'crimson' is the edition's rendering of the different word vermiculus.

old: Now they will make the shoulder vestment of gold, violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed crimson, and twisted fine linen, in variegated woven work.
new: Now they will make the shoulder vestment of gold, violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, in variegated woven work.
reason: cocco bis tincto = 'twice-dyed scarlet' elsewhere in the edition; 'crimson' is used for vermiculus.

old: The weaving itself also, and all the variety of the work, will be of gold, violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed crimson, and twisted fine linen.
new: The weaving itself also, and all the variety of the work, will be of gold, violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen.
reason: cocco bis tincto = 'twice-dyed scarlet' elsewhere in the edition; 'crimson' is used for vermiculus.

old: You will also make the breastpiece of judgment in variegated woven work, according to the weaving of the shoulder vestment, of gold, violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed crimson, and twisted fine linen.
new: You will also make the breastpiece of judgment in variegated woven work, according to the weaving of the shoulder vestment, of gold, violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen.
reason: cocco bis tincto = 'twice-dyed scarlet' elsewhere in the edition (incl. the parallel 36:15); 'crimson' is used for vermiculus.

old: Below, however, at the foot of that same tunic, all around, you will make, as it were, pomegranates, of violet-blue, purple, and twice-dyed crimson, with bells mingled in between,
new: Below, however, at the foot of that same tunic, all around, you will make, as it were, pomegranates, of violet-blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, with bells mingled in between,
reason: cocco bis tincto = 'twice-dyed scarlet' elsewhere in the edition; 'crimson' is used for vermiculus.

old: And you will place the turban on his head, and the holy plate upon the turban,
new: And you will place the headdress on his head, and the holy plate upon the headdress,
reason: tiara is 'headdress' in 28:37, 28:39 and 28:40 (the same item bearing the same plate); 'turban' is the edition's word for cidaris (28:4).

old: And you will receive all of them from their hands, and burn them upon the altar as a whole burnt offering, a most pleasing aroma in the sight of the Lord, because it is His offering.
new: And you will receive all of them from their hands, and burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering, a most pleasing aroma in the sight of the Lord, because it is His offering.
reason: in holocaustum: holocaustum is rendered 'burnt offering' throughout the edition; 'whole' is an added expansion.

old: with which Aaron and his sons were initiated, and they will fall to the share of Aaron and his sons by a perpetual right from the sons of Israel; because they are firstfruits and first portions from their peace sacrifices that they offer to the Lord.
new: with which Aaron and his sons were initiated, and they will fall to the share of Aaron and his sons by a perpetual right from the sons of Israel; because they are firstfruits and first portions from their peace offerings that they offer to the Lord.
reason: victimis pacificis: the edition's established rendering of pacifica is 'peace offerings'.

old: For seven days you will make atonement for the altar and sanctify it, and it will be the Holy of Holies; everyone who touches it will be sanctified.
new: For seven days you will make atonement for the altar and sanctify it, and it will be most holy; everyone who touches it will be sanctified.
reason: erit Sanctum sanctorum here is predicated of the altar (superlative 'most holy', as rendered in 30:10, 30:29, 30:36, 40:11); 'the Holy of Holies' wrongly names the inner sanctuary.

old: so that they may not die; it shall be an everlasting statute for him and for his offspring through successive generations."
new: so that they may not die; it shall be an everlasting statute for him and for his seed through successive generations."
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: and with it you shall anoint the tabernacle of the testimony, and the ark of the testament,
new: and with it you shall anoint the tabernacle of the testimony, and the ark of the covenant,
reason: arca testamenti is rendered 'ark of the covenant' in this edition.

old: And rising in the morning, they offered burnt offerings and peace sacrifices; and the people sat down to eat and drink, and got up to play.
new: And rising in the morning, they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and drink, and got up to play.
reason: hostias pacificas: the edition's established rendering of pacificæ hostiæ is 'peace offerings'.

old: They have quickly departed from the way that you showed them; and they have made for themselves a cast calf, and worshiped it, and sacrificing offerings to it, they said, 'These are your gods, Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt.'
new: They have quickly departed from the way that you showed them; and they have made for themselves a cast calf, and worshiped it, and sacrificing offerings to it, they said, 'These are your gods, Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt.'"
reason: The critical text has 32:9 (Rursumque ait Dominus..., shown after 32:8), a narrative line that opens a new speech, so the Lord's speech begun in 32:7 must close here; the matching closing quote at 32:9 is removed.

old: And once again the Lord said to Moses, "I perceive that this people is stiff-necked."
new: And once again the Lord said to Moses, "I perceive that this people is stiff-necked.
reason: The Latin ends with a colon and the Lord's speech continues in 32:10 (dimitte me...), which closes the quotation; the closing quote here left 32:10 unbalanced (32:8 now closes the speech begun in 32:7).

old: Verse 32:9 ("Again the Lord said to Moses: I see that this people is stiff-necked") is absent from the Clementine Vulgate, so 32:10 follows directly upon 32:8.
reason: False for the Latin: the critical text has 32:9 (Rursumque ait Dominus ad Moysen: Cerno quod populus iste duræ cervicis sit), displayed after 32:8.

old: Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Your servants, to whom You swore by Yourself, saying, 'I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven; and all this land about which I have spoken I will give to your offspring, and you will possess it forever.'"
new: Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Your servants, to whom You swore by Yourself, saying, 'I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven; and all this land about which I have spoken I will give to your seed, and you will possess it forever.'"
reason: Latin semen/semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "let loose" or "out of control" as "stripped naked" (nudatus) and adds the parenthetical explanation that Aaron had despoiled them "on account of the disgrace of filth" (propter ignominiam sordis) and set them naked among their enemies.
new: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "let loose" (or "out of control") as "stripped naked" (nudatus) and "had despoiled" (spoliaverat), and reads "on account of the disgrace of filth" (propter ignominiam sordis) where the Hebrew speaks of a derision among their enemies.
reason: The Hebrew also has an explanatory clause (Aaron had let them loose, for a derision among their enemies), so the Vulgate does not 'add' the parenthesis; it renders it differently.

old: And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, "Go, go up from this place, you and your people whom you led out of the land of Egypt, into the land that I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your offspring I will give it';
new: And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, "Go, go up from this place, you and your people whom you led out of the land of Egypt, into the land that I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your seed I will give it';
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: and you may enter a land flowing with milk and honey. For I will not go up with you, because you are a hard-necked people; otherwise I might destroy you on the way."
new: and you may enter a land flowing with milk and honey. For I will not go up with you, because you are a stiff-necked people; otherwise I might destroy you on the way."
reason: populus duræ cervicis is 'stiff-necked' at 32:9, 34:9 and elsewhere in the edition; 'hard-necked' occurs only here and in 33:5.

old: And the Lord said to Moses, "Speak to the sons of Israel: 'You are a hard-necked people; once I will go up in your midst and blot you out. Right now lay aside your adornment, so that I may know what I should do to you.'"
new: And the Lord said to Moses, "Speak to the sons of Israel: 'You are a stiff-necked people; once I will go up in your midst and blot you out. Right now lay aside your adornment, so that I may know what I should do to you.'"
reason: populus duræ cervicis is 'stiff-necked' at 32:9, 34:9 and elsewhere in the edition.

old: The Vulgate famously renders the Hebrew verb qaran ('shone, sent forth rays') as cornuta ('horned', from the related Hebrew root qeren, 'horn'), a reading repeated in vv. 30 and 35.
new: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew verb qaran ('shone, sent forth rays') as cornuta ('horned', from the related Hebrew root qeren, 'horn'), a reading repeated in vv. 30 and 35.
reason: 'famously' is commentary; notes should be neutral and factual.

old: Latin 'rationale' (reflecting Greek 'logeion', "oracle-piece" or "piece of reason") denotes the high priest's breastpiece. In vv. 18-20, the Vulgate gemstone sequence follows the Greek tradition rather than the Hebrew order (for example, placing 'jaspis' in row two, 'ligurius' or "ligure" in row three, and 'beryllus' in row four).
new: Latin 'rationale' (reflecting Greek 'logeion', "oracle-piece" or "piece of reason") denotes the high priest's breastpiece. In vv. 17-20, the Vulgate's names for the gems follow the Greek tradition rather than the Hebrew (for example, 'jaspis' in row two and 'beryllus' in row four, where the Hebrew has jasper last).
reason: The rows begin at v. 17, and 'ligurius' stands in the same position as Hebrew leshem, so it does not illustrate a difference; the difference lies in the stone names, not the order.

old: four-cornered, doubled, of a span's measure.
new: four-cornered, doubled, of a palm's measure.
reason: mensuræ palmi: palmus is 'palm' in the parallel 28:16 ('the measure of a palm') for the same breastpiece.

old: Latin 'de janthinis pellibus' ('of violet-colored skins,' from Greek 'ianthinos') preserves a distinctive Vulgate and Septuagint color rendering of Hebrew 'tahash', often translated as fine leather or sea-mammal skins.
new: Latin 'de janthinis pellibus' ('of violet-colored skins,' from Greek 'ianthinos') preserves a distinctive Vulgate and Septuagint color rendering of Hebrew 'tahash', a term of uncertain meaning.
reason: Notes should not report what translations do ('often translated as'); the neutral fact is that the Hebrew term is uncertain.

old: Vulgate reads "ad placandum sibi Dominum" ("to make the Lord favorable to himself"), interpreting the Hebrew phrase usually rendered "for his acceptance before the Lord."
new: Vulgate reads "ad placandum sibi Dominum" ("to make the Lord favorable to himself"), where the Hebrew reads "for his acceptance before the Lord."
reason: Removes a claim about how the Hebrew is 'usually rendered' by translations; keeps the neutral Latin/Hebrew comparison.

old: and he shall bring it to the doorway of the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord, and he shall place his hand upon its head and sacrifice it to the Lord.
new: and he shall bring it to the doorway of the tabernacle of the testimony before the Lord, and he shall place his hand upon its head and sacrifice it to the Lord.
reason: tabernaculum testimonii is rendered "tabernacle of the testimony" throughout the edition (e.g. 1:1, 1:3, 3:2).

old: Vulgate tabernaculi testimonii ("tabernacle of testimony") follows the Septuagint tradition, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "tent of meeting."
new: Vulgate tabernaculi testimonii ("tabernacle of the testimony") follows the Septuagint tradition, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "tent of meeting."
reason: Gloss aligned with the edition's standard rendering of tabernaculum testimonii.

old: He shall also draw from the blood of the calf, bringing it into the tabernacle of testimony.
new: He shall also draw from the blood of the calf, bringing it into the tabernacle of the testimony.
reason: tabernaculum testimonii → "tabernacle of the testimony" (edition standard).

old: And he shall put some of that same blood upon the horns of the altar of incense most pleasing to the Lord, which is in the tabernacle of testimony; but all the remaining blood he shall pour onto the base of the altar of burnt offering at the entrance of the tabernacle.
new: And he shall put some of that same blood upon the horns of the altar of incense most pleasing to the Lord, which is in the tabernacle of the testimony; but all the remaining blood he shall pour onto the base of the altar of burnt offering at the entrance of the tabernacle.
reason: tabernaculo testimonii → "tabernacle of the testimony" (edition standard).

old: And he shall remove the fat of the calf for sin, both that which covers the vital organs and all things that are inside:
new: And he shall remove the fat of the calf for sin, both that which covers the internal organs and all things that are inside:
reason: vitalia in this same sacrificial formula is "internal organs" in 3:3, 3:10, 3:14.

old: the two kidneys and the caul that is over them beside the flanks, and the fat of the liver with the kidneys,
new: the two kidneys and the membrane that is over them beside the flanks, and the fat of the liver with the kidneys,
reason: reticulum quod est super eos juxta ilia is rendered "the membrane that is over them beside the flanks" in 3:15; reticulum is "membrane" throughout.

old: the priest who is anointed shall bring some of its blood into the tabernacle of testimony,
new: the priest who is anointed shall bring some of its blood into the tabernacle of the testimony,
reason: tabernaculum testimonii → "tabernacle of the testimony" (edition standard).

old: And he shall put some of that same blood on the horns of the altar that is before the Lord in the tabernacle of testimony; but the remaining blood he shall pour beside the base of the altar of burnt offerings, which is at the doorway of the tabernacle of testimony.
new: And he shall put some of that same blood on the horns of the altar that is before the Lord in the tabernacle of the testimony; but the remaining blood he shall pour beside the base of the altar of burnt offerings, which is at the doorway of the tabernacle of the testimony.
reason: tabernaculo/tabernaculi testimonii (twice) → "tabernacle of the testimony" (edition standard).

old: And removing all the fat, just as it is customarily removed from the victims of peace offerings, he shall burn it upon the altar for an aroma of sweetness to the Lord; and he shall pray for him, and it will be forgiven him.
new: And removing all the fat, just as it is customarily removed from the victims of peace offerings, he shall burn it upon the altar for a fragrance of sweetness to the Lord; and he shall pray for him, and it will be forgiven him.
reason: in odorem suavitatis is "a fragrance of sweetness" in 2:9, 2:12, 8:28.

old: Vulgate arietis ("ram") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Septuagint read "lamb."
new: Vulgate arietis ("ram") is a distinctive reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "lamb" and the Septuagint "sheep."
reason: The Septuagint here has probaton ("sheep"), not "lamb"; the comparison is corrected to be accurate.

old: "If a soul sins, and hears the voice of one swearing, and is a witness because he either saw it himself or is aware of it: unless he discloses it, he will bear his iniquity.
new: "If a soul sins, and hears the voice of one swearing, and is a witness of what he either saw himself or is aware of: unless he discloses it, he will bear his iniquity.
reason: In testis fuerit quod aut ipse vidit, aut conscius est, quod is the relative object ("of what he saw"), not causal "because".

old: let him do penance for the sin,
new: let him repent for the sin,
reason: pœnitentiam agere is rendered "repent" in this edition; "do penance" imports technical vocabulary the Latin does not require.

old: Vulgate agat poenitentiam ("let him do penance") is a distinctive Latin rendering; the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Septuagint speak of confessing the sin.
new: Vulgate agat poenitentiam ("let him repent") is a distinctive Latin rendering; the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Septuagint speak of confessing the sin.
reason: Gloss aligned with the corrected verse and the edition's standard rendering of pœnitentiam agere.

old: In this versification (matching the Hebrew Masoretic Text), Leviticus 5 continues through 5:26; many modern English Bibles number 5:20-26 as Leviticus 6:1-7.
new: In this versification (matching the Hebrew Masoretic Text), Leviticus 5 continues through 5:26; other versifications number 5:20-26 as 6:1-7.
reason: Removes a claim about what English Bibles do while keeping the factual versification information.

old: In the Vulgate (following the Septuagint), Leviticus chapter 6 begins here (corresponding to Hebrew MT 6:8), because MT 6:1-7 appear as Vulgate 5:20-26.
new: In this versification (matching the Hebrew Masoretic Text), chapter 6 begins here; other versifications number this verse 6:8.
reason: The note was false for this text: here 5:20-26 and 6:1 follow the Hebrew numbering (this verse is MT 6:1, not MT 6:8), as the 5:20 note itself states.

old: The priest will take a handful of the fine flour that has been moistened with oil, and all the frankincense that has been placed on the fine flour, and he will burn it on the altar as a memorial of a most pleasing aroma to the Lord;
new: The priest will take a handful of the fine flour that has been moistened with oil, and all the frankincense that has been placed on the fine flour, and he will burn it on the altar as a memorial of a very sweet fragrance to the Lord;
reason: odor suavissimus is "a very sweet fragrance" in 1:13, 1:17, 2:2, 3:5, 3:16; "most pleasing" is used for gratissimus (4:7).

old: which, moistened with oil, will be fried in a frying pan. And it will be offered hot for a most pleasing aroma to the Lord
new: which, moistened with oil, will be fried in a frying pan. And it will be offered hot for a very sweet fragrance to the Lord
reason: in odorem suavissimum → "a very sweet fragrance" as elsewhere in chs. 1-3.

old: For a sacrifice that is killed for sin, whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of testimony to make atonement in the sanctuary, will not be eaten, but will be burned up with fire.'"
new: For a sacrifice that is killed for sin, whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of the testimony to make expiation in the sanctuary, will not be eaten, but will be burned up with fire.'"
reason: tabernaculum testimonii → "tabernacle of the testimony" (edition standard); ad expiandum is expiare, rendered "expiation" in 1:4 and 5:13, not the Hebrew-based "atonement".

old: They will offer from it the tail and the fat that covers the inward parts,
new: They will offer from it the tail and the fat that covers the internal organs,
reason: adipem qui operit vitalia is "the fat that covers the internal organs" in 3:3.

old: But the fat that was on the vital organs, and the membrane of the liver, and the two kidneys with their suet, he burned on the altar,
new: But the fat that was on the internal organs, and the membrane of the liver, and the two kidneys with their suet, he burned on the altar,
reason: vitalia is "internal organs" in 3:3, 3:10, 3:14.

old: "Wine, and anything that can intoxicate, you and your sons shall not drink when you enter the tabernacle of testimony, so that you may not die; for it is an everlasting command throughout your generations,
new: "Wine, and anything that can intoxicate, you and your sons shall not drink when you enter the tabernacle of the testimony, so that you may not die; for it is an everlasting command throughout your generations,
reason: tabernaculum testimonii → "tabernacle of the testimony" (edition standard, cf. 9:23).

old: The Vulgate renders Hebrew "strong drink" descriptively as "anything that can intoxicate" (omne quod inebriare potest), and renders the "tent of meeting" as "tabernacle of testimony" (tabernaculum testimonii), following the Septuagint.
new: The Vulgate renders Hebrew "strong drink" descriptively as "anything that can intoxicate" (omne quod inebriare potest), and renders the "tent of meeting" as "tabernacle of the testimony" (tabernaculum testimonii), following the Septuagint.
reason: Gloss aligned with the edition's standard rendering of tabernaculum testimonii.

old: The Vulgate adds "and the rest" (et cetera) after the camel, and in 11:5-6 reverses the order of the Hebrew text by placing the hare (lepus) before the rock badger (choerogryllus, from Greek choirogryllios, the Syrian rock hyrax).
new: The Vulgate adds "and the rest" (et cetera) after the camel; in 11:5 choerogryllus (from Greek choirogryllios) denotes the rock hyrax.
reason: False for this Latin: 11:5 is Chœrogryllus and 11:6 Lepus, the same order as the Hebrew (rock badger, then hare).

old: The hare also, for it too chews the cud, but does not divide the hoof.
new: The rock badger, which chews the cud and does not divide the hoof, is unclean.
reason: The English of 11:5 and 11:6 was swapped: Latin 11:5 is "Chœrogryllus qui ruminat, ungulamque non dividit, immundus est" (the rock badger).

old: The rock badger, which chews the cud and does not divide the hoof, is unclean.
new: The hare also, for it too chews the cud, but does not divide the hoof.
reason: The English of 11:5 and 11:6 was swapped: Latin 11:6 is "Lepus quoque: nam et ipse ruminat, sed ungulam non dividit" (the hare).

old: In 11:13-19 the Vulgate follows the Septuagint's Greek bird names, yielding several renderings distinct from modern translations of the Hebrew, including "griffin" (gryphem, understood in antiquity as a giant vulture or bird of prey), "ostrich" (struthionem), "ibis" (ibin), "swan" (cygnum), and "purple gallinule" (porphyrionem).
new: In 11:13-19 the Vulgate follows the Septuagint's Greek bird names, yielding several renderings that differ from the Hebrew, including "griffin" (gryphem, understood in antiquity as a giant vulture or bird of prey), "ostrich" (struthionem), "ibis" (ibin), "swan" (cygnum), and "purple gallinule" (porphyrionem).
reason: Removes a comparison with modern translations; keeps the neutral comparison with the Hebrew.

old: And when the priest purifying the man has set him and all these things before the Lord at the doorway of the tabernacle of testimony,
new: And when the priest purifying the man has set him and all these things before the Lord at the doorway of the tabernacle of the testimony,
reason: tabernaculi testimonii → "tabernacle of the testimony" (edition standard, cf. 12:6, 15:14).

old: and he will offer them on the eighth day of his purification to the priest, at the doorway of the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord.
new: and he will offer them on the eighth day of his purification to the priest, at the doorway of the tabernacle of the testimony before the Lord.
reason: tabernaculi testimonii → "tabernacle of the testimony" (edition standard).

old: and commanded him, saying: "Speak to Aaron your brother, that he not enter at all times into the sanctuary that is inside the veil before the propitiatory by which the ark is covered, so that he may not die (for I will appear in a cloud over the oracle),
new: and commanded him, saying: "Speak to Aaron your brother, that he not enter at all times into the sanctuary that is inside the veil before the mercy seat by which the ark is covered, so that he may not die (for I will appear in a cloud over the oracle),
reason: propitiatorium has the edition's established rendering "mercy seat".

old: Throughout this chapter the Vulgate alternates between "propitiatorium" ("propitiatory", vv. 2, 14) and "oraculum" ("oracle", vv. 2, 13, 15) to render the single Hebrew term for the cover of the ark.
new: Throughout this chapter the Vulgate alternates between "propitiatorium" ("mercy seat", vv. 2, 14) and "oraculum" ("oracle", vv. 2, 13, 15) to render the single Hebrew term for the cover of the ark.
reason: Gloss brought into line with the verse's established rendering of propitiatorium as "mercy seat".

old: Vulgate "capro emissario" ("for the emissary goat", the origin of the English term "scapegoat") interprets Hebrew "la'azazel" ("for Azazel") as a goat designated to be sent away; see also verses 10 and 26.
new: Vulgate "capro emissario" ("for the emissary goat") interprets Hebrew "la'azazel" ("for Azazel") as a goat designated to be sent away; see also verses 10 and 26.
reason: The aside on the origin of the English word "scapegoat" is English Bible history, not an explanation of the Latin.

old: He will also take some of the blood of the calf, and sprinkle with his finger seven times facing the propitiatory toward the east.
new: He will also take some of the blood of the calf, and sprinkle with his finger seven times facing the mercy seat toward the east.
reason: propitiatorium has the edition's established rendering "mercy seat".

old: You shall not give any of your offspring to be consecrated to the idol Molech, nor shall you pollute the name of your God. I am the Lord.
new: You shall not give any of your seed to be consecrated to the idol Molech, nor shall you pollute the name of your God. I am the Lord.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Vulgate uniquely uses 'amicum tuum' ('your friend') here rather than 'proximum tuum' ('your neighbor', used in vv. 11, 13, 15, and 16) to render the same Hebrew noun.
new: Vulgate here uses 'amicum tuum' ('your friend'), where vv. 13 and 16 render the same Hebrew noun with forms of 'proximus' ('neighbor').
reason: Inaccurate: v. 11 reads 'proximum suum', and vv. 11 and 15 render a different Hebrew noun ('amit), so only vv. 13 and 16 share the Hebrew noun of v. 18.

old: If a man sleeps with a woman in an intercourse of seed, who is a servant woman even of marriageable age, and yet not redeemed by a price nor granted freedom, both shall be beaten, and they shall not die, because she was not free.
new: If a man sleeps with a woman in an intercourse of seed, who is a slave woman even of marriageable age, and yet not redeemed by a price nor granted freedom, both shall be beaten, and they shall not die, because she was not free.
reason: ancilla here stands in an explicit slave/free contrast (libertate donata, non fuit libera), where the edition uses "slave".

old: Vulgate describes the servant woman as 'etiam nubilis' ('even of marriageable age') and prescribes 'vapulabunt ambo' ('both shall be beaten'), whereas the Hebrew text refers to a slave woman designated for a man and states that there shall be an inquiry or punishment.
new: Vulgate describes the slave woman as 'etiam nubilis' ('even of marriageable age') and prescribes 'vapulabunt ambo' ('both shall be beaten'), whereas the Hebrew text refers to a slave woman designated for a man and states that there shall be an inquiry or punishment.
reason: Keeps the note in step with the corrected verse rendering of ancilla.

old: "You shall speak these things to the sons of Israel: 'If any man from the sons of Israel, and from the strangers who live in Israel, gives from his offspring to the idol Molech, he shall surely die; the people of the land shall stone him.
new: "You shall speak these things to the sons of Israel: 'If any man from the sons of Israel, and from the strangers who live in Israel, gives from his seed to the idol Molech, he shall surely die; the people of the land shall stone him.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And I will set My face against him and will cut him off from the midst of his people, because he has given from his offspring to Molech, and has contaminated My sanctuary, and has defiled My holy name.
new: And I will set My face against him and will cut him off from the midst of his people, because he has given from his seed to Molech, and has contaminated My sanctuary, and has defiled My holy name.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And if the people of the land, being negligent and as if thinking little of My command, lets go the man who gave from his offspring to Molech, and refuses to kill him,
new: And if the people of the land, being negligent and as if thinking little of My command, lets go the man who gave from his seed to Molech, and refuses to kill him,
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin "sed nec in principe populi sui contaminabitur" ("but not even for a ruler of his people shall he be defiled") resolves a notoriously difficult Hebrew clause (often rendered "as a husband/chief among his people, so as to profane himself") as a prohibition against defilement even for a deceased ruler.
new: Latin "sed nec in principe populi sui contaminabitur" ("but not even for a ruler of his people shall he be defiled") renders a difficult Hebrew clause (literally "a husband/chief shall not defile himself among his people, so as to profane himself") as a prohibition against defilement even for a deceased ruler.
reason: Replaces a vague claim about how translations render the clause ("often rendered") with a neutral literal gloss of the Hebrew.

old: "On the tenth day of this seventh month, the day of atonements will be most celebrated, and it will be proclaimed holy; and you will afflict your souls on it, and you will offer a burnt offering to the Lord.
new: "On the tenth day of this seventh month, the day of expiations will be most celebrated, and it will be proclaimed holy; and you will afflict your souls on it, and you will offer a burnt offering to the Lord.
reason: expiationum is from expiatio, rendered "expiation" throughout Leviticus 16 (vv. 16, 27, 30); "atonements" brings in other wording.

old: The Clementine Vulgate includes the concluding colophon ("These are the judgments...") within verse 45, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most modern English Bibles number it separately as verse 46.
new: The Clementine Vulgate includes the concluding colophon ("These are the judgments...") within verse 45, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text numbers it separately as verse 46.
reason: Removes the claim about what English Bibles do; the comparison with the Hebrew numbering is kept.

old: Everything that is consecrated to the Lord, whether it is a person, or an animal, or a field, will not be sold, nor can it be redeemed. Whatever has once been consecrated will be most holy to the Lord;
new: Everything that is consecrated to the Lord, whether it is a person, or an animal, or a field, will not be sold, nor can it be redeemed. Whatever has once been consecrated will be a holy of holies to the Lord;
reason: Sanctum sanctorum is kept literal as "a holy of holies", as at 24:9; the idiom stays clear.

old: from Benjamin, Abidan, son of Gideoni;
new: from Benjamin, Abidan, son of Gideon;
reason: Gedeonis is the genitive of Gedeon ("Gideon"), as the verse's own note says; "Gideoni" follows the Hebrew name, not the Latin.

old: The Vulgate calls the sanctuary "tabernaculum foederis" (tabernacle of the covenant) here and "tabernaculum testimonii" (tabernacle of testimony) in 2:17, where the Hebrew has "tent of meeting" in both verses.
new: The Vulgate calls the sanctuary "tabernaculum foederis" (tabernacle of the covenant) here and "tabernaculum testimonii" (tabernacle of the testimony) in 2:17, where the Hebrew has "tent of meeting" in both verses.
reason: Note house style: "tabernacle of the testimony" for tabernaculum testimonii.

old: Then the tabernacle of testimony will be lifted up through the services of the Levites and their companies; just as it will be erected, so also it will be taken down. Each will set out by their places and ranks.
new: Then the tabernacle of the testimony will be lifted up through the services of the Levites and their companies; just as it will be erected, so also it will be taken down. Each will set out by their places and ranks.
reason: tabernaculum testimonii is rendered "tabernacle of the testimony" in this edition (as at 1:50, 1:53).

old: Distinctively, the Vulgate describes the tabernacle of testimony being lifted up through the services of the Levites and taken down just as it will be erected, whereas the Hebrew describes the tent of meeting setting out with the camp of the Levites in the midst of the camps, setting out just as they camp.
new: Distinctively, the Vulgate describes the tabernacle of the testimony being lifted up through the services of the Levites and taken down just as it will be erected, whereas the Hebrew describes the tent of meeting setting out with the camp of the Levites in the midst of the camps, setting out just as they camp.
reason: Note house style: "tabernacle of the testimony" for tabernaculum testimonii.

old: In the tribe of the sons of Benjamin, the leader was Abidan son of Gideoni.
new: In the tribe of the sons of Benjamin, the leader was Abidan son of Gideon.
reason: Gedeonis is the genitive of Gedeon ("Gideon"), as the note says; "Gideoni" follows the Hebrew name, not the Latin.

old: and observe whatever pertains to the service of the multitude before the tabernacle of testimony,
new: and observe whatever pertains to the service of the multitude before the tabernacle of the testimony,
reason: tabernaculum testimonii is rendered "tabernacle of the testimony" in this edition (as at 1:50, 1:53).

old: The Vulgate renders Hebrew ohel mo'ed ("tent of meeting") here and in 3:38 as tabernaculum foederis ("tabernacle of the covenant")—and in 3:26 as tectum foederis ("shelter of the covenant")—whereas in 3:7 it renders the same Hebrew phrase as tabernaculum testimonii ("tabernacle of testimony").
new: The Vulgate renders Hebrew ohel mo'ed ("tent of meeting") here and in 3:38 as tabernaculum foederis ("tabernacle of the covenant")—and in 3:26 as tectum foederis ("shelter of the covenant")—whereas in 3:7 it renders the same Hebrew phrase as tabernaculum testimonii ("tabernacle of the testimony").
reason: Note house style: "tabernacle of the testimony" for tabernaculum testimonii.

old: Then on the eighth day he shall offer two turtledoves or two young doves to the priest at the entrance of the covenant of testimony.
new: Then on the eighth day he shall offer two turtledoves or two young doves to the priest at the entrance of the covenant of the testimony.
reason: fœderis testimonii is rendered "the covenant of the testimony" at 4:30, matching the edition's "tabernacle of the testimony" for testimonii.

old: The Vulgate uniquely reads in introitu foederis testimonii ("at the entrance of the covenant of testimony") where the Hebrew text has "at the entrance of the tent of meeting."
new: The Vulgate uniquely reads in introitu foederis testimonii ("at the entrance of the covenant of the testimony") where the Hebrew text has "at the entrance of the tent of meeting."
reason: Note gloss updated to match the corrected verse wording.

old: On the ninth day the chief of the sons of Benjamin, Abidan son of Gideoni,
new: On the ninth day the chief of the sons of Benjamin, Abidan son of Gideon,
reason: Gedeonis is the genitive of Gedeon ("Gideon"), as the verse's own note says; "Gideoni" follows the Hebrew name, not the Latin.

old: and for sacrifices of peace offerings two oxen, five rams, five male goats, five one-year-old lambs. This was the offering of Abidan son of Gideoni.
new: and for sacrifices of peace offerings two oxen, five rams, five male goats, five one-year-old lambs. This was the offering of Abidan son of Gideon.
reason: filii Gedeonis = "son of Gedeon (Gideon)"; "Gideoni" follows the Hebrew name, not the Latin (see note at 7:60).

old: And in the tribe of Benjamin, the commander was Abidan the son of Gideoni.
new: And in the tribe of Benjamin, the commander was Abidan the son of Gideon.
reason: filius Gedeonis = "son of Gedeon (Gideon)"; "Gideoni" follows the Hebrew name, not the Latin (cf. notes at 1:11, 2:22, 7:60).

old: Latin faciam principem super gentem magnam specifies making Moses a ruler over a greater nation, whereas the Hebrew reads making him into a greater and mightier nation.
new: Latin faciam principem super gentem magnam specifies making Moses a ruler over a great nation, whereas the Hebrew reads making him into a greater and mightier nation.
reason: The Latin has the positive gentem magnam ("a great nation"), not a comparative; the note misdescribes the Latin.

old: My servant Caleb, who is full of another spirit and has followed Me, I will lead into this land that he traversed; and his offspring will possess it.
new: My servant Caleb, who is full of another spirit and has followed Me, I will lead into this land that he traversed; and his seed will possess it.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: But they, darkened, went up to the summit of the mountain. Yet the ark of the testament of the Lord and Moses did not depart from the camp.
new: But they, darkened, went up to the summit of the mountain. Yet the ark of the covenant of the Lord and Moses did not depart from the camp.
reason: arca testamenti is rendered "ark of the covenant" in this edition; "testament" is kept only where a will is meant.

old: But when you make a burnt offering or a sacrifice from the oxen, to fulfill a vow or peace sacrifices,
new: But when you make a burnt offering or a sacrifice from the oxen, to fulfill a vow or peace offerings,
reason: pacificas victimas is the standard peace-offering term, rendered "peace offerings" in this edition.

old: Unlike the Hebrew negative ("you have not brought us"), the Vulgate renders Dathan and Abiram's words as biting sarcasm with Revera induxisti nos ("Indeed, you have brought us") and reads "our eyes" (oculos nostros) rather than "the eyes of these men."
new: Unlike the Hebrew negative ("you have not brought us"), the Vulgate has the affirmative Revera induxisti nos ("Indeed, you have brought us") and reads "our eyes" (oculos nostros) rather than "the eyes of these men."
reason: "biting sarcasm" is interpretive comment on tone; the note should state only what the Latin reads.

old: Latin in infernum ("into the underworld," also traditionally rendered "hell") is the Vulgate's standard term for the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol), and blasphemaverint ("have blasphemed") renders Hebrew "have despised/spurned."
new: Latin in infernum ("into the underworld") is the Vulgate's standard term for the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol), and blasphemaverint ("have blasphemed") renders Hebrew "have despised/spurned."
reason: Remove the remark about how translations traditionally render the word; the note should explain the Latin only.

old: In Clementine Vulgate versification, Numbers 16 ends at 16:35; the subsequent account of the bronze censers (16:36-50 in most English Bibles) begins Numbers 17.
new: In this versification, as in the Hebrew, Numbers 16 ends at 16:35, and the subsequent account of the bronze censers begins Numbers 17.
reason: Remove the claim about "most English Bibles"; the Hebrew also ends chapter 16 at verse 35, so the break is not distinctive to the Vulgate.

old: In the Clementine Vulgate, Numbers 17:1-15 corresponds to 16:36-50 in the Hebrew numbering, while 17:16-28 corresponds to 17:1-13; verse number 17:8 is omitted because its substance is merged into 17:7.
new: As in the Hebrew numbering, Numbers 17 here contains the censers and the plague (17:1-15) and Aaron's rod (17:16-28); verse number 17:8 is not used because its substance is merged into 17:7.
reason: False claim: the Hebrew also numbers these sections 17:1-15 and 17:16-28; 16:36-50 and 17:1-13 belong to a different versification, not the Hebrew.

old: so that afterward the sons of Israel might have things by which to be reminded that no outsider, and no one who is not of the offspring of Aaron, may approach to offer incense to the Lord, so that he may not suffer as Korah and all his assembly suffered, as the Lord spoke to Moses.
new: so that afterward the sons of Israel might have things by which to be reminded that no outsider, and no one who is not of the offspring of Aaron, may approach to offer incense to the Lord, so that he may not suffer as Korah and all his congregation suffered, as the Lord spoke to Moses.
reason: congregatio ejus is Korah's band, rendered "congregation" in 16:16 and 16:21; "assembly" is reserved for ecclesia.

old: so that afterward the sons of Israel might have things by which to be reminded that no outsider, and no one who is not of the offspring of Aaron, may approach to offer incense to the Lord, so that he may not suffer as Korah and all his congregation suffered, as the Lord spoke to Moses.
new: so that afterward the sons of Israel might have things by which to be reminded that no outsider, and no one who is not of the seed of Aaron, may approach to offer incense to the Lord, so that he may not suffer as Korah and all his congregation suffered, as the Lord spoke to Moses.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Throughout Chapter 18 (18:8, 11, 12, 19, 26, 28, 30), the Vulgate translates the Hebrew term for "contribution" or "heave offering" ("terumah") as "primitiae" ("firstfruits").
new: Throughout Chapter 18 (18:8, 11, 19, 26, 28, 30), the Vulgate translates the Hebrew term for "contribution" or "heave offering" ("terumah") as "primitiae" ("firstfruits").
reason: In 18:12 primitiarum renders Hebrew reshit ("firstfruits"), not terumah, so the verse does not belong in this list.

old: However, the firstborn of an ox, and of a sheep, and of a goat, you shall not have redeemed, because they have been sanctified to the Lord. Their blood alone you shall pour out upon the altar, and their fat you shall burn as a most pleasing aroma to the Lord.
new: However, the firstborn of an ox, and of a sheep, and of a goat, you shall not have redeemed, because they have been sanctified to the Lord. Their blood alone you shall pour out upon the altar, and their fat you shall burn as a most sweet fragrance to the Lord.
reason: in suavissimum odorem is rendered "a most sweet fragrance" in 15:24 (and odor suavitatis "fragrance of sweetness"); keep the sacrificial formula consistent.

old: The Vulgate reads immundus erit usque ad vesperum ("he will be unclean until evening"), matching verses 7, 8, 10, 21, and 22, whereas the Hebrew and Septuagint state that he will be "clean at evening."
new: The Vulgate reads immundus erit usque ad vesperum ("he will be unclean until evening"), as in verses 8, 10, 21, and 22, whereas the Hebrew states that he will be "clean at evening."
reason: Verse 7 reads commaculatus, not immundus; and the Septuagint here also reads "unclean until evening," so only the Hebrew differs.

old: Vulgate Tolletur propter Agag, rex ejus, et auferetur regnum illius ("His king will be removed because of Agag, and his kingdom will be taken away") diverges sharply from the Hebrew ("his king will be higher than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted"), reflecting an interpretation alluding to Saul losing the kingship after sparing Agag (1 Samuel 15).
