new: Vulgate Tolletur propter Agag, rex ejus, et auferetur regnum illius ("His king will be removed because of Agag, and his kingdom will be taken away") differs from the Hebrew ("his king will be higher than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted").
reason: The allusion to Saul is interpretive speculation not stated by the Latin; keep the note to the textual difference.

old: Vulgate quid populus tuus populo huic faciat ("what your people will do to this people") reverses the subject and object of the Hebrew ("what this people will do to your people"), linking Balaam's counsel to Moab's entrapment of Israel in chapter 25.
new: Vulgate quid populus tuus populo huic faciat ("what your people will do to this people") reverses the subject and object of the Hebrew ("what this people will do to your people").
reason: The link to chapter 25 is interpretive comment, not something the Latin of this verse states.

old: The Vulgate uniquely renders Hebrew Kittim as Italia ("Italy"), specifies in trieribus ("in triremes"), and translates Hebrew Eber as Hebraeos ("the Hebrews").
new: The Vulgate renders Hebrew Kittim as Italia ("Italy"), specifies in trieribus ("in triremes"), and translates Hebrew Eber as Hebraeos ("the Hebrews").
reason: "uniquely" is inaccurate for Hebraeos, which the Septuagint shares (Hebraious); the note should not overstate.

old: and there will be both for him and for his offspring an everlasting pact of the priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and atoned for the crime of the sons of Israel.'"
new: and there will be both for him and for his offspring an everlasting covenant of the priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and atoned for the crime of the sons of Israel.'"
reason: pactum is rendered "covenant" in this edition (cf. pactum salis, "covenant of salt," 18:19).

old: and there will be both for him and for his offspring an everlasting covenant of the priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and atoned for the crime of the sons of Israel.'"
new: and there will be both for him and for his seed an everlasting covenant of the priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and atoned for the crime of the sons of Israel.'"
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And the Lord said to him, "Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom the Spirit is, and place your hand on him.
new: And the Lord said to him, "Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom the spirit is, and place your hand on him.
reason: Latin has bare spiritus with no Dei or Sanctus; capital "Spirit" silently decides a disputed referent, so lowercase keeps the Latin's openness.

old: In the Clementine Vulgate, chapter 30 begins with this verse (corresponding to Numbers 29:40 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text), so Vulgate 30:2-17 correspond to Hebrew 30:1-16.
new: As in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, chapter 30 begins with this verse; in the alternative versification it is numbered 29:40, and verses 30:2-17 here are numbered 30:1-16.
reason: The Hebrew text also numbers this verse 30:1 (and its chapter 30 has 17 verses like the Vulgate); 29:40 is the alternative English versification, so the note's claim about the Masoretic numbering is false.

old: The Vulgate adds atque vicissent ("and were victorious") and omits the Hebrew clause "as the LORD commanded Moses."
new: The Vulgate adds atque vicissent ("and were victorious") and omits the Hebrew clause "as the Lord commanded Moses."
reason: Edition style forbids capital LORD in notes; use "the Lord".

old: The Vulgate translates the final two golden ornaments as dextralia ("bracelets" for the right arm or wrist) and muraenulas ("chain necklaces"), and renders the closing purpose clause as a request for Moses's intercession (ut depreceris pro nobis Dominum, "so that you may pray to the Lord for us") rather than Hebrew "to make atonement for our souls before the LORD."
new: The Vulgate translates the final two golden ornaments as dextralia ("bracelets" for the right arm or wrist) and muraenulas ("chain necklaces"), and renders the closing purpose clause as a request for Moses's intercession (ut depreceris pro nobis Dominum, "so that you may pray to the Lord for us") rather than Hebrew "to make atonement for our souls before the Lord."
reason: Edition style forbids capital LORD in notes; use "the Lord".

old: The Vulgate reading contra fontem Daphnim ("opposite the spring Daphnis") identifies Hebrew Ain ("spring") with the celebrated spring of Daphne near Riblah.
new: The Vulgate reads contra fontem Daphnim ("opposite the spring Daphnis"), naming the spring where the Hebrew has only Ain ("spring").
reason: The famous spring of Daphne lies near Antioch, not near Riblah; the note should state only what the Latin reads against the Hebrew.

old: Look,' He said, 'I have delivered it to you: go in and possess it, concerning which the Lord swore to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, that He would give it to them and to their offspring after them.'
new: Look,' He said, 'I have delivered it to you: go in and possess it, concerning which the Lord swore to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, that He would give it to them and to their seed after them.'
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: so that, lifting your eyes to heaven, you might not see the sun and the moon and all the stars of heaven, and, deceived by error, worship them and serve what the Lord your God created for the service of all the peoples who are under heaven.
new: so that, lifting your eyes to heaven, you might not see the sun and the moon and all the stars of heaven, and, deceived by error, worship them and serve what the Lord your God created for the service of all the nations that are under heaven.
reason: cunctis gentibus is "all the nations" (the edition's rendering of gentes, as at 7:1, 7:7, 14:2); "peoples" is used for populi.

old: The Vulgate distinctively reads tota tribulatione animæ tuæ ("with all the affliction of your soul"), emphasizing penitential distress where the Hebrew has simply "with all your soul."
new: The Vulgate reads tota tribulatione animæ tuæ ("with all the affliction of your soul") where the Hebrew has simply "with all your soul."
reason: "emphasizing penitential distress" is interpretive comment; the note should only state the Latin reading.

old: from Aroer, which is situated on the bank of the torrent Arnon, as far as Mount Sion, which is also Hermon,
new: from Aroer, which is situated on the bank of the stream of Arnon, as far as Mount Sion, which is also Hermon,
reason: torrentis Arnon is rendered "the stream of Arnon" everywhere else in this edition (2:24, 2:36, 3:8, 3:12, 3:16).

old: Latin 'caeremonias' ("ceremonies," used consistently throughout chs. 5-6) is the Vulgate's characteristic rendering of the Hebrew term usually translated "statutes."
new: Latin 'caeremonias' ("ceremonies," used consistently throughout chs. 5-6) is the Vulgate's characteristic rendering of the Hebrew term chuqqim ("statutes").
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: Not with our fathers did He enter into the pact, but with us who are here at the present time and live.
new: Not with our fathers did He enter into the covenant, but with us who are here at the present time and live.
reason: pactum is rendered "covenant" in this edition (cf. fœdus in 5:2, pactum in 4:13, 4:23, 4:31).

old: Latin 'eruntque et movebuntur' ("and they shall be and move") follows the Septuagint rendering of the rare Hebrew term usually translated "frontlets"; likewise, v. 9 reads 'in limine, et ostiis' ("on the threshold and the doors") rather than Hebrew "doorposts" and "gates."
new: Latin 'eruntque et movebuntur' ("and they shall be and move") stands where the Hebrew has a rare noun for bands or frontlets; likewise, v. 9 reads 'in limine, et ostiis' ("on the threshold and the doors") rather than Hebrew "doorposts" and "gates."
reason: The Septuagint here reads "they shall be immovable" (asaleuta), the opposite of movebuntur, so "follows the Septuagint" is inaccurate; "usually translated" is a claim about translations.

old: and the Lord your God hands them over to you, you shall strike them down to utter destruction. You shall not enter into a treaty with them, nor show mercy to them,
new: and the Lord your God hands them over to you, you shall strike them down to utter destruction. You shall not enter into a covenant with them, nor show mercy to them,
reason: fœdus is rendered "covenant" in this edition (as in 5:2); "treaty" departs from the established rendering.

old: but because the Lord loved you and kept the oath that He swore to your fathers; and He brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh, king of Egypt.
new: but because the Lord loved you and kept the oath that He swore to your fathers; and He brought you out with a strong hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh, king of Egypt.
reason: in manu forti is "with a strong hand" elsewhere in this edition (5:15, 6:21, 9:26).

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads Domini tui ("your Lord") without Dei ("God"), and reads de quibus facta sunt ("from which they are made") rather than the Hebrew "which is on them."
new: This Latin text reads Domini tui ("your Lord") without Dei ("God"), and reads de quibus facta sunt ("from which they are made") rather than the Hebrew "which is on them."
reason: The reading Domini tui belongs to the critical text in the input; common Clementine printings read Domini Dei tui, so the note should not attribute it to "the Clementine Vulgate".

old: Listen, Israel: you will cross the Jordan today to possess very great nations, stronger than you, huge cities, walled all the way to heaven,
new: Hear, Israel: you will cross the Jordan today to possess very great nations, stronger than you, huge cities, walled all the way to heaven,
reason: Audi, Israël is rendered "Hear, Israel" at 5:1, 6:3 and 6:4.

old: Yet they are Your people and Your inheritance, whom You brought out in Your great strength and with Your outstretched arm."
new: They are Your people and Your inheritance, whom You brought out in Your great strength and with Your outstretched arm."
reason: qui sunt populus tuus is a plain relative clause ("who are Your people"); the adversative "Yet" has no Latin basis.

old: and yet the Lord was closely joined to your fathers, and loved them, and chose their offspring after them, that is, you, from all the nations, just as is confirmed today.
new: and yet the Lord was closely joined to your fathers, and loved them, and chose their seed after them, that is, you, from all the nations, just as is confirmed today.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: The Vulgate includes "alone" (ei soli, "Him alone"), agreeing with the Septuagint and Christ's quotation in Matthew 4:10 and Luke 4:8, where the Masoretic Hebrew has simply "Him."
new: The Vulgate includes "alone" (ei soli, "Him alone"), agreeing with the Septuagint and the quotation in Matthew 4:10 and Luke 4:8, where the Masoretic Hebrew has simply "Him."
reason: Keep the comparison neutral: "Christ's quotation" is confessional framing; the factual reference is the quotation in Matthew 4:10 and Luke 4:8.

old: and may live for a long time in it, the land that the Lord promised under oath to your fathers and to their offspring, flowing with milk and honey.
new: and may live for a long time in it, the land that the Lord promised under oath to your fathers and to their seed, flowing with milk and honey.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: In the Vulgate, chapter 13 begins with this verse (numbered 12:32 in Hebrew and most modern English Bibles), shifting the rest of the chapter's numbering by one. Latin "do this alone for the Lord" (hoc tantum facito Domino) adds "for the Lord" and "alone" where the Hebrew reads "observe to do all the word."
new: As in the Hebrew, chapter 13 begins with this verse (numbered 12:32 in some other versifications), so the rest of the chapter is numbered one higher. Latin "do this alone for the Lord" (hoc tantum facito Domino) adds "for the Lord" and "alone" where the Hebrew reads "observe to do all the word."
reason: The Hebrew Masoretic Text also numbers this verse 13:1, so "numbered 12:32 in Hebrew" is false; the claim about "most modern English Bibles" is a claim about translations.

old: But if it is unwilling to enter into a treaty and begins war against you, you shall attack it.
new: But if it is unwilling to enter into a covenant and begins war against you, you shall attack it.
reason: fœdus inire: fœdus is rendered "covenant" edition-wide.

old: In the Vulgate chapter 23 begins here (corresponding to 22:30 in Hebrew and most English Bibles), so the verses of chapter 23 are numbered one higher than in the Hebrew text.
new: In the Latin, as in the Hebrew text, chapter 23 begins with this verse.
reason: The Hebrew text also begins chapter 23 here, so the claim that the Latin numbering is one higher than the Hebrew is false, and the brief excludes claims about English Bibles.

old: Latin Syrus persequebatur patrem meum ("A Syrian was persecuting my father") reflects an ancient interpretive tradition referring to Laban pursuing Jacob, whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered "A wandering (or perishing) Aramean was my father."
new: Latin Syrus persequebatur patrem meum ("A Syrian was persecuting my father") reflects an ancient interpretive tradition referring to Laban pursuing Jacob, whereas the Hebrew reads "A wandering (or perishing) Aramean was my father."
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate gives an explicit anatomical periphrasis, partem corporis, per quam stercora egeruntur ('the part of the body through which excrement is discharged'), for the Hebrew term usually translated 'tumors' or 'hemorrhoids'.
new: The Vulgate gives an explicit anatomical periphrasis, partem corporis, per quam stercora egeruntur ('the part of the body through which excrement is discharged'), for the Hebrew term meaning 'tumors' or 'hemorrhoids.'
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: And they will be signs and wonders upon you, and upon your offspring forever,
new: And they will be signs and wonders upon you, and upon your seed forever,
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: the Lord will increase your plagues and the plagues of your offspring, great and persistent plagues, most severe and perpetual sicknesses,
new: the Lord will increase your plagues and the plagues of your seed, great and persistent plagues, most severe and perpetual sicknesses,
reason: Latin seminis (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Following the Hebrew versification, the Vulgate concludes chapter 28 with this summary verse (28:69), which most English Bibles number as Deuteronomy 29:1.
new: As in the Hebrew text, this summary verse concludes chapter 28 in the Latin (28:69).
reason: The note's claim about how most English Bibles number the verse is the kind of statement the brief excludes; the factual point about the Latin following the Hebrew numbering is kept.

old: The Vulgate compresses the longer Hebrew wording ('both with him who stands here with us today before the LORD our God and with him who is not here with us today') into the concise phrase sed cunctis praesentibus et absentibus ('but with all who are present and absent').
new: The Vulgate compresses the longer Hebrew wording ('both with him who stands here with us today before the Lord our God and with him who is not here with us today') into the concise phrase sed cunctis praesentibus et absentibus ('but with all who are present and absent').
reason: Capital LORD is not used in this edition, in verses or notes.

old: The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your descendants, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may be able to live.
new: The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may be able to live.
reason: Latin seminis (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: I call heaven and earth as witnesses today that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose life, therefore, so that both you and your descendants may live,
new: I call heaven and earth as witnesses today that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose life, therefore, so that both you and your seed may live,
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And he commanded them, saying, "After seven years, in the year of remission, at the festival of tabernacles,
new: And he commanded them, saying, "After seven years, in the year of remission, at the solemn feast of Tabernacles,
reason: in solemnitate tabernaculorum is rendered "the solemn feast of Tabernacles" elsewhere in this book (16:13, 16:16).

old: And the Lord said to Moses, "Look, the days of your death are near; call Joshua, and stand in the tabernacle of testimony, so that I may command him." So Moses and Joshua went and stood in the tabernacle of testimony.
new: And the Lord said to Moses, "Look, the days of your death are near; call Joshua, and stand in the tabernacle of the testimony, so that I may command him." So Moses and Joshua went and stood in the tabernacle of the testimony.
reason: tabernaculum testimonii has the established rendering "tabernacle of the testimony" (both occurrences in the verse).

old: For I will bring them into the land for which I swore to their fathers, flowing with milk and honey. And when they have eaten and been satisfied and grown fat, they will turn aside to foreign gods and serve them, and they will revile Me and nullify My pact.
new: For I will bring them into the land for which I swore to their fathers, flowing with milk and honey. And when they have eaten and been satisfied and grown fat, they will turn aside to foreign gods and serve them, and they will revile Me and nullify My covenant.
reason: pactum is rendered "covenant" in this edition (compare irritum faciet fœdus, "nullify the covenant," in v. 16).

old: After many evils and afflictions have found them, this song, which no forgetfulness will erase from the mouth of their offspring, will answer them as a witness. For I know their thoughts, what they are about to do today, before I bring them into the land that I have promised them."
new: After many evils and afflictions have found them, this song, which no forgetfulness will erase from the mouth of their seed, will answer them as a witness. For I know their thoughts, what they are about to do today, before I bring them into the land that I have promised them."
reason: Latin seminis (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: A fire has been kindled in My fury, and it will burn all the way to the lowest depths of the netherworld; and it will devour the earth with its growth, and burn up the foundations of the mountains.
new: A fire has been kindled in My fury, and it will burn all the way to the lowest depths of the underworld; and it will devour the earth with its growth, and burn up the foundations of the mountains.
reason: infernus has the established rendering "the underworld".

old: From the vine of Sodom is their vine, and from the outskirts of Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their clusters are most bitter.
new: From the vineyard of Sodom is their vineyard, and from the outskirts of Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their clusters are most bitter.
reason: The Latin has vinea ("vineyard") twice, as everywhere else in Deuteronomy; "vine" follows the Hebrew gefen rather than the Latin.

old: This is the blessing of Judah: "Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him in to his people; his hands will fight for him, and He will be his helper against his adversaries."
new: This is the blessing of Judah: "Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him in to his people; his hands will fight for him, and his helper will be against his adversaries."
reason: et adjutor illius contra adversarios ejus erit has adjutor as the subject of a third-person erit, parallel to manus ejus pugnabunt; supplying a capitalized "He" adds a subject the Latin lacks and settles the referent.

old: Of Levi he also said: "Your perfection and Your teaching belong to Your holy man, whom You proved in testing and judged at the waters of contradiction.
new: Of Levi he also said: "Your perfection and Your teaching belong to Your holy man, whom You proved in testing and judged at the waters of Contradiction.
reason: ad aquas contradictionis is rendered "the waters of Contradiction" in 32:51 (and in the note at 32:49); same name, same capitalization.

old: And he saw his preeminence, that in his portion the teacher was laid up, who was with the leaders of the people, and carried out the righteous deeds of the Lord and His judgment with Israel."
new: And he saw his preeminence, that in his portion the teacher was laid up, who was with the leaders of the people, and carried out the righteous deeds of the Lord and his judgment with Israel."
reason: judicium suum is reflexive, so it refers to the subject of fecit (the one in Gad's portion), not to the Lord; the capital follows the Hebrew mishpatav instead of the Latin.

old: And the Lord said to him: "This is the land about which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your offspring I will give it.' You have seen it with your eyes, and you will not cross over to it."
new: And the Lord said to him: "This is the land about which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your seed I will give it.' You have seen it with your eyes, and you will not cross over to it."
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin nec dentes illius moti sunt ("nor were his teeth loosened") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew clause usually translated "nor had his vigor fled."
new: Latin nec dentes illius moti sunt ("nor were his teeth loosened") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew clause "nor had his vigor fled."
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate renders this clause 'ut intelligas cuncta quæ agis' ('so that you may understand all that you do'), and similarly in 1:8 'diriges viam tuam, et intelliges eam' ('you will direct your way, and you will understand it'), emphasizing practical understanding where the Hebrew is commonly rendered 'succeed' or 'prosper.'
new: The Vulgate renders this clause 'ut intelligas cuncta quæ agis' ('so that you may understand all that you do'), and similarly in 1:8 'diriges viam tuam, et intelliges eam' ('you will direct your way, and you will understand it'), where the Hebrew verb means 'act wisely' or 'prosper.'
reason: Removes the claim about how the Hebrew is 'commonly rendered' (a statement about translations) and the interpretive 'emphasizing' remark; keeps a neutral lexical comparison.

old: Latin juxta numerum filiorum Israël ("according to the number of the sons of Israel") omits "tribes," referring directly to the twelve patriarchs; the same Vulgate reading recurs in 4:8.
new: Latin juxta numerum filiorum Israël ("according to the number of the sons of Israel") lacks the Hebrew's "tribes"; the same Vulgate reading recurs in 4:8.
reason: "referring directly to the twelve patriarchs" is an interpretation the Latin does not state (filii Israël may equally mean the people); the note should stay factual.

old: were uncircumcised during the forty years of the journey through the vast wilderness, until those were consumed who had not listened to the voice of the Lord, and to whom He had previously sworn that He would not show them a land flowing with milk and honey.
new: were uncircumcised during the forty years of the journey through the very vast wilderness, until those were consumed who had not listened to the voice of the Lord, and to whom He had previously sworn that He would not show them a land flowing with milk and honey.
reason: latissimæ is superlative ("very vast"); plain "vast" drops the degree, unlike the parallel longissimos ("very long") in 5:4.

old: "So long a day" preserves Vulgate "tam longa dies" (Hebrew: "a day like it"). Verse 10:15 of the Hebrew text (reporting Joshua's return to Gilgal) is absent from the Clementine Vulgate, which proceeds directly to 10:16.
new: "So long a day" preserves Vulgate "tam longa dies" (Hebrew: "a day like it").
reason: False claim: the critical text has 10:15 (Reversusque est Josue cum omni Israël in castra Galgalæ), carried in this edition as an additional verse after 10:14.

old: he said to them again, "Do not fear, nor be terrified; be strengthened and be strong, for thus the Lord will do to all your enemies against whom you fight."
new: he said to them again, "Do not fear, nor be terrified; be strengthened and be resolute, for thus the Lord will do to all your enemies against whom you fight."
reason: robusti is rendered "resolute" in this book (esto robustus, 1:6, 1:7, 1:9) and in Deut 31:7, 31:23 ("Be strengthened and be resolute"); "strong" here blurs confortamini/robusti.

old: And when the sun was setting, he commanded his companions to take them down from the gallows. Having taken them down, they threw them into the cave in which they had hidden, and placed huge stones over its mouth, which remain until the present.
new: And when the sun was setting, he commanded his companions to take them down from the gibbets. Having taken them down, they threw them into the cave in which they had hidden, and placed huge stones over its mouth, which remain until the present.
reason: patibulum is "gibbet" in 8:29 (and Deut 21:22); same Latin term, same English.

old: Therefore Joshua struck all the hill country and the south and the plains, and Asedoth, with their kings; he did not leave in it any remnant, but he killed everything that could breathe, just as the Lord God of Israel had commanded him,
new: Therefore Joshua struck all the hill country and the south and the plains, and Ashdoth, with their kings; he did not leave in it any remnant, but he killed everything that could breathe, just as the Lord God of Israel had commanded him,
reason: The same Latin name Asedoth is "Ashdoth" in 12:3, 12:8 and 13:20; harmonize the spelling.

old: "Asedoth" preserves the Vulgate treatment of the Hebrew geographic common noun "ashedot" ("the slopes" or "foothills") as a proper place name.
new: "Ashdoth" (Latin Asedoth) preserves the Vulgate treatment of the Hebrew geographic common noun "ashedot" ("the slopes" or "foothills") as a proper place name.
reason: Keeps the note in step with the harmonized spelling Ashdoth.

old: "Fought for him" reflects Vulgate "pugnavit pro eo" (Hebrew: "fought for Israel"). Verse 10:43 of the Hebrew text (the return to Gilgal) is absent from the Clementine Vulgate.
new: "Fought for him" reflects Vulgate "pugnavit pro eo" (Hebrew: "fought for Israel").
reason: False claim: the critical text has 10:43 (Reversusque est cum omni Israël ad locum castrorum in Galgala), carried in this edition as an additional verse after 10:42.

old: Latin "vulnerandos" ("to be wounded") renders Hebrew "chalalim" ("pierced/killed"), whereas the Septuagint reads "put to flight" and most modern versions translate "killed" or "defeated."
new: Latin "vulnerandos" ("to be wounded") renders Hebrew "chalalim" ("pierced/killed"), where the Septuagint reads "put to flight."
reason: Removes the claim about what "most modern versions" do; keeps the neutral Hebrew/Greek comparison.

old: These are the kings whom the sons of Israel struck down, and whose land they possessed beyond the Jordan toward the rising of the sun, from the torrent of Arnon as far as Mount Hermon, and all the eastern region that faces the wilderness.
new: These are the kings whom the sons of Israel struck down, and whose land they possessed beyond the Jordan toward the rising of the sun, from the stream of Arnon as far as Mount Hermon, and all the eastern region that faces the wilderness.
reason: torrens (Arnon, Jabbok, Egypt) is "stream" elsewhere in Joshua (13:9, 13:16, 15:4, 15:7, 15:47, 17:9) and Deuteronomy; 12:1-2 are the only "torrent" outliers.

old: Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, ruled from Aroer, which is situated on the bank of the torrent of Arnon, and over the middle part in the valley, and over half of Gilead, as far as the torrent of Jabbok, which is the border of the sons of Ammon;
new: Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, ruled from Aroer, which is situated on the bank of the stream of Arnon, and over the middle part in the valley, and over half of Gilead, as far as the stream of Jabbok, which is the border of the sons of Ammon;
reason: torrentis Arnon / torrentem Jaboc: same Latin as 13:9, 13:16 ("stream of Arnon") and Deut 2:37, 3:16 ("stream of Jabbok").

old: and from the wilderness as far as the Sea of Chinneroth toward the east, and as far as the sea of the desert, which is the very salty sea, toward the eastern region by the road that leads to Beth-jeshimoth, and on the southern side, which lies beneath Ashdoth-pisgah.
new: and from the wilderness as far as the Sea of Chinneroth toward the east, and as far as the sea of the desert, which is the Saltiest Sea, toward the eastern region by the road that leads to Beth-jeshimoth, and on the southern side, which lies beneath Ashdoth, Pisgah.
reason: Latin "Asedoth, Phasga" gives two names (as rendered in 13:20 "Ashdoth, Pisgah"); the compound "Ashdoth-pisgah" follows the Hebrew. mare salsissimum is "the Saltiest Sea" in 15:2, 15:5, 16:8, 18:19.

old: Latin "mare salsissimum" ("the very salty sea") uses a superlative for Hebrew "yam hammelach" ("the Salt Sea"). Both here ("Asedoth, Phasga") and in 12:8 ("In Asedoth"), the Vulgate retains Hebrew "ashedoth" ("slopes") as a proper name, Ashdoth.
new: Latin "mare salsissimum" ("the Saltiest Sea") uses a superlative for Hebrew "yam hammelach" ("the Salt Sea"). Both here ("Asedoth, Phasga") and in 12:8 ("In Asedoth"), the Vulgate retains Hebrew "ashedoth" ("slopes") as a proper name, Ashdoth.
reason: Keeps the note in step with the harmonized rendering "the Saltiest Sea."

old: And the border of Manasseh was from Asher to Michmethath, which faces Shechem; and it goes out to the right beside the inhabitants of the spring of Tappuah.
new: And the border of Manasseh was from Asher, Michmethath, which faces Shechem; and it goes out to the right beside the inhabitants of the spring of Tappuah.
reason: Latin ab Aser, Machmethath has no "to"; the names stand in apposition (as kept at 16:2 "from Bethel, Luz"); "to" follows the Hebrew.

old: And it goes down to the part of the mountain that faces the valley of the sons of Hinnom, and it is toward the northern side at the farthest part of the valley of Rephaim. And it goes down to Ge-hinnom (that is, the valley of Hinnom) along the flank of the Jebusite to the south, and reaches the spring of Rogel,
new: And it goes down to the part of the mountain that faces the valley of the sons of Hinnom, and it is toward the northern side at the farthest part of the valley of Rephaim. And it goes down to Gehennom (that is, the valley of Hinnom) along the flank of the Jebusite to the south, and reaches the spring of Rogel,
reason: Same Latin Geennom is "Gehennom" in 15:8 (and its note); harmonize the form.

old: so that whoever has struck a person unknowingly may flee to them, and may be able to escape the wrath of the kinsman who is the avenger of blood.'"
new: so that whoever has struck a person unknowingly may flee to them, and may be able to escape the wrath of the kinsman who is the avenger of blood.
reason: The Latin of v. 3 ends with a colon and the Lord's speech continues in the critical text's additional vv. 4-6 (shown after 20:3: stabit, non tradent, habitabit...); the closing marks belong at the end of 20:6 (paired change at Joshua 20:6), keeping quotes balanced.

old: And he will live in that city until he stands before the court, rendering an account of his deed, and until the high priest who is in office at that time dies; then the killer will return and enter his city and his house, from which he had fled.
new: And he will live in that city until he stands before the court, rendering an account of his deed, and until the high priest who is in office at that time dies; then the killer will return and enter his city and his house, from which he had fled.'"
reason: Vv. 4-6 (shown after 20:3) are still the Lord's words opened in 20:1-2; the closing single and double quotes move here from 20:3 (paired change at Joshua 20:3).

old: so that after you have gone in to the peoples who will be among you, you do not swear by the name of their gods, nor serve them, nor worship them,
new: so that after you have gone in to the nations who will be among you, you do not swear by the name of their gods, nor serve them, nor worship them,
reason: Latin gentes is rendered "nations" in this edition (Joshua 24:18; Judges 2:21; 3:1), while "peoples" is used for populi (Joshua 24:17; Judges 2:12).

old: And then the Lord God will remove in your sight great and very strong peoples, and no one will be able to resist you.
new: And then the Lord God will remove in your sight great and very strong nations, and no one will be able to resist you.
reason: gentes magnas et robustissimas: gentes = "nations" per the edition's rendering; "peoples" is reserved for populi.

old: But if you choose to cling to the errors of these peoples who dwell among you, and to join in marriage with them, and to form friendships,
new: But if you choose to cling to the errors of these nations who dwell among you, and to join in marriage with them, and to form friendships,
reason: gentium harum = "of these nations" (gentes = "nations" in this edition).

old: So I took your father Abraham from the borders of Mesopotamia, and brought him into the land of Canaan, and multiplied his offspring,
new: So I took your father Abraham from the borders of Mesopotamia, and brought him into the land of Canaan, and multiplied his seed,
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin suspirasset sedens in asino ("sighed while sitting on the donkey") reflects Jerome's understanding of the rare Hebrew verb tsanach, usually rendered as alighting from the donkey; similarly, in 1:11, 1:17, and 1:35 the Vulgate adds etymological glosses (civitas litterarum, anathema, and testaceo, reading Heres as "earthen" rather than "sun").
new: Latin suspirasset sedens in asino ("sighed while sitting on the donkey") reflects Jerome's understanding of the rare Hebrew verb tsanach (apparently "got down" from the donkey); similarly, in 1:11, 1:17, and 1:35 the Vulgate adds etymological glosses (civitas litterarum, anathema, and testaceo, reading Heres as "earthen" rather than "sun").
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: provided only that you would not strike a treaty with the inhabitants of this land, but would overthrow their altars; yet you were unwilling to listen to My voice. Why have you done this?
new: provided only that you would not strike a covenant with the inhabitants of this land, but would overthrow their altars; yet you were unwilling to listen to My voice. Why have you done this?
reason: fœdus is rendered "covenant" in this edition (pactum/fœdus → covenant; cf. Judges 8:33 cum Baal fœdus = "a covenant with Baal").

old: Latin Thamnathsare corresponds to "Timnath-serah" (agreeing with Joshua 19:50 and 24:30), whereas the Masoretic Text of Judges 2:9 reads "Timnath-heres."
new: Latin Thamnathsare corresponds to "Timnath-serah" (agreeing with Joshua 19:50 and 24:31), whereas the Masoretic Text of Judges 2:9 reads "Timnath-heres."
reason: In this critical text the burial in Thamnathsare is Joshua 24:31 (24:30 is Joshua's death), so the cross-reference is corrected.

old: The Vulgate presents Deborah's opening words as a direct statement ('has commanded you') rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's rhetorical question ('Has not the LORD commanded?').
new: The Vulgate presents Deborah's opening words as a direct statement ('has commanded you') rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's rhetorical question ('Has not the Lord commanded?').
reason: House rule: never capital LORD in verses or notes.

old: The Vulgate reads "The Lord chose new wars, and He Himself overthrew the gates of the enemies," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly rendered "they chose new gods; then war was in the gates." The conditional clause "if shield and spear appeared" reproduces a Hebraistic rhetorical idiom implying that none were seen.
new: The Vulgate reads "The Lord chose new wars, and He Himself overthrew the gates of the enemies," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "they chose new gods; then war was in the gates." The conditional clause "if shield and spear appeared" reproduces a Hebraistic rhetorical idiom implying that none were seen.
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate renders Hebrew qedumim (commonly translated "ancient" or "onrushing") as a proper name, torrens Cadumim ("the torrent of Kedumim").
new: The Vulgate renders Hebrew qedumim (meaning "ancient" or "onrushing") as a proper name, torrens Cadumim ("the torrent of Kedumim").
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew altar name YHWH-Shalom into Latin as Domini pax ("The Lord's Peace"), attaches "until the present day" to the naming, and joins "while he was still in Ophrah" to the Lord's nighttime command in 6:25.
new: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew altar name ("the Lord is peace") into Latin as Domini pax ("The Lord's Peace"), attaches "until the present day" to the naming, and joins "while he was still in Ophrah" to the Lord's nighttime command in 6:25.
reason: House rule bars Yahweh/Jehovah forms in notes; the tetragrammaton transliteration YHWH is replaced with "the Lord."

old: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew clause commonly translated "whoever contends for him" as qui adversarius est ejus ("Whoever is his adversary"), preserving the literal Latin syntax of Joash's challenge.
new: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew clause "whoever contends for him" as qui adversarius est ejus ("Whoever is his adversary"), preserving the literal Latin syntax of Joash's challenge.
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: Latin consistently gives the name of Gaal's father as Obed (vv. 26, 28, 30, 31, 35), following a Greek textual tradition, whereas the Hebrew reads Ebed.
new: Latin consistently gives the name of Gaal's father as Obed (vv. 26, 28, 30, 31, 35), whereas the Hebrew reads Ebed.
reason: The claim that Obed follows a Greek tradition is unsupported (the main Septuagint witnesses read Abed/Iobel); keep only the accurate Latin-Hebrew comparison.

old: The Vulgate reads 'Chanaan' ('Canaan,' agreeing with the Septuagint) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'Maon' (the Maonites).
new: The Vulgate reads 'Chanaan' ('Canaan') where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'Maon' (the Maonites).
reason: The Septuagint here reads Midian (Madiam), not Canaan, so 'agreeing with the Septuagint' is false.

old: Therefore, having called all the men of Gilead to himself, he fought against Ephraim; and the men of Gilead struck down Ephraim, because they had said, "Gilead is a fugitive from Ephraim and lives in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh."
new: Therefore, having called all the men of Gilead to himself, he fought against Ephraim; and the men of Gilead struck down Ephraim, because Ephraim had said, "Gilead is a fugitive from Ephraim and lives in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh."
reason: dixerat is singular with Ephraim as subject; English 'they' after 'the men of Gilead struck' wrongly points to the Gileadites.

old: Elon the Zebulunite succeeded him, and he judged Israel for ten years,
new: Aijalon the Zebulunite succeeded him, and he judged Israel for ten years,
reason: The Latin names the judge Ahialon (= Aijalon, cf. Aialon elsewhere), not Elon; 'Elon' follows the Masoretic vocalization instead of the Latin.

old: Vulgate spells the judge's name Ahialon (reflecting the Hebrew consonants of Elon/Aijalon), and in 12:12 states simply in Zabulon ("in Zebulun"), omitting the Hebrew place name "in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun."
new: Vulgate names the judge Ahialon (Aijalon), where the Hebrew vocalizes the name as Elon; in 12:12 it states simply in Zabulon ("in Zebulun"), omitting the Hebrew place name "in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun."
reason: Note updated to match the verse now following the Latin name Ahialon (Aijalon).

old: Now his parents did not know that the matter was coming about from the Lord, and that He was seeking an occasion against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.
new: Now his parents did not know that the matter was coming about from the Lord, and that he was seeking an occasion against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.
reason: The subject of quæreret is unexpressed (the Lord or Samson) and the referent is disputed; the capital 'He' silently settles it (flagged).

old: Now after a short time, when the days of the wheat harvest were at hand, Samson came, wanting to visit his wife, and he brought her a kid from the goats. And when he wanted to enter her inner room as usual, her father stopped him, saying,
new: Now after a short time, when the days of the wheat harvest were at hand, Samson came, wanting to visit his wife, and he brought her a young goat from the goats. And when he wanted to enter her inner room as usual, her father stopped him, saying,
reason: hædum de capris is rendered 'a young goat from the goats' in 13:15, 13:19 (and hædum 'young goat' in 14:6); keep the same English.

old: The Clementine Vulgate prints eam ('her') here, a well-known printing slip for eum ('him'), which the context and the following verse require.
new: The Latin text reads eam ('her') here, evidently a slip for eum ('him'), which the context and the following verse require.
