new: The Clementine Vulgate does not have this material at 2:35; following this edition's Greek-based verse arrangement, the English here joins Vulgate 2:35 with 9:23 and 9:25 (the five hundred and fifty chief officers, the thrice-yearly sacrifices, and the completion of the temple). The Septuagint has similar material in its additions after 2:35.
reason: The old note falsely says the Vulgate retains this summary at 2:35; the Latin shown comes from CT 9:23 and 9:25.

old: The Clementine Vulgate appends a summary of Solomon's prosperous reign (paralleling 1 Kings 4:20-21, 25 in the Hebrew text and the Septuagint miscellany at 2:46) and reads a flumine terrae Philisthiim ("from the river of the land of the Philistines"), where Hebrew 4:21 reads "from the River [Euphrates] to the land of the Philistines."
new: The Clementine Vulgate does not have this material at 2:46; following this edition's Greek-based verse arrangement, the English here joins Vulgate 2:46 with 4:20, 5:1 and 5:5 (the Septuagint has a similar summary in its additions after 2:46). The Latin reads a flumine terrae Philisthiim ("from the river of the land of the Philistines"), where the Hebrew reads "from the River to the land of the Philistines."
reason: The old note falsely says the Vulgate appends this summary at 2:46; the Latin shown comes from CT 4:20, 5:1 and 5:5 (also drops the wrong 'Hebrew 4:21' numbering and brackets).

old: look, I have done for you according to your words, and I have given you a wise and understanding heart, to such an extent that no one like you has existed before you, nor will arise after you.
new: look, I have done for you according to your words, and I have given you a wise and understanding heart, to such an extent that no one like you has been before you, nor will arise after you.
reason: fuerit is simply 'has been'; 'existed' interprets.

old: And these were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim.
new: And these were their names: Ben-hur, in Mount Ephraim.
reason: in monte Ephraim is 'in Mount Ephraim' (as at 2 Sam 20:21); 'hill country' follows the Hebrew/familiar English Bibles.

old: And the above-mentioned governors of the king provided food for them; moreover, they also supplied the necessities of the table of King Solomon with immense care in their due time. Barley also, and straw for the horses and beasts of burden, they brought to the place where the king was, according to what was appointed for them.
new: And the above-mentioned prefects of the king provided food for them; moreover, they also supplied the necessities of the table of King Solomon with immense care in their due time. Barley also, and straw for the horses and beasts of burden, they brought to the place where the king was, according to what was appointed for them.
reason: praefecti is rendered 'prefects' for these same officers at 4:7.

old: And the Lord gave wisdom to Solomon, just as He had spoken to him; and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them struck a covenant.
new: The Lord also gave wisdom to Solomon, just as He had spoken to him; and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them struck a covenant.
reason: quoque ('also') was not represented (cf. 5:9 Dedit quoque Deus, 'God also gave').

old: the son of a widowed woman from the tribe of Naphtali, whose father was a Tyrian, a bronze craftsman, and full of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge for making every work of bronze. When he had come to King Solomon, he did all his work.
new: the son of a widowed woman from the tribe of Naphtali, whose father was a Tyrian; he was a bronze craftsman, and full of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge for making every work of bronze. When he had come to King Solomon, he did all his work.
reason: artificem aerarium is accusative in apposition to filium (the son), not to the ablative patre Tyrio; the English let 'a bronze craftsman' attach to the father.

old: He also made ten bronze basins: one basin held forty baths, and it was of four cubits; and he placed each basin upon each one, that is, the ten bases.
new: He also made ten bronze basins: one basin held forty baths, and it was of four cubits; and he also placed each basin upon each one, that is, the ten bases.
reason: singulos quoque luteres ... posuit: quoque ("also") was not represented.

old: Latin literally reads in manibus ejus ("in/with his hands"), using the non-reflexive pronoun ejus and plural manibus; the context and the parallel in 8:24 indicate God's own hands, though some Latin readers have linked ejus to David.
new: Latin in manibus ejus ("in/with his hands") uses the non-reflexive ejus, which could grammatically point to David; the parallel in 8:24 (manibus perfecisti, "with Your hands You have fulfilled") indicates God's own hands.
reason: Removes the unsupported claim about what "some Latin readers" have done and keeps the note to the Latin grammar and the 8:24 parallel.

old: Now therefore, Lord God of Israel, keep for Your servant my father David what You spoke to him, saying, 'A man will not be taken away from you before Me to sit on the throne of Israel, only if your sons keep their way, so that they walk before Me just as you walked in My sight.'
new: Now therefore, Lord God of Israel, keep for Your servant my father David what You spoke to him, saying, 'A man will not be taken away from you before Me to sit on the throne of Israel, yet only if your sons keep their way, so that they walk before Me just as you walked in My sight.'
reason: ita tamen si: tamen ("yet/however") was not represented.

old: If Your people Israel flee from their enemies (because they will sin against You), and, doing penance and confessing Your name, come and pray and make supplication to You in this house,
new: If Your people Israel flee from their enemies (because they will sin against You), and, repenting and confessing Your name, come and pray and make supplication to You in this house,
reason: agentes pœnitentiam: the edition renders pœnitentiam agere as "repent"; "doing penance" brings in technical vocabulary the Latin does not require.

old: Latin distinctively reads fugerit inimicos suos ("flee from their enemies"), the future periphrastic quia peccaturus est tibi ("because they will sin against You"), and agentes poenitentiam ("doing penance"), whereas the Hebrew has "are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and turn back to You."
new: Latin distinctively reads fugerit inimicos suos ("flee from their enemies"), the future periphrastic quia peccaturus est tibi ("because they will sin against You"), and agentes poenitentiam ("repenting"), whereas the Hebrew has "are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and turn back to You."
reason: Brings the note into line with the corrected verse (pœnitentiam agere = "repent").

old: If heaven is shut up, and it does not rain because of their sins, and praying in this place they do penance to Your name, and turn back from their sins because of their affliction,
new: If heaven is shut up, and it does not rain because of their sins, and praying in this place they repent to Your name, and turn back from their sins because of their affliction,
reason: pœnitentiam egerint nomini tuo: pœnitentiam agere is rendered "repent" in this edition, not "do penance".

old: and they do penance in their heart in the place of captivity, and turning back they make supplication to You in their captivity, saying, 'We have sinned; we have acted iniquitously, we have done wickedly,'
new: and they repent in their heart in the place of captivity, and turning back they make supplication to You in their captivity, saying, 'We have sinned; we have acted iniquitously, we have done wickedly,'
reason: egerint pœnitentiam in corde suo: pœnitentiam agere is rendered "repent" in this edition, not "do penance".

old: The opening sentence on Solomon's forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand riding horses stands here following the Septuagint 3 Kingdoms placement (compare 1 Kings 4:26 in the Hebrew text), and the Vulgate reads "fortified cities" (civitates munitas) where the Hebrew has "chariot cities."
new: The opening sentence on Solomon's forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand riding horses (numbered 5:6 in the Saints Latin Critical Text) stands here following the Septuagint 3 Kingdoms placement, and the Vulgate reads "fortified cities" (civitates munitas) where the Hebrew has "chariot cities."
reason: The sentence comes from CT 5:6, so the cross-reference "1 Kings 4:26 in the Hebrew text" is wrong (4:26 is the English-Bible number; Hebrew and the critical text have 5:6).

old: And this is the cause of the rebellion against him: that Solomon built the Millo and leveled the chasm of the city of David his father.
new: And this is the cause of the rebellion against him: that Solomon built Millo and leveled the chasm of the city of David his father.
reason: Mello is rendered "Millo" without the article in 9:9 and 10:22; keep it the same here.

old: and I will afflict the offspring of David because of this, yet not for all days.
new: and I will afflict the seed of David because of this, yet not for all days.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: The Vulgate reads "because the Lord had turned away from him" (quoniam aversatus fuerat eum Dominus), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "for it was a turn of affairs from the LORD."
new: The Vulgate reads "because the Lord had turned away from him" (quoniam aversatus fuerat eum Dominus), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "for it was a turn of affairs from the Lord."
reason: Capital LORD is not allowed in notes; use "the Lord".

old: Verse 6 is absent in this Clementine Vulgate text, with the battle notice between Abijam and Jeroboam appearing at the end of verse 7. The Vulgate's 'book of the words of the days' (in libro verborum dierum) literally reflects the Hebrew title for the royal annals or chronicles.
new: Latin verse 6 (on war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam) is given among this book's additional verses; the battle notice between Abijam and Jeroboam stands at the end of verse 7. The Vulgate's 'book of the words of the days' (in libro verborum dierum) literally reflects the Hebrew title for the royal annals or chronicles.
reason: False claim: the critical text does have 15:6 (Attamen bellum fuit inter Roboam et Jeroboam...); this edition lists it as an additional verse.

old: "There is a treaty between me and you, and between my father and your father; therefore I have sent you gifts, silver and gold, and I ask that you come and make void the treaty that you have with Baasha king of Israel, so that he may withdraw from me."
new: "There is a covenant between me and you, and between my father and your father; therefore I have sent you gifts, silver and gold, and I ask that you come and make void the covenant that you have with Baasha king of Israel, so that he may withdraw from me."
reason: Fœdus ... fœdus: fœdus is rendered "covenant" edition-wide.

old: Verse 32 (which in the Hebrew repeats the war notice between Asa and Baasha from verse 16) is absent from this Clementine Vulgate text.
new: Latin verse 32, which repeats the war notice between Asa and Baasha from verse 16, is given among this book's additional verses.
reason: False claim: the critical text does have 15:32 (Fuitque bellum inter Asa, et Baasa...); this edition lists it as an additional verse.

old: Major textual addition in this Latin text: following Omri's death and Ahab's accession, material parallel to 1 Kings 22:46-49 concerning Jehoshaphat (whose name appears midway through the addition, with 'Asa his father' signaling the shift in subject) is inserted here, reflecting the Septuagint placement of the Jehoshaphat summary.
new: Following the Septuagint (3 Kingdoms) placement of the Jehoshaphat summary, the material numbered 22:47-50 in the Saints Latin Critical Text stands here after Omri's death and Ahab's accession; 'Asa his father' signals the shift of subject to Jehoshaphat, whose name appears midway through.
reason: The note called this an addition "in this Latin text" and cited 22:46-49; the critical text has it at 22:47-50, and the edition has moved it here (16:28 in the CT is only Omri's death).

old: For the Lord God of Israel says this: 'The jar of flour will not run out, nor will the flask of oil be reduced, until the day on which the Lord will give rain upon the face of the earth.'"
new: For this is what the Lord God of Israel says: 'The jar of flour will not run out, nor will the flask of oil be reduced, until the day on which the Lord will give rain upon the face of the earth.'"
reason: Latin "Hæc autem dicit Dominus Deus Israël" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: And when it was already noon, Elijah mocked them, saying, "Shout with a louder voice, for he is a god; and perhaps he is talking, or he is at an inn, or on a journey, or surely he is asleep and must be awakened."
new: And when it was already noon, Elijah mocked them, saying, "Shout with a louder voice, for he is a god; and perhaps he is talking, or he is at an inn, or on a journey, or surely he is asleep, so that he may be awakened."
reason: ut excitetur is a purpose clause ("so that he may be awakened"); "must be awakened" turns it into necessity.

old: Following the chapter order of the Septuagint (3 Kingdoms), the Naboth's vineyard narrative appears here as chapter 20 rather than chapter 21 as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and standard Sixto-Clementine Vulgate numbering.
new: Following the chapter order of the Septuagint (3 Kingdoms), the Saints Latin Critical Text places the narrative of Naboth's vineyard in chapter 20, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text and the standard Sixto-Clementine numbering have chapter 21.
reason: Fixes the grammar ("the Naboth's vineyard narrative") and says plainly that the critical text itself numbers this chapter 20.

old: And he said to him, "The cities that my father took from your father I will return, and make streets for yourself in Damascus, just as my father did in Samaria; and I, bound by a treaty, will depart from you." Therefore he made a treaty and let him go.
new: And he said to him, "The cities that my father took from your father I will return, and make streets for yourself in Damascus, just as my father did in Samaria; and I, bound by a covenant, will depart from you." Therefore he made a covenant and let him go.
reason: fœdus (pepigit fœdus; fœderatus) is rendered "covenant" in this edition, as at 2 Kings 3:5 and 11:4; context does not require "treaty".

old: In the Vulgate (et ego foederatus recedam a te), Ben-hadad continues speaking ("and I, bound by a treaty, will depart from you"), whereas in the Hebrew Masoretic Text Ahab speaks this clause ("and I will let you go with this treaty").
new: In the Vulgate (et ego foederatus recedam a te), Ben-hadad continues speaking ("and I, bound by a covenant, will depart from you"), whereas in the Hebrew Masoretic Text Ahab speaks this clause ("and I will let you go with this covenant").
reason: Keeps the note in step with the verse's "covenant" for fœdus/fœderatus.

old: And Micaiah said, "You will see on that day when you enter a room within a room to hide yourself."
new: And Micaiah said, "You will see on that day when you enter a chamber within a chamber to hide yourself."
reason: cubiculum intra cubiculum is the same phrase rendered "a chamber that was inside a chamber" at 21:30; the echo should be kept.

old: Now it happened, when the Lord was about to lift Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, that Elijah and Elisha were going from Gilgal.
new: Now it happened, when the Lord willed to lift Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, that Elijah and Elisha were going from Gilgal.
reason: cum levare vellet Dominus expresses the Lord's will (vellet, "willed/wished"); "was about to" drops the volition.

old: And when the king of Israel had read the letter, he tore his garments and said, "Am I God, that I can kill and make alive, that this man has sent to me to cure a man of his leprosy? Take note and see that he is seeking pretexts against me."
new: And when the king of Israel had read the letter, he tore his garments and said, "Am I a god, that I can kill and make alive, that this man has sent to me to cure a man of his leprosy? Take note and see that he is seeking pretexts against me."
reason: The critical text prints lowercase deus ("Numquid deus ego sum"), as it does for "a god" elsewhere (e.g. Judges 6:31 si deus est); "Am I God" follows the Hebrew/familiar Bibles instead.

old: Yet the leprosy of Naaman will also cling to you and to your offspring forever." And he went out from him, leprous like snow.
new: Yet the leprosy of Naaman will also cling to you and to your seed forever." And he went out from him, leprous like snow.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Now it happened that when one had cut down a piece of timber, the iron of the axe fell into the water; and he cried out and said, "Oh no! Oh no! Oh no, my lord! And I had borrowed this very thing."
new: Now it happened that when one had cut down a piece of timber, the iron of the axe fell into the water; and he cried out and said, "Alas! Alas! Alas, my lord! And I had borrowed this very thing."
reason: Heu! heu! heu! is rendered "Alas! Alas! Alas!" at 3:10 and elsewhere in the edition.

old: Now the attendant of the man of God, rising at dawn and going out, saw an army all around the city, and horses and chariots; and he reported to him, saying, "Oh no! Oh no! Oh no, my lord! What shall we do?"
new: Now the attendant of the man of God, rising at dawn and going out, saw an army all around the city, and horses and chariots; and he reported to him, saying, "Alas! Alas! Alas, my lord! What shall we do?"
reason: Heu! heu! heu! is rendered "Alas! Alas! Alas!" at 3:10 and elsewhere in the edition.

old: The Clementine Latin prints Stetique ("and I stood"), a known orthographic variant for Stetitque ("and he stood"); the Vulgate also reads "was troubled to the flushing of his face" (conturbatus est usque ad suffusionem vultus), where the Hebrew reads "fixed his gaze until he was ashamed."
new: The critical text prints Stetique (literally "and I stood"), evidently for Stetitque ("and he stood"), which the third-person narrative requires; the Vulgate also reads "was troubled to the flushing of his face" (conturbatus est usque ad suffusionem vultus), where the Hebrew reads "fixed his gaze until he was ashamed."
reason: The claim that Stetique is "a known orthographic variant" is unsupported; state neutrally what the critical text prints and why "he stood" is rendered.

old: The Vulgate coordinates both kings in the genitive ("of Joram... and of Jehoshaphat king of Judah"), reflecting a difficult chronological clause in Hebrew often rendered "while Jehoshaphat was king of Judah."
new: The Vulgate coordinates both kings in the genitive ("of Joram... and of Jehoshaphat king of Judah"), reflecting a difficult chronological clause in the Hebrew.
reason: Removes the claim about how the clause is "often rendered" by translations; keeps the factual point about the Latin.

old: Vulgate 'civitatem templi Baal' ("the city of the temple of Baal") literally renders the Hebrew expression for the inner citadel or sanctuary precinct of Baal's temple; in 10:26-27 the Vulgate also reads singular 'statuam' ("statue") where the Hebrew has plural pillars.
new: Vulgate 'civitatem templi Baal' ("the city of the temple of Baal") literally renders the Hebrew expression for the inner citadel or sanctuary precinct of Baal's temple; in 10:26 the Vulgate also reads singular 'statuam' ("statue") where the Hebrew has plural pillars.
reason: statuam occurs only in 10:26 (10:27 has eam), and the Hebrew of 10:27 is itself singular, so the reference "10:26-27" is inaccurate.

old: Now the rest of the accounts of Jehoahaz, and all that he did, and his might, are these not written in the book of the accounts of the days of the kings of Israel?
new: Now the rest of the accounts of Jehoahaz, and all that he did, and his might, are these not written in the book of the words of the days of the kings of Israel?
reason: The chronicle title libro sermonum dierum is rendered "the book of the words of the days" elsewhere in this edition (e.g. 14:15, 14:18); "accounts" here is inconsistent.

old: Now the rest of the accounts of Joash, and all that he did, and his might, how he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are these not written in the book of the accounts of the days of the kings of Israel?
new: Now the rest of the accounts of Joash, and all that he did, and his might, how he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are these not written in the book of the words of the days of the kings of Israel?
reason: The chronicle title libro sermonum dierum is rendered "the book of the words of the days" elsewhere in this edition; "accounts" here is inconsistent.

old: However, he did not kill the sons of those who had killed him, according to what is written in the book of the law of Moses, just as the Lord commanded, saying, "Fathers will not die for sons, nor will sons die for fathers; rather, each one will die in his own sin."
new: However, he did not kill the sons of those who had killed, according to what is written in the book of the law of Moses, just as the Lord commanded, saying, "Fathers will not die for sons, nor will sons die for fathers; rather, each one will die in his own sin."
reason: qui occiderant has no expressed object; the added "him" naturally points to Amaziah (the subject) rather than his father, who was the one killed.

old: In the days of Pekah, king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came and captured Ijon, and Abel House of Maacah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, and carried them away to the Assyrians.
new: In the days of Pekah, king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came and captured Ijon, and Abel House, Maacah and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, and carried them away to the Assyrians.
reason: The critical text reads Abel Domum, Maacha et Janoë, punctuating Maacha as a separate name paired with Janoë; the supplied "of" merges them into the Hebrew Abel-beth-maacah.

old: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew town name Abel-beth-maacah partly into Latin as "Abel Domum, Maacha" ("Abel House of Maacah," with a comma after "Domum" in the Clementine text), and renders the destination as "in Assyrios" ("to the Assyrians").
new: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew town name Abel-beth-maacah partly into Latin as "Abel Domum, Maacha" ("Abel House, Maacah," with a comma after "Domum" in the Clementine text, so that Maacha stands as a separate name), and renders the destination as "in Assyrios" ("to the Assyrians").
reason: Note updated to match the corrected verse, which follows the critical text's punctuation.

old: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew idiom for child sacrifice doubly as 'consecrated... passing him through the fire' (consecravit, transferens per ignem). It also reads 'idols' (idola) with neuter plural 'which' (quae) where the Hebrew has 'abominations' of the nations whom the Lord drove out.
new: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew idiom for child sacrifice doubly as 'consecrated... passing him through the fire' (consecravit, transferens per ignem). It also reads 'idols' (idola) where the Hebrew has 'abominations' of the nations whom the Lord drove out.
reason: quæ is grammatically ambiguous (neuter plural with idola or feminine plural with gentium; cf. quas … gentium in 21:2), so the note should not assert it is neuter.

old: Then the king of the Assyrians commanded, saying, "Lead one of the priests whom you brought captive from there to that place, and let him go and live with them, and let him teach them the ordinances of the God of the land."
new: Then the king of the Assyrians commanded, saying, "Lead to that place one of the priests whom you brought captive from there, and let him go and live with them, and let him teach them the ordinances of the God of the land."
reason: illuc goes with Ducite ("lead to that place"); placed at the end, "to that place" wrongly reads as the destination of the captives' deportation (inde captivos adduxistis).

old: Vulgate reads transite ad dominum meum ("come over to my lord"), diverging from the Hebrew idiom commonly translated "make a wager with my master."
new: Vulgate reads transite ad dominum meum ("come over to my lord"), diverging from the Hebrew idiom "make a wager with my master."
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: Therefore Isaiah the prophet called upon the Lord, and He brought the shadow back along the lines by which it had already gone down on the sundial of Ahaz, backward by ten degrees.
new: Therefore Isaiah the prophet called upon the Lord, and he brought the shadow back along the lines by which it had already gone down on the sundial of Ahaz, backward by ten degrees.
reason: reduxit has no expressed subject and grammatically continues Isaias propheta as subject; the capital "He" settles the referent as the Lord where the Latin leaves it open.

old: In the Clementine Vulgate, the opening sentence ("And they reported to the king what she had said") begins 23:1, whereas in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most modern English Bibles it concludes 22:20.
new: In the Clementine Vulgate, the opening sentence ("And they reported to the king what she had said") begins 23:1, whereas in the Hebrew Masoretic Text it concludes 22:20.
reason: Notes should not make claims about what English translations do; the factual comparison with the Hebrew is kept.

old: And the king stood upon the step and made a covenant before the Lord, that they would walk after the Lord and keep His precepts and testimonies and ceremonies with all their heart and with their whole soul, and re-establish the words of this covenant that were written in that book; and the people agreed to the pact.
new: And the king stood upon the step and made a covenant before the Lord, that they would walk after the Lord and keep His precepts and testimonies and ceremonies with all their heart and with their whole soul, and re-establish the words of this covenant that were written in that book; and the people agreed to the covenant.
reason: pactum is rendered "covenant" in this edition (pactum/fœdus → covenant), and here it refers to the fœdus just made.

old: Now the rest of the accounts of Jehoiakim, and all that he did, are these not written in the book of the accounts of the days of the kings of Judah? And Jehoiakim slept with his fathers,
new: Now the rest of the accounts of Jehoiakim, and all that he did, are these not written in the book of the words of the days of the kings of Judah? And Jehoiakim slept with his fathers,
reason: The chronicle title libro sermonum dierum is rendered "the book of the words of the days" elsewhere in this edition (e.g. 23:28, 21:25); "accounts" here is inconsistent.

old: Vulgate "locksmith" (clusorem, also in v. 16) is a literal coinage from Latin claudere ("to shut/lock") for the Hebrew term masger, commonly rendered "smiths" or "metalworkers."
new: Vulgate "locksmith" (clusorem, also in v. 16) is a literal coinage from Latin claudere ("to shut/lock") for the Hebrew term masger ("smiths" or "metalworkers").
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: Vulgate preserves the proper name Aram, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Oren.
new: Vulgate reads the proper name Aram, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Oren.
reason: 'preserves' implies a judgment that Aram is the original reading; state the reading neutrally.

old: These were the sons of Caleb, the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim;
new: These were the sons of Caleb, the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim;
reason: filii Hur parallels filii Caleb (nominative plural, 'the sons of Hur'); 'Caleb, the son of Hur' reverses 2:19, where Ephratha bore Hur to Caleb and Hur is the firstborn of Ephratha.

old: Vulgate treats Asir ('Assir') as the proper name of Jeconiah's first son, whereas many translations of the Hebrew take it as an epithet ('Jeconiah the captive').
new: Vulgate treats Asir ('Assir') as the proper name of Jeconiah's first son; the Hebrew 'assir can also be read as an epithet of Jeconiah, 'the captive.'
reason: Removes a claim about what translations do; states the Latin and Hebrew facts only.

old: In the Clementine Vulgate, 1 Chronicles 5:27-41 concludes chapter 5 with the Levitical genealogy; in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most modern English Bibles, these verses are numbered 1 Chronicles 6:1-15.
new: This text numbers these verses 5:27-41, as the Hebrew does; the printed Sixto-Clementine edition numbers them 6:1-15.
reason: The note's numbering claim is false: the Hebrew text numbers these verses 5:27-41 (as this Latin text does), while the printed Clementine edition numbers them 6:1-15.

old: In the Vulgate, 1 Chronicles 6:1-33 corresponds to 6:16-48 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most English translations, because the Vulgate includes the Aaronite high-priestly genealogy at 5:27-41.
new: This text follows the Hebrew numbering of chapter 6 (6:1-66); the printed Sixto-Clementine edition numbers these verses 6:16-81.
reason: The note's numbering claim is false: this text and the Hebrew both number this chapter 6:1-66 and both contain 5:27-41; only the printed Clementine (and other) numbering differs.

old: The Vulgate preserves several distinct proper names here and in vv. 29-31: 'Thohu' ('Tohu', matching 1 Sam 1:1) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'Toah'; in v. 29 'Cusi' ('Cushi', related to 'Kushaiah' in 1 Chr 15:17) for Hebrew 'Kishi'; and in v. 31 'Amasai' for Hebrew 'Amzi.'
new: The Vulgate has several distinct proper names here and in vv. 29-31: 'Thohu' ('Tohu', matching 1 Sam 1:1) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'Toah'; in v. 29 'Cusi' ('Cushi', related to 'Kushaiah' in 1 Chr 15:17) for Hebrew 'Kishi'; and in v. 31 'Amasai' for Hebrew 'Amzi.'
reason: 'preserves' implies a judgment that the Latin names are original; state the readings neutrally.

old: and also Aijalon with its outskirts, and Gath-rimmon in the same manner.
new: and also Helon with its outskirts, and Gath-rimmon in the same manner.
reason: The Latin reads Helon (contrast Ajalon in 8:13); 'Aijalon' follows the Hebrew instead of this text.

old: And he went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Beriah, because he had been born in the misfortunes of his house.
new: And he went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Beriah, because he had been born in the misfortunes of his house.
reason: quæ concepit, et peperit filium, et vocavit: one subject (quæ, the wife) governs all three verbs; 'he called' follows the Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate reads "before the Lord" (coram Domino), combining elements that the Hebrew Masoretic Text divides as "in time past; the LORD was with him."
new: The Vulgate reads "before the Lord" (coram Domino), combining elements that the Hebrew Masoretic Text divides as "in time past; the Lord was with him."
reason: Capital LORD is not used in this edition's notes; use 'the Lord'.

old: The Vulgate reads "and did not hope in the Lord" (nec speraverit in Domino), whereas the Hebrew reads "and did not inquire of the LORD."
new: The Vulgate reads "and did not hope in the Lord" (nec speraverit in Domino), whereas the Hebrew reads "and did not inquire of the Lord."
reason: Capital LORD is not used in this edition's notes; use 'the Lord'.

old: The Clementine Vulgate omits "Eliphal the son of Ur" present here in the Hebrew Masoretic Text; in this warrior roster it also preserves distinct proper-name readings including Pharonite (11:27), Thosaite (11:45), and Mahumite, Josaia, and Masobia (11:46).
new: This Latin text lacks "Eliphal the son of Ur," present here in the Hebrew Masoretic Text; in this warrior roster it also has distinct proper-name readings including Pharonite (11:27), Thosaite (11:45), and Mahumite, Josaia, and Masobia (11:46).
reason: State only what this Latin text has (it lacks Eliphal son of Ur) rather than a claim about the Clementine edition, and avoid 'preserves', which implies the readings are original.

old: The Clementine Vulgate combines what are verses 4 and 5 in Hebrew and most modern editions into 12:4 (leaving no separate 12:5), and reads Samaias (Shemaiah) where the Hebrew has Ishmaiah.
new: Here 12:4 contains what the Hebrew divides into verses 4 and 5, so there is no separate 12:5; the Latin reads Samaias (Shemaiah) where the Hebrew has Ishmaiah.
reason: Removes the claim about "most modern editions" (in common English numbering 12:4 already includes these names) and states the verse-division fact as it stands in this text.

old: Moreover, some from the Gadites also defected to David while he was hiding in the wilderness, very strong men and the finest fighters, holding shield and spear; their faces were like the face of a lion, and they were swift like gazelles on the mountains:
new: Moreover, some from the Gadites also defected to David while he was hiding in the wilderness, very strong men and the finest fighters, holding shield and spear; their faces were like the face of a lion, and they were swift like roe deer on the mountains:
reason: Latin capreæ is rendered "roe deer", the edition's rendering of caprea (Deut 12:15, 2 Sam 2:18, Song 2:9, Sirach 11:30).

old: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders the Hebrew baca-trees (often translated balsam or mulberry trees) as 'pear trees' (pyrorum) here and in verse 15.
new: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders the Hebrew baca-trees (perhaps balsam or mulberry trees) as 'pear trees' (pyrorum) here and in verse 15.
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: Vulgate partem assae carnis bubalae, et frixam oleo similam ("a portion of roasted beef, and fine flour fried in oil") translates two rare Hebrew food terms often rendered "a portion of meat" (or "date cake") and "a raisin cake."
new: Vulgate partem assae carnis bubalae, et frixam oleo similam ("a portion of roasted beef, and fine flour fried in oil") translates two rare Hebrew food terms probably meaning "a portion of meat" (or "date cake") and "a raisin cake."
reason: Replaces a claim about how translations render the Hebrew with a neutral statement of its probable meaning.

old: offspring of Israel, His servant, sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.
new: seed of Israel, His servant, sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Verse 24 of the Hebrew text ("Declare His glory among the nations, His marvelous works among all the peoples") is omitted in the Clementine Vulgate, which passes directly from 16:23 to 16:25.
reason: False for this Latin: the text has 16:24 (narrate in gentibus gloriam ejus; in cunctis populis mirabilia ejus), placed as an additional verse after 16:23, so nothing is omitted.

old: Vulgate Et dicat omnis populo: Amen, et hymnum Domino ("And let all the people say, 'Amen,' and a hymn to the Lord") uses a jussive subjunctive (dicat) rather than the Hebrew past narrative ("and all the people said... and praised the Lord"), and preserves the Clementine Vulgate form omnis populo for omnis populus.
new: Vulgate Et dicat omnis populo: Amen, et hymnum Domino ("And let all the people say, 'Amen,' and a hymn to the Lord") uses a jussive subjunctive (dicat) rather than the Hebrew past narrative ("and all the people said... and praised the Lord"), and the text here reads omnis populo where omnis populus would be expected.
reason: Describes the form as it stands in this Latin text instead of an unverified claim that it is the Clementine reading.

old: The Vulgate reads pharetras aureas ("golden quivers"), whereas the Hebrew term is usually translated "golden shields."
new: The Vulgate reads pharetras aureas ("golden quivers"), whereas the Hebrew term probably means "golden shields."
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate adds "so that they were cut in pieces and crushed," explicitly interpreting the treatment of the Ammonite captives as execution rather than forced labor.
new: The Vulgate adds "so that they were cut in pieces and crushed" (ita ut dissecarentur et contererentur).
reason: Removes the interpretive comment ("explicitly interpreting ... as execution rather than forced labor"); keeps the factual description of the Latin.

old: The Vulgate reads "took pity" (misertus est), emphasizing divine compassion over the calamity where the Hebrew verb denotes relenting or grieving.
new: The Vulgate reads "took pity" (misertus est) where the Hebrew verb denotes relenting or grieving.
reason: Removes the interpretive "emphasizing divine compassion"; keeps the neutral comparison with the Hebrew.

old: Although the text counts six sons of Jeduthun, only five are named here (the sixth, Shimei, appears in the tenth lot in 25:17). The Vulgate also renders the final phrase with plural participles ('super confitentes et laudantes', 'over those giving thanks to and praising'), whereas the Hebrew has infinitives ('in giving thanks and praising').
new: Although the text counts six sons of Jeduthun, only five are named here (the sixth is presumably Shemaiah, Latin Semeias, who receives the tenth lot in 25:17, where the Hebrew has Shimei). The Vulgate also renders the final phrase with plural participles ('super confitentes et laudantes', 'over those giving thanks to and praising'), whereas the Hebrew has infinitives ('in giving thanks and praising').
reason: Brings the note into line with the Latin name at 25:17 (Semeiæ = Shemaiah, not Shimei).

old: The tenth for Shimei, his sons and his brothers, twelve.
new: The tenth for Shemaiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve.
reason: The Latin has Semeiæ (Semeias), which this edition renders Shemaiah everywhere else (15:8, 24:6, 26:4); Shimei (Latin Semei) is the Hebrew name here.

old: and over the cultivators of the vineyards, Shimei the Ramathite; and over the wine cellars, Zabdi the Aphonite.
new: and over the cultivators of the vineyards, Shemaiah the Ramathite; and over the wine cellars, Zabdi the Aphonite.
reason: The Latin reads Semeias Romathites; Semeias is Shemaiah throughout this edition, while Shimei (Latin Semei) is the Hebrew reading.

old: And when the king had risen and stood up, he said, "Listen to me, my brothers and my people: I planned to build a house in which the ark of the covenant of the Lord and the footstool of our God might rest, and I prepared everything for building.
new: And when the king had risen and stood up, he said, "Listen to me, my brothers and my people: I planned to build a house in which the ark of the covenant of the Lord and the footstool of the feet of our God might rest, and I prepared everything for building.
reason: scabellum pedum Dei nostri includes pedum ("of the feet"), rendered elsewhere in the edition as "the footstool of His/My feet".

old: And you, my son Solomon, know the God of your father and serve Him with a complete heart and a willing spirit; for the Lord examines all hearts and understands all the thoughts of minds. If you seek Him, you will find Him; but if you abandon Him, He will cast you away forever.
new: And you, my son Solomon, know the God of your father and serve Him with a perfect heart and a willing spirit; for the Lord examines all hearts and understands all the thoughts of minds. If you seek Him, you will find Him; but if you abandon Him, He will cast you away forever.
reason: corde perfecto is "with a perfect heart" in 12:39, 29:19, 2 Kings 20:3 and 2 Chronicles 16:9 and 19:9.

old: The Vulgate reads "Deo nostro" ("our God") where the Hebrew has "your God," and adds "deinde" ("and then") before "the king" to distinguish the assembly's worship ("adoraverunt") of God from royal homage to David.
new: The Vulgate reads "Deo nostro" ("our God") where the Hebrew has "your God," and adds "deinde" ("then") before "the king."
reason: Removed the interpretive claim that deinde serves 'to distinguish' worship of God from homage to David; the note now states only the textual facts.

old: And he went with the whole multitude to the high place of Gibeon, where the tent of the covenant of God was, which Moses the servant of God made in the wilderness.
new: And he went with the whole multitude to the high place of Gibeon, where the tabernacle of the covenant of God was, which Moses the servant of God made in the wilderness.
reason: tabernaculum foederis is rendered 'tabernacle of the covenant' throughout this edition; this is the sacred tabernacle, not an ordinary tent.

old: Latin tabernaculum foederis ('tent of the covenant,' also in 1:6, 1:13) is a distinctly Vulgate rendering of Hebrew 'tent of meeting.'
new: Latin tabernaculum foederis ('tabernacle of the covenant,' also in 1:6, 1:13) is a distinctly Vulgate rendering of Hebrew 'tent of meeting.'
reason: Note updated to match the corrected verse rendering of tabernaculum foederis.

old: The bronze altar also, which Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had fashioned, was there before the tent of the Lord; and Solomon and the whole assembly sought it out.
new: The bronze altar also, which Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had fashioned, was there before the tabernacle of the Lord; and Solomon and the whole assembly sought it out.
reason: coram tabernaculo Domini refers to the sacred tabernacle of 1:3; the edition's rendering of tabernaculum is 'tabernacle' ('tent' only for ordinary tents).

old: And Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the tent of the covenant of the Lord, and offered one thousand sacrifices on it.
new: And Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the tabernacle of the covenant of the Lord, and offered one thousand sacrifices on it.
reason: tabernaculum foederis Domini = 'tabernacle of the covenant of the Lord', per the edition's established rendering.

old: So Solomon came from the high place of Gibeon to Jerusalem, before the tent of the covenant, and reigned over Israel.
new: So Solomon came from the high place of Gibeon to Jerusalem, before the tabernacle of the covenant, and reigned over Israel.
reason: coram tabernaculo foederis = 'before the tabernacle of the covenant', per the edition's established rendering.

old: Latin reads in Jerusalem coram tabernaculo foederis ('to Jerusalem, before the tent of the covenant'), placing coram ('before') after in Jerusalem rather than 'from before the tent of meeting' as in the Hebrew.
new: Latin reads in Jerusalem coram tabernaculo foederis ('to Jerusalem, before the tabernacle of the covenant'), placing coram ('before') after in Jerusalem rather than 'from before the tent of meeting' as in the Hebrew.
reason: Note updated to match the corrected verse rendering of tabernaculo foederis.

old: Latin renders Hebrew 'resident aliens' with the Septuagint-influenced term proselytos ('proselytes'), and divides the total as 'one hundred fifty thousand, and three thousand six hundred' in anticipation of 2:17.
new: Latin renders Hebrew 'resident aliens' with the Septuagint-influenced term proselytos ('proselytes').
reason: Removed the claim that the Latin 'divides the total ... in anticipation of 2:17'; the Hebrew has the same division (150,000 and 3,600), so it is not a Vulgate feature.

old: also the lampstands with their lamps, of the purest gold, so that they might shine before the inner sanctuary according to the rite;
new: also the lampstands with their lamps, of the purest gold, so that they might shine before the oracle according to the rite;
reason: oraculum is rendered 'oracle' throughout the edition (including 2 Chr 3:16 and the parallel 1 Kgs 7:49 and 8:6, 8:8); 'inner sanctuary' explains the Hebrew debir rather than translating the Latin.

old: And the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord into its place, that is, to the inner sanctuary of the temple, into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim,
new: And the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord into its place, that is, to the oracle of the temple, into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim,
reason: ad oraculum templi = 'to the oracle of the temple', matching the edition's rendering of oraculum (cf. 1 Kgs 8:6 'into the oracle of the temple').

old: Now the ends of the poles by which the ark was carried, because they were a little longer, were visible before the inner sanctuary; but if anyone was a little outside, he could not see them. So the ark has been there until the present day.
new: Now the ends of the poles by which the ark was carried, because they were a little longer, were visible before the oracle; but if anyone was a little outside, he could not see them. So the ark has been there until the present day.
reason: ante oraculum = 'before the oracle', matching the edition's rendering of oraculum (cf. 1 Kgs 8:8).

old: The Vulgate reads "when the Lord gave the law" (legem dedit) where the Hebrew reads "when the LORD made a covenant."
new: The Vulgate reads "when the Lord gave the law" (legem dedit) where the Hebrew reads "when the Lord made a covenant."
reason: Notes must not use capital LORD; the edition uses 'the Lord'.

old: The Vulgate expands the musical account with "voice," "instruments, and various kinds of music," and "the sound was heard far away," and in 5:14 shifts from "cloud" (nube) to "thick darkness" (caliginem).
new: The Vulgate reads nube ("cloud") here but caliginem ("thick darkness") in 5:14, where the Hebrew has "cloud" in both verses.
reason: The note's claim that the Vulgate 'expands' the account with 'voice' and 'instruments' is inaccurate (the Hebrew also has voice/sound and instruments of music); kept only the accurate cloud/thick darkness comparison.

old: For indeed Solomon had made a bronze platform and had placed it in the middle of the basilica, measuring five cubits in length, five cubits in width, and three cubits in height; and he stood upon it, and then, with bent knees facing the entire multitude of Israel and with palms raised toward heaven,
new: For indeed Solomon had made a bronze platform and had placed it in the middle of the hall, measuring five cubits in length, five cubits in width, and three cubits in height; and he stood upon it, and then, with bent knees facing the entire multitude of Israel and with palms raised toward heaven,
reason: basilica is rendered 'hall' at 2 Chr 4:9 (basilicam grandem ... in basilica) and Esth 5:1; 'basilica' is an anachronistic loanword for the same Latin term.

old: And the priests were standing in their duties, and the Levites at the instruments of the songs of the Lord, which King David made to praise the Lord, "For His mercy is eternal," singing the hymns of David by their hands; moreover, the priests were sounding trumpets before them, and all Israel was standing.
new: And the priests were standing in their duties, and the Levites at the instruments of the songs of the Lord, which King David made to praise the Lord, "For His mercy is forever," singing the hymns of David by their hands; moreover, the priests were sounding trumpets before them, and all Israel was standing.
reason: Quoniam in aeternum misericordia ejus is rendered 'His mercy is forever' elsewhere (5:13, 7:3 and throughout the edition).

old: In the Clementine Vulgate, chapter 14 begins at verse 2 of the Hebrew and modern English numbering (since Hebrew 14:1 stands at Vulgate 13:23). The Vulgate also reads 'his God' (Dei sui) and 'altars of foreign worship' (altaria peregrini cultus).
new: The Vulgate reads 'in the sight of his God' (in conspectu Dei sui) where the Hebrew has 'the Lord his God,' and 'altars of foreign worship' (altaria peregrini cultus).
reason: The claim that chapter 14 begins at Hebrew 14:2 is false: the Hebrew, like the Vulgate, places 'Abijah slept...' at 13:23 and begins chapter 14 with this verse; removed the numbering claim and made the remaining comparison explicit.

old: Vulgate reads "some of the Ammonites" (de Ammonitis), reflecting the consonantal Hebrew text; many modern translations emend this to "Meunites" based on the Septuagint.
new: Vulgate reads "some of the Ammonites" (de Ammonitis), as does the Hebrew Masoretic Text, where the Septuagint reads "Meunites."
reason: Removed the claim about what 'many modern translations' do; kept a neutral comparison with the Hebrew and Greek.

old: Then Eliezer son of Dodavahu, from Mareshah, prophesied to Jehoshaphat, saying, "Because you have had an alliance with Ahaziah, the Lord has struck your works." And the ships were shattered, and they could not go to Tarshish.
new: Then Eliezer son of Dodavahu, from Mareshah, prophesied to Jehoshaphat, saying, "Because you have had a covenant with Ahaziah, the Lord has struck your works." And the ships were shattered, and they could not go to Tarshish.
reason: fœdus is rendered "covenant" in this edition, including political treaties (2 Chr 16:3).

old: Vulgate preserves "forty-two" (quadraginta duorum) in agreement with the Hebrew Masoretic Text here, in contrast to "twenty-two" in 2 Kings 8:26 and the Septuagint.
new: Vulgate preserves "forty-two" (quadraginta duorum) in agreement with the Hebrew Masoretic Text here, in contrast to "twenty-two" in 2 Kings 8:26.
reason: The main Septuagint text of 2 Chr 22:2 reads "twenty," not "twenty-two"; the claim about the Septuagint is inaccurate.

old: So the whole multitude entered into a pact in the house of God with the king, and Jehoiada said to them, "Look, the son of the king will reign, just as the Lord spoke concerning the sons of David.
new: So the whole multitude entered into a covenant in the house of God with the king, and Jehoiada said to them, "Look, the son of the king will reign, just as the Lord spoke concerning the sons of David.
reason: pactum is rendered "covenant" in this edition (cf. fœdus "covenant" in 23:1 and 23:16 of the same episode).

old: The Vulgate translates the difficult Hebrew clause as a clear conditional statement ("if you think that wars depend on the strength of an army"), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew is usually rendered "if you go, act, be strong for battle."
new: The Vulgate translates the difficult Hebrew clause as a clear conditional statement ("if you think that wars depend on the strength of an army"), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "if you go, act, be strong for battle."
reason: Notes should state what the Hebrew reads, not how it is usually rendered by translations.

old: Latin intelligentis et videntis Deum literally reads "who understood and saw God," where the Masoretic Hebrew is commonly rendered "who instructed him in the fear of God" (or "in visions of God").
new: Latin intelligentis et videntis Deum literally reads "who understood and saw God," where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "who had understanding in the visions of God."
reason: Removes a claim about common translations; the Masoretic Text (bir'ot) reads "visions/seeing of God," while "fear of God" is a variant reading, not the MT.

old: The Clementine Vulgate moves directly from 27:7 to 27:9, omitting the duplicate summary of Jotham's age and length of reign numbered 27:8 in the Masoretic Hebrew (already stated in 27:1).
reason: False for the critical text: the Latin does contain 27:8 (Viginti quinque annorum erat cum regnare cœpisset...), supplied as an additional verse.

old: "Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, declares these things: In what are you placing confidence as you sit besieged in Jerusalem?
new: "This is what Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, says: In what are you placing confidence as you sit besieged in Jerusalem?
reason: Hæc dicit X is rendered "This is what X says" in this edition (cf. Hæc dicit Cyrus in 36:23).

old: The Vulgate spells Isaiah's father's name as 'Amos' (identical to the prophet Amos), whereas standard English distinguishes him as Amoz following the Hebrew.
new: The Vulgate spells Isaiah's father's name as 'Amos' (identical to the prophet Amos), whereas the Hebrew distinguishes Amoz from Amos.
reason: Replaces a claim about English usage with the factual Hebrew distinction (Amotz vs. Amos).

old: After he was brought into dire distress, he prayed to the Lord his God and did deep penance before the God of his fathers.
new: After he was brought into dire distress, he prayed to the Lord his God and repented greatly before the God of his fathers.
reason: pœnitentiam agere is rendered "repent" in this edition; "did penance" imports technical vocabulary, and valde is "greatly".

old: Vulgate 'egit pœnitentiam' ("did penance," repeated in 33:19) renders the Hebrew verb meaning "humbled himself."
new: Vulgate 'egit pœnitentiam' ("repented," repeated in 33:19) renders the Hebrew verb meaning "humbled himself."
reason: Note aligned with the verse change: pœnitentiam agere = "repent".

old: Furthermore, he restored the altar of the Lord and sacrificed upon it victims, peace offerings, and praise; and he commanded Judah to serve the Lord, the God of Israel.
new: Furthermore, he restored the altar of the Lord and sacrificed upon it victims, peace offerings, and praise; and he commanded Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel.
reason: Domino Deo Israël is rendered "the Lord God of Israel" throughout this edition.

old: Now the rest of the deeds of Manasseh, and his supplication to his God, and also the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, are contained in the records of the kings of Israel.
new: Now the rest of the deeds of Manasseh, and his supplication to his God, and also the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the Lord God of Israel, are contained in the records of the kings of Israel.
reason: Domini Dei Israël is rendered "the Lord God of Israel" throughout this edition.

old: His prayer as well and its favorable hearing, and all his sins and acts of contempt, and also the sites where he built high places and made sacred groves and statues before he did penance, are written in the records of Hozai.
new: His prayer as well and its favorable hearing, and all his sins and acts of contempt, and also the sites where he built high places and made sacred groves and statues before he repented, are written in the records of Hozai.
reason: antequam ageret pœnitentiam: pœnitentiam agere is rendered "repent" in this edition.

old: The Vulgate reads Cariathiarim ("Kiriath-jearim", matching Nehemiah 7:29), whereas the Hebrew Ketiv in Ezra 2:25 reads the shorter form Kiriath-arim.
new: The Vulgate reads Cariathiarim ("Kiriath-jearim", matching Nehemiah 7:29), whereas the Hebrew text of Ezra 2:25 reads the shorter form Kiriath-arim.
reason: The Hebrew of Ezra 2:25 simply reads Kiriath-arim; it is not a Ketiv/Qere case, so 'Ketiv' is inaccurate.

old: And these are the ones who went up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer; and they could not declare the house of their fathers and their lineage, whether they were from Israel.
new: And these are the ones who went up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer; and they could not declare the house of their fathers and their seed, whether they were from Israel.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And Joshua and his sons and his brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, and the sons of Judah stood as one man to oversee those who were doing the work in the temple of God: the sons of Henadad, and their sons, and their brothers the Levites.
new: And Joshua and his sons and his brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, and the sons of Judah stood as one man to urge on those who were doing the work in the temple of God: the sons of Henadad, and their sons, and their brothers the Levites.
reason: ut instarent super eos = 'to press upon / urge on' them (cf. ut urgerent opus in 3:8); 'to oversee' follows the Hebrew lenatseach rather than the Latin.

old: Retaining the first-person plural respondimus ("we answered"), the Vulgate presents this verse as the Jews' reply giving the builders' names, whereas many modern versions emend the Aramaic to third person ("they asked") following the Septuagint.
new: Retaining the first-person plural respondimus ("we answered") of the Aramaic, the Vulgate presents this verse as the Jews' reply giving the builders' names, whereas the Septuagint has the third person ("they said").
reason: Notes must not make claims about what modern versions do; restated as a neutral comparison of the Latin with the Aramaic and Greek.

old: Now on the fourth day, the silver, and the gold, and the vessels were weighed out in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites,
new: Now on the fourth day, the silver, and the gold, and the vessels were weighed out in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were Jozabad the son of Joshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites,
reason: Latin Josue is rendered "Joshua" throughout this edition of Ezra-Nehemiah (Ezra 2:2, 2:40, 3:2, 3:9; Neh 7:7, 7:43, with notes at Ezra 2:2 and 3:2); "Jeshua" follows the Hebrew form instead.

old: And now make confession to the Lord, the God of your fathers, and do His pleasure, and separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign wives."
new: And now make confession to the Lord God of your fathers, and do His pleasure, and separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign wives."
reason: Domino Deo patrum vestrorum = "the Lord God of your fathers" (cf. 7:27, 8:28); the appositional "the Lord, the God of" follows the Hebrew phrasing.

old: And among the sons of the priests there were found those who had married foreign wives. Of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah.
new: And among the sons of the priests there were found those who had married foreign wives. Of the sons of Joshua the son of Jozadak, and his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah.
reason: Josue filii Josedec is the same high priest rendered "Joshua son of Jozadak" at 3:2, 3:8 and 5:2 (with a note on Josue = Joshua); "Jeshua" follows the Hebrew.

old: And of the sons of Harim: Eliezer, Jeshua, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Simeon,
new: And of the sons of Harim: Eliezer, Joshua, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Simeon,
reason: Latin Josue is rendered "Joshua" elsewhere in this edition of Ezra-Nehemiah.

old: The Vulgate reads Josue ("Jeshua," matching 10:18 and the Septuagint), whereas the Hebrew text reads "Isshijah."
new: The Vulgate reads Josue ("Joshua," as in 10:18), whereas the Hebrew text reads "Isshijah."
reason: Updated to match the verse's rendering of Josue; the unverified claim about the Septuagint (which appears to have a form of Isshijah) is dropped.

old: "They left Jerusalem as far as the wall of the broader street" translates the Vulgate's dimiserunt ... murum plateae latioris, whereas many modern translations of the Hebrew render "they restored Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall."
new: "They left Jerusalem as far as the wall of the broader street" translates the Vulgate's dimiserunt ... murum plateae latioris, whereas the Hebrew is often understood as "they restored Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall."
reason: Notes must not make claims about what modern translations do; restated as a neutral comparison with the Hebrew.

old: and next to him Ezer son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, built a second measure, opposite the ascent of the strongest corner.
new: and next to him Ezer son of Joshua, ruler of Mizpah, built a second measure, opposite the ascent of the strongest corner.
reason: Latin Josue is rendered "Joshua" elsewhere in this edition of Ezra-Nehemiah (e.g. Neh 7:7, 7:39, 7:43); "Jeshua" follows the Hebrew form.

old: In 3:34-36 (numbered 4:2-4 in Hebrew and most English Bibles), the Vulgate preserves several distinctive readings: "Will the nations let them alone?" (Hebrew "Will they restore it for themselves?"), "build the stones" (Hebrew "revive the stones"), "it will leap over" (transiliet in 3:35, Hebrew "break down"), and "to contempt" (in despectionem in 3:36, Hebrew "to plunder").
new: In 3:34-36 the Vulgate preserves several distinctive readings: "Will the nations let them alone?" (Hebrew "Will they restore it for themselves?"), "build the stones" (Hebrew "revive the stones"), "it will leap over" (transiliet in 3:35, Hebrew "break down"), and "to contempt" (in despectionem in 3:36, Hebrew "to plunder").
reason: The parenthesis is false for the Hebrew, which also numbers these verses 3:34-36, and it is a claim about English Bibles; removed.

old: Now these are the ones who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, and they could not show the house of their fathers and their lineage, whether they were from Israel:
new: Now these are the ones who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, and they could not show the house of their fathers and their seed, whether they were from Israel:
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: You Yourself are the Lord God, who chose Abram, and brought him out from the fire of the Chaldeans, and gave him the name Abraham;
new: It is You Yourself, Lord God, who chose Abram, and brought him out from the fire of the Chaldeans, and gave him the name Abraham;
reason: Domine Deus is vocative (as Domine in 9:6: 'Tu ipse, Domine'), not a predicate; 'You Yourself are the Lord God' follows the Hebrew.

old: In the Vulgate, chapter 10 begins one verse earlier than in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (where this verse is 9:38), shifting all subsequent verse numbers in the chapter by one. Latin foedus renders Hebrew amanah ('binding agreement') with the standard covenant term.
new: As in the Hebrew, chapter 10 begins with this verse. Latin foedus renders Hebrew amanah ('binding agreement') with the standard covenant term.
reason: The note's claim that the Vulgate begins chapter 10 one verse earlier than the Hebrew is false: the Hebrew Masoretic Text also numbers this verse 10:1.

old: all who were able to understand, pledged on behalf of their brothers, their nobles, and came to promise and to swear that they would walk in the law of God, which He had given by the hand of Moses the servant of God, that they would do and keep all the commandments of the Lord our God, and His judgments and His ceremonies,
new: all who were able to understand, pledging on behalf of their brothers, their nobles, and those who came to promise and to swear that they would walk in the law of God, which He had given by the hand of Moses the servant of God, that they would do and keep all the commandments of the Lord our God, and His judgments and His ceremonies,
reason: spondentes is a participle ('pledging') and 'et qui veniebant' is a further listed group ('and those who came'), not finite verbs of the same subject.

old: The Vulgate reads 'for praising and for giving thanks' (ad laudandum et ad confitendum), reflecting tehillah ('praise') where the Masoretic Text vocalizes techillah ('beginning').
new: The Vulgate reads 'for praising and for giving thanks' (ad laudandum et ad confitendum), reflecting tehillah ('praise') where the Masoretic Text has techillah ('beginning').
reason: tehillah and techillah differ by a consonant (he vs. heth), not merely by vocalization.

old: and what they endured, and what was afterward changed, the Jews took upon themselves and their offspring, and upon all who wished to be joined to their religion, so that no one is permitted to pass these two days without solemn observance, which the writing attests and fixed times require, as the years continually succeed one another.
new: and what they endured, and what was afterward changed, the Jews took upon themselves and their seed, and upon all who wished to be joined to their religion, so that no one is permitted to pass these two days without solemn observance, which the writing attests and fixed times require, as the years continually succeed one another.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: observing the days of lots, and that they should celebrate them in their proper time with joy, just as Mordecai and Esther had appointed; and they accepted to be observed by themselves and by their offspring the fasts, and the cries, and the days of lots,
new: observing the days of lots, and that they should celebrate them in their proper time with joy, just as Mordecai and Esther had appointed; and they accepted to be observed by themselves and by their seed the fasts, and the cries, and the days of lots,
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: The Vulgate adds "entire" (omnem) and "all" (cunctas) and renders "islands of the sea" (maris insulas) with "made ... subject to tribute" (fecit tributarias), where the Hebrew MT has "laid a tribute on the land and the coastlands of the sea."
new: The Vulgate adds "entire" (omnem) and "all" (cunctas) and reads "made ... subject to tribute" (fecit tributarias), where the Hebrew MT has "laid a tribute on the land and the coastlands of the sea."
reason: The note garbles the comparison, saying maris insulas ('islands of the sea') is rendered with 'made ... subject to tribute'.

old: and how Mordecai, of Jewish descent, was second to King Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews, and pleasing to the populace of his brothers, seeking good things for his people and speaking the things that pertained to the peace of his offspring. And Mordecai said, "These things have been done by God. I remembered the dream that I had seen, which signified these same things, and not one of them was in vain. The little spring, which grew into a river, and was turned into light and the sun, and overflowed into abundant waters, is Esther, whom the king took as a wife and willed to be queen. Now the two dragons are I and Haman. The nations that had assembled are those who attempted to blot out the name of the Jews. But my nation is Israel, which cried out to the Lord, and the Lord saved His people; and He freed us from all evils and performed great signs and wonders among the nations; and He commanded that there be two lots, one for the people of God, and the other for all the nations. And these days will be observed in the month of Adar on the fourteenth and fifteenth day of the same month, with all eagerness and joy, in one assembly of the gathered people, for all succeeding generations of the people of Israel."
