old: And he gathered power and an exceedingly strong army, and his heart was exalted and lifted up.
new: And he gathered a force and an exceedingly strong army, and his heart was exalted and lifted up.
reason: congregavit virtutem uses virtus in its concrete military sense, rendered "force" elsewhere in this book (3:10, 3:40, 4:3, 6:6); "gathered power" is abstract.

old: And the inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them, and she became a dwelling of strangers, and she became a stranger to her own offspring, and her children abandoned her.
new: And the inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them, and she became a dwelling of strangers, and she became a stranger to her own seed, and her children abandoned her.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin directa est (lit. "was directed" or "was guided straight") is a biblical Latin idiom expressing divinely guided success or prosperity.
new: Latin directa est (lit. "was directed" or "was guided straight") is an idiom expressing success or prosperity.
reason: "divinely guided" adds a theological interpretation that the Latin directa est salus in manu ejus does not state.

old: The Vulgate reads plural "Leave no man behind" (Neminem hominem reliqueritis), whereas the Greek reads singular "Do not allow any man to encamp."
new: The Vulgate reads "Leave no man behind" (Neminem hominem reliqueritis), whereas the Greek reads "Do not allow any man to encamp."
reason: The Greek verb (aphete) is also second person plural, so the plural/singular contrast in the note is inaccurate.

old: and the men of the force encamped, and he assaulted that city all day and all night, and the city was delivered into his hand;
new: and the men of valor encamped, and he assaulted that city all day and all night, and the city was delivered into his hand;
reason: viri virtutis is the idiom "men of valor/strength", rendered "men of valor" at 6:37; "men of the force" misreads it.

old: However, they themselves were not of the offspring of those men through whom deliverance came about in Israel.
new: However, they themselves were not of the seed of those men through whom deliverance came about in Israel.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: so crush this army in our sight today, and let the rest know that he has spoken evil against Your sanctuary, and judge him according to his wickedness."
new: so crush this army in our sight today, and let the rest know that he has spoken evil against Your holy places, and judge him according to his wickedness."
reason: sancta tua is neuter plural, rendered "Your holy places" in 3:51 and throughout this book; "sanctuary" is reserved for sanctificatio/sanctuarium.

old: And Jonathan sent his brother, the leader of the people, and asked the Nabateans, his friends, that they might entrust to them their equipment, which was abundant.
new: And Jonathan sent his brother, the leader of the people, and asked the Nabateans, his friends, that they might lend them their equipment, which was abundant.
reason: commodarent illis is "lend them"; "entrust" bends the Latin toward the Greek (depositing baggage), and as written it even reverses the note's own sense.

old: Latin commodarent (literally "lend") here carries the late-Latin sense of "entrust" or "deposit for safekeeping," meaning Jonathan's party asked to leave their abundant equipment (apparatum) with the Nabateans.
new: Latin commodarent means "lend"; the Greek has Jonathan's party asking to leave its abundant baggage with the Nabateans.
reason: The claimed late-Latin sense "entrust/deposit" is an unsupported harmonization with the Greek; replaced with a neutral factual comparison.

old: Because you have kept the pact with us, and have remained in our friendship, and have not gone over to our enemies, we have heard and have rejoiced.
new: Because you have kept the covenant with us, and have remained in our friendship, and have not gone over to our enemies, we have heard and have rejoiced.
reason: servastis ad nos pactum: pactum is rendered "covenant" edition-wide.

old: And he sent envoys to Demetrius, saying, "Come, let us make a pact between us, and I will give you my daughter, whom Alexander has, and you will reign in your father's kingdom;
new: And he sent envoys to Demetrius, saying, "Come, let us make a covenant between us, and I will give you my daughter, whom Alexander has, and you will reign in your father's kingdom;
reason: componamus inter nos pactum: pactum is rendered "covenant" edition-wide.

old: And Demetrius began to reign in the one hundred sixty-seventh year.
new: And Demetrius began to reign in the one hundred and sixty-seventh year.
reason: anno centesimo ... is rendered "the one hundred and ...th year" throughout this book (9:3, 10:1, 10:57, 10:67, 13:41).

old: "King Demetrius to his brother Jonathan, greeting, and to the nation of the Jews.
new: "King Demetrius to his brother Jonathan, greetings, and to the nation of the Jews.
reason: salutem in letter openings is "greetings" everywhere else in this book (10:18, 10:25, 12:6, 13:36, 15:2, 15:16).

old: 'King Demetrius to his father Lasthenes, greeting.
new: 'King Demetrius to his father Lasthenes, greetings.
reason: salutem in letter openings is "greetings" elsewhere in this book.

old: And those who were of the city assembled, one hundred twenty thousand men, and they wanted to kill the king.
new: And those who were of the city assembled, one hundred and twenty thousand men, and they wanted to kill the king.
reason: centum viginti millia is "one hundred and twenty thousand" in 15:13; same number style.

old: And the young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan, saying, "I confirm to you the priesthood, and I appoint you over the four cities, so that you may be among the friends of the king."
new: And the young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan, saying, "I establish for you the priesthood, and I appoint you over the four cities, so that you may be among the friends of the king."
reason: Constituo tibi sacerdotium is "I establish for you the priesthood" (cf. 11:27 statuit ei ... "established for him"); "confirm" follows familiar English renderings of the Greek.

old: But Jonathan and those who were with him did not know until morning, for they saw the lights burning.
new: But Jonathan and those who were with him did not know until morning, and they saw the lights burning.
reason: videbant autem is connective, not causal; "for" imports the Greek gar instead of the Latin autem.

old: And they gathered together to build the city; and the wall that was above the brook on the east collapsed, and he repaired the one that is called Caphetetha.
new: And they gathered together to build the city; and the wall that was above the brook on the east collapsed, and he repaired it, the one that is called Caphetetha.
reason: reparavit eum, qui vocatur Caphetetha: eum ("it", the fallen wall) was omitted, making the repaired wall seem a different one as in the Greek.

old: Therefore I will vindicate my nation and the holy places, and our children and wives as well, because all the nations have gathered together to crush us out of hostility."
new: Therefore I will avenge my nation and the holy places, and our children and wives as well, because all the nations have gathered together to crush us out of hostility."
reason: Vindicabo here is "I will avenge" (as vindicare is rendered in 9:26, 9:42); modern "vindicate" means to clear of blame, the wrong sense.

old: In the one hundred seventy-second year, King Demetrius gathered his army and departed into Media to assemble auxiliary forces for himself, so that he might defeat Trypho.
new: In the one hundred and seventy-second year, King Demetrius gathered his army and departed into Media to assemble auxiliary forces for himself, so that he might defeat Trypho.
reason: anno centesimo ... is rendered "the one hundred and ...th year" throughout this book (13:41, 13:51, 15:10).

old: And this is the copy of the writing: "On the eighteenth day of the month of Elul, in the one hundred seventy-second year, in the third year under Simon the great priest in Asaramel,
new: And this is the copy of the writing: "On the eighteenth day of the month of Elul, in the one hundred and seventy-second year, in the third year under Simon the great priest in Asaramel,
reason: anno centesimo septuagesimo secundo: same year formula as elsewhere, "the one hundred and ...th year".

old: And King Demetrius confirmed the high priesthood for him.
new: And King Demetrius established the high priesthood for him.
reason: statuit illi summum sacerdotium is "established ... for him" (cf. 11:27 statuit ei principatum sacerdotii, "established for him"); "confirmed" follows familiar English renderings of the Greek.

old: and they contained this wording: "King Antiochus to Simon the high priest and to the nation of the Jews, greetings.
new: and they contained this wording: "King Antiochus to Simon the great priest and to the nation of the Jews, greetings.
reason: Simoni sacerdoti magno is "the great priest" as in 12:20, 14:20, 14:23, 14:27; "high priest" is reserved for summus sacerdos.

old: Since indeed wicked men have taken possession of the kingdom of our fathers, I intend to reclaim the kingdom and restore it as it was before; and I have formed a chosen multitude of an army, and I have built warships.
new: Since indeed pestilent men have taken possession of the kingdom of our fathers, I intend to reclaim the kingdom and restore it as it was before; and I have formed a chosen multitude of an army, and I have built warships.
reason: pestilentes is "pestilent men" in 10:61; "wicked men" is this edition's rendering of iniqui.

old: Now therefore I confirm to you all the offerings which all the kings before me remitted to you, and whatever other gifts they remitted to you;
new: Now therefore I establish for you all the offerings which all the kings before me remitted to you, and whatever other gifts they remitted to you;
reason: statuo tibi is "I establish for you" (as statuere/constituere in 11:27, 11:57, 14:38); "confirm" follows familiar English renderings of the Greek.

old: Envoys of the Jews, our friends, have come to us, renewing the former friendship and alliance, sent by Simon the high priest and the people of the Jews.
new: Envoys of the Jews, our friends, have come to us, renewing the former friendship and alliance, sent by Simon the chief priest and the people of the Jews.
reason: Simone principe sacerdotum is "chief priest" (as principem sacerdotum in 14:35), not summus sacerdos "high priest"; "high priest" follows the Greek archiereus.

old: If therefore any wicked men have fled from their country to you, hand them over to Simon the high priest, so that he may punish them according to his law."
new: If therefore any pestilent men have fled from their country to you, hand them over to Simon the chief priest, so that he may punish them according to his law."
reason: pestilentes is "pestilent men" (10:61) and Simoni principi sacerdotum is "chief priest" (14:35), not summus sacerdos.

old: And they wrote a copy of them to Simon the high priest and to the people of the Jews.
new: And they wrote a copy of them to Simon the chief priest and to the people of the Jews.
reason: Simoni principi sacerdotum is "chief priest" (as in 14:35), distinct from summus sacerdos "high priest".

old: and grant to all of you a heart to worship Him and carry out His will with a generous heart and a willing spirit.
new: and grant to all of you a heart to worship Him and carry out His will with a great heart and a willing spirit.
reason: corde magno is literally "with a great heart"; "generous" narrows the sense interpretively.

old: The Vulgate identifies Simon as from 'the tribe of Benjamin' (de tribu Benjamin) and states that he strove 'to contrive something unjust in the city' (iniquum aliquid in civitate moliri), whereas the Greek Septuagint assigns him to the priestly clan of Bilgah and describes a dispute over the supervision of the city market.
new: The Vulgate states that Simon strove 'to contrive something unjust in the city' (iniquum aliquid in civitate moliri), whereas the Greek describes a dispute with the high priest over the administration of the city market.
reason: The Greek manuscripts also read 'of the tribe of Benjamin' (Bilgah comes from Old Latin/Armenian witnesses), so the contrast drawn on Simon's tribe is false; the accurate market-dispute comparison is kept.

old: The Vulgate reads 'Tharseas' (Tharsææ), a distinct spelling corresponding to 'Thraseas' in the Greek Septuagint.
new: The Latin reads Tharsææ ('of Tharseas'), matching the Greek manuscripts' Tharseou; some modern editions of the Greek emend the name to 'Thraseas.'
reason: The Greek manuscripts read Tharseou, not Thraseas (an editorial emendation), so the note's comparison was inaccurate.

old: but you, wait patiently, and you will see His great power, how He will torture you and your offspring."
new: but you, wait patiently, and you will see His great power, how He will torture you and your seed."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And while they were holding victory celebrations in Jerusalem, they burned the one who had burned the sacred gates, that is, Callisthenes, when he had fled into a small house, a fitting reward having been repaid to him for his ungodly deeds.
new: And while they were holding victory celebrations in Jerusalem, they burned the one who had burned the sacred gates, that is, Callisthenes, when he had fled into a certain dwelling, a fitting reward having been repaid to him for his ungodly deeds.
reason: Latin quoddam domicilium is "a certain dwelling"; "small house" follows the Greek oikidion, not the Latin.

old: The Clementine Vulgate prints Ora (an orthographic variant for Oro, "I implore"), pairing in the first-person singular with et peto ("and ask") and taking the accusative vos ("you").
new: The Latin prints Ora (imperative in form), evidently for Oro ("I implore"), as the parallel first-person et peto ("and ask") and the accusative vos ("you") require.
reason: Ora is not an orthographic variant of Oro but a different (imperative) form; the note's description of the Latin was inaccurate.

old: And because he was not senseless, considering within himself the loss that had happened to him, and understanding that the Hebrews were invincible, relying on the help of almighty God, he sent to them,
new: And because he was not senseless, considering within himself the loss that had happened to him, and understanding that the Hebrews were invincible, relying on the help of Almighty God, he sent to them,
reason: omnipotentis Dei is rendered "Almighty God" elsewhere in this book (3:22, 3:24, 5:20, 7:35); established rendering of omnipotens is "Almighty".

old: and so, turning to prayer, they asked that the offense that had been committed be given over to oblivion. And the most valiant Judas urged the people to keep themselves without sin, seeing before their eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who were struck down.
new: and so, turning to prayer, they asked that the offense that had been committed be given over to oblivion. But the most valiant Judas urged the people to keep themselves without sin, seeing before their eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who were struck down.
reason: At vero is adversative ("but"), not a simple "and".

old: since indeed they feared being deprived of the law, their homeland, and the holy temple, and that He would not allow the people, who had recently caught their breath a little, to be subjected again to blasphemous nations.
new: since indeed they feared being deprived of the law, their homeland, and the holy temple; and so that He would not allow the people, who had recently caught their breath a little, to be subjected again to blasphemous nations.
reason: ac ... ne sineret continues the purpose clause of v. 10 (quo ... adjuvaret), not the object of vererentur; "feared ... and that He would not allow" makes them fear the opposite of what they prayed for.

old: But when he came to Ptolemais, the people of Ptolemais took the agreement of friendship badly, being indignant, for fear that perhaps they might violate the treaty.
new: But when he came to Ptolemais, the people of Ptolemais took the agreement of friendship badly, being indignant, for fear that perhaps they might violate the covenant.
reason: ne forte fœdus irrumperent: fœdus is rendered "covenant" edition-wide.

old: The Vulgate clause indignantes ne forte foedus irrumperent ('being indignant, for fear that perhaps they might violate the treaty') diverges in syntax from the Greek, which states that they were angry at the stipulations and wanted to annul the agreements.
new: The Vulgate clause indignantes ne forte foedus irrumperent ('being indignant, for fear that perhaps they might violate the covenant') diverges in syntax from the Greek, which states that they were angry at the stipulations and wanted to annul the agreements.
reason: Note quotation updated to match the verse (fœdus = "covenant").

old: Therefore, when a shout was raised and a commotion was stirred up, they blessed the almighty Lord in their native tongue.
new: Therefore, when a shout was raised and a commotion was stirred up, they blessed the Almighty Lord in their native tongue.
reason: omnipotens is rendered "Almighty" (capitalized) in this edition, as in 15:8 and throughout 2 Maccabees ("the Almighty Lord", "Almighty God").

old: And after showing the head of Nicanor, and the wicked hand which he had stretched out against the holy house of almighty God as he boasted grandly,
new: And after showing the head of Nicanor, and the wicked hand which he had stretched out against the holy house of Almighty God as he boasted grandly,
reason: omnipotentis Dei is rendered "Almighty God" (capitalized) elsewhere in the edition.

old: In the Clementine Vulgate, this verse consists of an ablative absolute (ostenso capite...) and a relative clause without its own finite verb (unlike the Greek main verb "he displayed"), so it is linked grammatically to the main verb "ordered" in verse 33.
new: The Latin verse has no main verb of its own: ostenso capite... is an ablative absolute and gloriatus est belongs to the relative clause, so the sentence continues with jussit ("ordered") in verse 33.
reason: The relative clause does have a finite verb (gloriatus est), and the Greek also uses a participle here, not a main verb "he displayed"; both claims were false.

old: The Vulgate reads literally "all the heavens blessed the Lord" (Omnes igitur cæli), whereas the Greek has "all [the people], looking toward heaven, blessed the manifest Lord."
new: Omnes igitur cæli can be construed "all the heavens" (as here) or, taking cæli as genitive with Dominum, "all blessed the Lord of heaven"; the Greek has "all [the people], looking toward heaven, blessed the manifest Lord."
reason: The Latin is grammatically ambiguous (cæli nominative plural with omnes, or genitive with Dominum); the note should not present one construal as the only literal reading.

old: The Clementine Vulgate ends this verse after "without celebration," omitting the Greek specification of the date (the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, the day before Mordecai's day).
new: The Latin text here ends the sentence after "without celebration" and has no equivalent of the Greek specification of the date (the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, the day before Mordecai's day).
reason: The printed Clementine Vulgate does carry the date clause (habere autem celebritatem tertiadecima die mensis Adar...); the note should describe the critical text as given, not attribute the omission to the Clementine.

old: The Vulgate translates a rare Hebrew word for a faint whisper as "venas susurri ejus" ("the veins of its whisper"), an image Jerome uses again in Job 26:14.
new: The Vulgate translates a rare Hebrew word for a faint whisper as "venas susurri ejus" ("the veins of its whisper").
reason: False cross-reference: Job 26:14 in this Latin reads parvam stillam ("a small drop"), not venas susurri.

old: The Vulgate renders the difficult Hebrew phrase (often translated "egg white" or "juice of the purslane") as quod gustatum affert mortem ("what, once tasted, brings death").
new: The Vulgate renders the difficult Hebrew phrase (possibly "egg white" or "juice of the purslane") as quod gustatum affert mortem ("what, once tasted, brings death").
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: My flesh is clothed with decay and the filth of dust; my skin has dried up and contracted.
new: My flesh is clothed with decay, and with the filth of dust my skin has dried up and contracted.
reason: In the Latin sordibus pulveris goes with the second clause (et sordibus pulveris cutis mea aruit et contracta est); attaching it to "clothed" follows the Hebrew line division.

old: He is higher than heaven, and what will you do? Deeper than hell, and how will you come to know?
new: He is higher than heaven, and what will you do? Deeper than the underworld, and how will you come to know?
reason: infernus is rendered "the underworld" in this edition; "hell" imports a later theological sense.

old: The Vulgate concludes cum ipse dederit omnia in manus eorum ("although He Himself has given all things into their hands"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered "those who bring their god in their hand."
new: The Vulgate concludes cum ipse dederit omnia in manus eorum ("although He Himself has given all things into their hands"), whereas the Hebrew reads "those who bring their god in their hand."
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: Look, my eye has seen all these things, and my ear has heard, and I have understood each one.
new: "Look, my eye has seen all these things, and my ear has heard, and I have understood each one.
reason: Job's speech continues from ch. 12, but 12:25 closes the quotation; following the edition's practice at chapter breaks (e.g. 9:35/10:1), the quotation must reopen here to keep quotation marks balanced.

old: Vulgate "in inferno" literally means "in the lower realm" or "underworld" (traditionally rendered "hell"), denoting the abode of the dead.
new: Vulgate "in inferno" literally means "in the lower realm" or "underworld," denoting the abode of the dead.
reason: Note gloss aligned with the edition's rendering of infernus as "the underworld"; the "hell" gloss (a claim about traditional English renderings) is removed.

old: Verse 8:33 (present in the Hebrew text and some other Latin witnesses) is omitted in this Clementine Vulgate text, which moves directly from 8:32 to 8:34.

old: Hand in hand, an evil person will not be guiltless, but the offspring of the righteous will be saved.

old: The soul that blesses will be enriched, and the one who satisfies with drink will himself also be satisfied.

old: The Vulgate renders a difficult Hebrew clause as 'Qui negligit damnum propter amicum, justus est' ('Whoever disregards loss for the sake of a friend is righteous'), whereas many modern renderings of the Hebrew read 'The righteous is a guide to his neighbor.'
new: The Vulgate renders a difficult Hebrew clause as 'Qui negligit damnum propter amicum, justus est' ('Whoever disregards loss for the sake of a friend is righteous'), whereas the Hebrew is commonly understood as 'The righteous is a guide to his neighbor.'
reason: Notes should not make claims about what (modern) translations do; restated as a neutral comparison with the Hebrew.

old: There is a way that appears right to a man, but its final ends lead down to death.
new: There is a way that appears just to a man, but its final ends lead down to death.
reason: The Latin here has justa ("just"), unlike recta ("right") at 16:25; the English should not level the two to the identical Hebrew wording.

old: Vulgate reads 'propter semetipsum' ('for His own sake'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly rendered 'for its own purpose.' This verse corresponds to 16:4 in the Hebrew text.
new: Vulgate reads 'propter semetipsum' ('for His own sake'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly understood as 'for its own purpose.' This verse corresponds to 16:4 in the Hebrew text.
reason: Avoid a claim about how translations render the Hebrew; state the comparison neutrally.

old: Following a distinct reading of the Hebrew, the Vulgate has "A needy person is merciful" (Homo indigens misericors est), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is generally translated "What is desired in a man is steadfast love."
new: Following a distinct reading of the Hebrew, the Vulgate has "A needy person is merciful" (Homo indigens misericors est), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is generally understood as "What is desired in a man is steadfast love."
reason: Avoid a claim about how translations render the Hebrew; state the comparison neutrally.

old: Latin gigantum ("giants") is the Vulgate's standard rendering of Hebrew rephaim, which Hebrew-based translations typically render as "the dead" or "shades."
new: Latin gigantum ("giants") renders Hebrew rephaim ("the dead" or "shades"), as also at 9:18.

old: The sacrifices of the wicked are detestable, because they are offered from wrongdoing.

old: There is no wisdom, there is no discernment, there is no plan against the Lord.
new: There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.
reason: prudentia and consilium are "prudence" and "counsel" throughout Proverbs in this edition (e.g. 8:14 consilium ... prudentia, 15:22 non est consilium).

old: The outcome of humility is the fear of the Lord, wealth, glory, and life.
new: The outcome of modesty is the fear of the Lord, wealth, glory, and life.
reason: The Latin has modestiæ ("modesty"), not humilitas (rendered "humility" at 11:2, 15:33); "humility" follows the Hebrew.

old: Latin tripliciter ("in a threefold way") is a famous Vulgate reading—contrasting with Masoretic Hebrew "thirty [sayings]" or "excellent things"—which early Christian interpreters often connected to the threefold sense of Scripture.
new: Latin tripliciter ("in a threefold way") is a distinctive Vulgate reading, contrasting with Masoretic Hebrew "thirty [sayings]" or "excellent things."
reason: Drops the evaluative "famous" and the comment on later Christian interpretation, which do not explain the Latin.

old: You will strike him with a rod, and you will rescue his soul from hell.
new: You will strike him with a rod, and you will rescue his soul from the underworld.
reason: de inferno: infernus is rendered "the underworld" in this edition (cf. 30:16); "hell" imports a later concept.

old: Verse 23:23 ("Buy truth and do not sell it...") is absent from the Clementine Vulgate text; numbering skips directly from 23:22 to 23:24.
reason: False: the critical text has 23:23 (Veritatem eme, et noli vendere sapientiam...), and the edition carries it as an additional verse after 23:22.

old: Vulgate detractoribus ("slanderers") translates a difficult Hebrew term commonly rendered "those who change" or "rebels," matching detractor ("slanderer") in 24:9.
new: Vulgate detractoribus ("slanderers") translates a difficult Hebrew term meaning "those who change" or "rebels," matching detractor ("slanderer") in 24:9.

new: The Vulgate reads in lectis argenteis ("on silver beds"), an interpretation of the Hebrew expression "in settings of silver."
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Hebrew.

old: and loses his cloak in the day of cold. Vinegar on soda: such is one who sings songs to a wicked heart. Just as a moth does to a garment and a worm to wood, so a man's sorrow harms the heart.
new: and loses his cloak in the day of cold. Vinegar on soda: such is one who sings songs to a very wicked heart. Just as a moth does to a garment and a worm to wood, so a man's sorrow harms the heart.

old: The Vulgate links "and loses his cloak in the day of cold" to v. 19, translates the Hebrew for a troubled heart literally as cordi pessimo ("a wicked heart"), and includes the final sentence on the moth, worm, and sorrow from the Septuagint.
new: The Vulgate links "and loses his cloak in the day of cold" to v. 19, renders the Hebrew for a troubled heart as cordi pessimo ("a very wicked heart"), and includes the final sentence on the moth, worm, and sorrow from the Septuagint.
reason: Align the note with the superlative pessimo in the verse; "literally" no longer fits a superlative rendering of the Hebrew.

old: Following the Hebrew ketiv ("to him") rather than the qere ("not"), the Vulgate omits any negation and reads in quempiam superveniet ("will come upon someone").
new: The Vulgate has no negation and reads in quempiam superveniet ("will come upon someone"), agreeing with the Hebrew qere ("to him") rather than the ketiv ("not").
reason: The note reverses the Hebrew forms: the written text (ketiv) is "not" and the marginal reading (qere) is "to him".

old: Where the Hebrew text is cryptic (commonly translated as an archer wounding passersby or one hiring a fool), the Vulgate preserves an entirely different proverb from the Old Latin tradition.
new: Where the Hebrew text is cryptic (commonly translated as an archer wounding passersby or one hiring a fool), the Vulgate has an entirely different proverb.
reason: The claim that the reading comes from the Old Latin is unsupported (it is Jerome's reading of the Hebrew); keep only the factual contrast.

old: Where the Hebrew text is cryptic (commonly translated as an archer wounding passersby or one hiring a fool), the Vulgate has an entirely different proverb.
new: Where the Hebrew text is cryptic (apparently of an archer wounding passersby or of one hiring a fool), the Vulgate has an entirely different proverb.

old: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads sub ascella sua ("under his armpit") where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in the dish."
new: The Vulgate reads sub ascella sua ("under his armpit") where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in the dish."

old: Just as if you wanted to adorn a clay vessel with impure silver, so are swelling lips allied with a wicked heart.
new: Just as if you wanted to adorn a clay vessel with impure silver, so are swelling lips allied with a very wicked heart.
reason: cum pessimo corde is superlative ("very wicked/worst"); plain "wicked" drops the degree (cf. 24:19 pessimis "most evil").

old: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads 'the hearts of people are evident to the prudent' (corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus), where the Hebrew reads 'the heart of man reflects man.'
new: The Vulgate reads 'the hearts of people are evident to the prudent' (corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus), where the Hebrew reads 'the heart of man reflects man.'

old: Hell and destruction are never filled; likewise, the eyes of people are also insatiable.
new: The underworld and destruction are never filled; likewise, the eyes of people are also insatiable.
reason: Infernus is rendered "the underworld" in this edition (cf. 30:16); "Hell" imports a later concept.

old: For a king who judges the poor in truth, his throne will be made firm forever.

old: The underworld, and the opening of the womb, and the earth that is not satisfied with water; and fire never says, 'It is enough.'
new: The underworld, and the opening of the womb, and the earth that is not satisfied with water; but fire never says, 'It is enough.'

old: The Vulgate reads "the childbirth of his mother" (partum matris suæ), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which is commonly rendered "obedience to a mother."
new: The Vulgate reads "the childbirth of his mother" (partum matris suæ), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "obedience to a mother."

old: Latin afflictio spiritus ("affliction of spirit") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of a Hebrew expression commonly translated "striving after wind."
new: Latin afflictio spiritus ("affliction of spirit") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew expression re'ut ruach ("striving after wind").

old: Distinctively in the Vulgate, Ecclesiastes resolves to withdraw his flesh from wine and avoid folly, whereas the Hebrew is usually translated as cheering his body with wine and laying hold on folly.
new: Distinctively in the Vulgate, Ecclesiastes resolves to withdraw his flesh from wine and avoid folly, whereas the Hebrew speaks of cheering his body with wine and laying hold on folly.

old: Latin scyphos, et urceos in ministerio ad vina fundenda ("cups and pitchers in service for pouring out wines") is Jerome's rendering of an obscure Hebrew phrase often translated "concubines" in modern versions.
new: Latin scyphos, et urceos in ministerio ad vina fundenda ("cups and pitchers in service for pouring out wines") is Jerome's rendering of an obscure Hebrew phrase often taken to mean "concubines."
reason: Notes should not make claims about what modern versions do; keep the factual point about the Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate's ut ego ("as I do") reflects the Hebrew reading mimmeni ("apart from me" or "more than I"), whereas some witnesses and modern versions read "apart from Him."
new: The Vulgate's ut ego ("as I do") reflects the Hebrew reading mimmeni ("apart from me" or "more than I"), whereas some witnesses read "apart from Him."

old: Latin mundum tradidit disputationi eorum ("handed the world over to their disputation") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew clause commonly translated "He has put eternity into their heart."
new: Latin mundum tradidit disputationi eorum ("handed the world over to their disputation") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew clause "He has put eternity into their heart."

old: Again I contemplated all the labors of people, and I noticed that endeavors are exposed to a neighbor's envy; therefore in this too there is futility and needless anxiety.

reason: cura superflua is rendered "superfluous care" at 2:26 (curam superfluam); same phrase, same sense.

old: In the Vulgate chapter division, 4:17 corresponds to 5:1 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (shifting the numbering of chapter 5 by one verse). The Vulgate also renders the clause with the explicit noun obedientia ("obedience").
new: This verse is 4:17 in both the Vulgate and the Hebrew Masoretic Text (5:1 in some other numberings). The Vulgate renders the clause with the explicit noun obedientia ("obedience").

old: Anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of face the spirit of the wrongdoer is corrected.
new: Anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of face the mind of the wrongdoer is corrected.
reason: animus delinquentis is "the mind" (as the note and elsewhere in the edition render animus); "spirit" suggests spiritus.

old: It is good for you to support the righteous man, and indeed do not withdraw your hand from him, because the one who fears God neglects nothing.
new: It is good for you to support the righteous man, but also do not withdraw your hand from him, because the one who fears God neglects nothing.
reason: sed et is "but also"; "and indeed" drops the adversative sed and adds an intensifier.

old: Also, do not direct your heart to all the words that are spoken, so that you do not happen to hear your servant cursing you,
new: But also, do not direct your heart to all the words that are spoken, so that you do not happen to hear your servant cursing you,
reason: Sed et: the adversative sed is not represented.

old: Vulgate reads utrum amore an odio dignus sit ("whether he is worthy of love or of hatred"), a distinctive reading prominent in Latin theology, where the Hebrew states that man does not know whether love or hatred awaits him.
new: Vulgate reads utrum amore an odio dignus sit ("whether he is worthy of love or of hatred"), where the Hebrew states that man does not know whether love or hatred awaits him.
reason: Remove commentary on the verse's theological reception; keep the factual Latin/Hebrew contrast.

old: Dying flies ruin the sweetness of ointment. More precious than wisdom and glory is a small and temporary folly.
new: Dying flies ruin the sweetness of ointment. Wisdom and glory are more precious than a small and temporary folly.
reason: In the Latin, sapientia et gloria is most naturally the subject of pretiosior est and parva et ad tempus stultitia the ablative of comparison (so Jerome and the Latin tradition read it); making folly the more precious imports the Hebrew sense.

old: Latin muscae morientes literally means "dying flies" (unlike Hebrew "dead flies"). In the second clause, following the Hebrew word order, sapientia et gloria acts as an ablative of comparison ("more precious than wisdom and glory is a small and temporary folly"), though the uninflected-looking feminine forms have sometimes been construed in reverse.
new: Latin muscae morientes literally means "dying flies" (unlike Hebrew "dead flies"). In the second sentence sapientia et gloria is taken as the subject and parva et ad tempus stultitia as the ablative of comparison; the Hebrew has the reverse sense ("a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor").
reason: Note updated to match the corrected verse; it had justified reading the Latin by the Hebrew word order.

old: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and deer of the fields, neither to rouse nor to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.
new: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roe deer and stags of the fields, neither to rouse nor to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.
reason: caprea is the roe deer and cervus the stag (so this edition at Song 4:5, 7:4, 8:14 and Deut 14:5); 'gazelle' renders the Hebrew tsebi, not the Latin.

old: My beloved is like a gazelle and a fawn of the deer. See, he himself stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, peering through the lattices.

old: My beloved belongs to me, and I to him, who grazes among the lilies,

old: until the day breathes and the shadows decline. Return; my beloved, be like a gazelle and a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bether.

old: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and deer of the fields, neither to rouse nor to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.

old: Latin lectulum ("bed") repeats the same noun used in 1:16 and 3:1, whereas modern translations from the Hebrew often render the term here as "litter."

old: My beloved is radiant and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.

old: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.

reason: The Latin repeats 2:6 word for word (Læva ejus sub capite meo...), which this edition renders 'beneath my head'.

old: Who is this who ascends from the desert, overflowing with delights, leaning on her beloved? Under the apple tree I roused you; there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated.

old: He: Her foes have been placed at the head; her enemies have grown wealthy, for the Lord has spoken against her because of the multitude of her iniquities. Her little ones have been led into captivity before the face of the oppressor.

old: Resh: See, Lord, and consider whom You have harvested in this way. Will women really eat their fruit, little ones the measure of a palm? Should priest and prophet be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?
new: Resh: See, Lord, and consider whom You have harvested in this way. Will women really eat their fruit, little ones the measure of a palm? Are priest and prophet killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?

old: Latin "Novi" is masculine plural referring back to the Lord's mercies and compassions in the preceding verse, and "diluculo" is singular ("at daybreak").

old: Vulgate "Nazirites" (Nazaraei) and "ancient ivory" (ebore antiquo) preserve distinctive renderings where the Hebrew is commonly translated "princes" (or "consecrated ones") and "corals" (or "rubies").
new: Vulgate "Nazirites" (Nazaraei) and "ancient ivory" (ebore antiquo) preserve distinctive renderings where the Hebrew has terms meaning "consecrated ones" (or "princes") and "corals" (or "rubies").

old: Vulgate "breath of our mouth" (Spiritus oris nostri), nominative "the anointed Lord" (christus Dominus, traditionally read as "Christ the Lord"), and "in our sins" (in peccatis nostris) follow the Septuagint and Patristic Christological tradition, whereas the Hebrew reads "breath of our nostrils," "the LORD's anointed," and "in their pits."

reason: Removes capital LORD and the 'Christological tradition' comment, and corrects the claim that 'mouth' and 'in our sins' follow the Septuagint (which has 'of our face' and 'in their corruptions').

old: For the endings of an unjust generation are dire.
new: For the endings of an unjust nation are dire.
reason: nationis is 'nation' (as nationes in 1:14); 'generation' follows the Greek geneas.

old: so we too, once born, immediately ceased to be; and indeed we were able to show no sign of virtue, but in our wickedness we were consumed." Such things those who sinned spoke in hell,

old: For there is in her a spirit of understanding, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, eloquent, mobile, undefiled, clear, sweet, loving the good, keen, which nothing hinders, doing good,
new: For there is in her a spirit of understanding, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, eloquent, mobile, undefiled, certain, sweet, loving the good, keen, which nothing hinders, doing good,

old: For she is a vapor of God's power, and a certain pure outflow of the splendor of almighty God; and therefore nothing defiled enters into her.
new: For she is a vapor of God's power, and a certain pure outflow of the splendor of Almighty God; and therefore nothing defiled enters into her.
reason: omnipotentis Dei: the edition renders omnipotens Deus as "Almighty God"

old: And since I was even more good, I came to an undefiled body.
new: And since I was more good, I came to an undefiled body.
reason: magis bonus is "more good"; "even" has no Latin basis (the note already gives the literal sense)

old: And when I knew that I could not otherwise be self-controlled unless God gives it, and that this very thing belonged to wisdom, to know whose gift this was, I approached the Lord and implored Him, and I spoke from my whole heart:
new: And when I knew that I could not otherwise be self-controlled unless God gives it—and this very thing belonged to wisdom, to know whose gift this was—I approached the Lord and implored Him, and I spoke from my whole heart:
reason: et hoc ipsum erat sapientiæ (indicative erat) is the author's own parenthetical remark, not a second object of scivi quoniam; "and that" made it part of what he knew

old: As a witness to their wickedness, a smoking deserted land still remains, and trees bearing fruit at an uncertain time, and a standing figure of salt, a memorial of an unbelieving soul.
new: As a witness to their wickedness, a smoking deserted land remains, and trees bearing fruit at an uncertain time, and a standing figure of salt, a memorial of an unbelieving soul.
reason: constat has no "adhuc"; "still" comes from the Greek eti, which the Latin lacks

old: She delivered a righteous people and a blameless offspring from the nations that oppressed them.
new: She delivered a righteous people and a blameless seed from the nations that oppressed them.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: for neither did they exist from the beginning, nor will they exist forever.
new: for neither were they from the beginning, nor will they be forever.
reason: neque erant ... neque erunt is simply "were ... will be"; "exist" interprets esse

old: Now the safety of the righteous indeed, but the destruction of the unrighteous, was awaited by Your people.
new: Now the safety of the righteous indeed, but the destruction of the unrighteous, was received by Your people.
reason: suscepta est means "was received/accepted"; "awaited" follows the Greek prosedechthe

old: Your all-powerful word sprang forth out of heaven, from the royal thrones, a stern warrior into the middle of the land of destruction,
new: Your almighty word sprang forth out of heaven, from the royal thrones, a stern warrior into the middle of the land of destruction,
reason: omnipotens is rendered "almighty" in this edition (cf. 11:17 "Your almighty hand")

old: In the Vulgate, gladius acutus ('a sharp sword') is nominative in apposition to the Word itself, whereas the Greek accusative makes the sword an object carried by the warrior.
new: In the Vulgate, gladius acutus ('a sharp sword') is nominative in apposition to sermo tuus ('Your word') itself, whereas the Greek accusative makes the sword an object carried by the warrior.
reason: The verse has lowercase "word" for sermo; the capitalized "Word" in the note silently imposes a Logos reading the Latin does not settle

old: Clementine Vulgate versification incorporates the clause numbered 19:14 in Greek editions into 19:13 (omitting verse number 14), and reads bonos hospites ('good guests') where Greek has 'guest-benefactors'.
new: In this critical text no verse 14 is numbered: this verse includes the material of Greek 19:14 (the Clementine numbers the following verse, beginning Et non solum hæc, as 19:14). The Latin reads bonos hospites ('good guests') where the Greek has 'guest-benefactors'.
reason: The Clementine does number a 19:14 (Et non solum hæc...); only this critical text's alignment leaves 14 unnumbered, so the note's claim about "Clementine Vulgate versification ... omitting verse number 14" is false

old: Clementine Vulgate merges Greek 19:22 into the end of verse 21, and reads bonam escam ('good food') where Greek has 'ambrosial/immortal food'.
new: This verse includes the material of Greek 19:22 (the Clementine numbers this whole verse 19:20, and no verse 22 is numbered here); the Latin reads bonam escam ('good food') where the Greek has 'ambrosial/immortal food'.
reason: The Clementine numbers this verse 19:20, not 21; the note's attribution of the 19:21 numbering to the Clementine is inaccurate

old: Humble your heart, and endure; incline your ear, and receive words of understanding; and do not hasten in the time of gloom.
new: Humble your heart, and endure; incline your ear, and receive words of understanding; and do not hasten in the time of calamity.
reason: in tempore obductionis is rendered "time of calamity" at 5:1 and "day of calamity" at 5:8; use the same English here

old: The clause "incline your ear, and receive words of understanding" is a Vulgate addition; "obductionis" ("gloom," literally "covering over" or "clouding over") is an Old Latin calque of Greek "epagōgē" ("calamity/affliction").
new: The clause "incline your ear, and receive words of understanding" is a Vulgate addition; "obductionis" ("calamity," literally "a covering over" or "a bringing upon") is an Old Latin calque of Greek "epagōgē" ("calamity/affliction").
reason: Note updated to match the verse rendering and the 5:1 note on obductio

old: Vulgate "nationes hominum" ("the nations of men") reflects an Old Latin rendering of Greek "archaias geneas" ("ancient generations") and adds "sons" ("filii"), while omitting two rhetorical questions that follow in the Greek.
new: Vulgate "nationes hominum" ("the nations of men") reflects an Old Latin rendering of Greek "archaias geneas" ("ancient generations") and adds "sons" ("filii"); this Latin text lacks the two rhetorical questions that follow in the Greek.
reason: The rhetorical questions are absent from this Latin text (CT 2:10-11); the note no longer asserts that the Vulgate as a whole omits them.

old: The Vulgate adds "saying, 'If we do not repent'" ("dicentes: Si pœnitentiam non egerimus," literally "do not do penance"), absent from the Greek, framing the verse as a conditional statement, and adds "with Him" ("cum ipso est") at the end.
new: The Vulgate adds "saying, 'If we do not repent'" ("dicentes: Si pœnitentiam non egerimus"), absent from the Greek, framing the verse as a conditional statement, and adds "with Him" ("cum ipso est") at the end.
reason: pœnitentiam agere is rendered "repent" in this edition; the "do penance" gloss imports confessional vocabulary the note does not need

old: For God honored the father over the children, and seeking out the judgment of the mother, He established it upon the children.
new: For God honored the father in the children, and seeking out the judgment of the mother, He established it upon the children.
reason: in filiis is "in the children"; "over" follows the Greek epi teknois

old: He who loves God will pray for atonement for sins, and will restrain himself from them, and in daily prayer he will be heard.
new: He who loves God will make entreaty for sins, and will restrain himself from them, and in daily prayer he will be heard.
reason: exorabit pro peccatis means "will entreat (successfully) for sins"; "atonement" imports the Greek exilasketai

old: and in righteousness it will be built up for you, and on the day of affliction you will be remembered, and like ice in clear weather, your sins will dissolve.
new: and in righteousness it will be built up for you, and on the day of tribulation you will be remembered, and like ice in clear weather, your sins will dissolve.
reason: in die tribulationis is rendered "day of tribulation" at 2:11 and 6:8

old: The Clementine Vulgate prints De propitiatio peccato (understood as a variant of propitiato peccato, "concerning a propitiated/forgiven sin"), differing from the Greek "concerning atonement."
new: This Latin text reads De propitiatio peccato (understood as a variant of propitiato peccato, "concerning a propitiated/forgiven sin"), differing from the Greek "concerning atonement."
reason: The form propitiatio is this Latin text's reading; the note no longer asserts what the printed Clementine Vulgate prints.

old: Do not let the injustice of the unjust please you, knowing that even down to the netherworld the ungodly man will not be pleasing.
new: Do not let the injustice of the unjust please you, knowing that even down to the underworld the ungodly man will not be pleasing.
reason: inferos is rendered "the underworld" in this edition (14:12; 21:10)

old: Guard yourself against a pestilent man, for he devises evil things, so that he may not bring mockery upon you forever.
new: Guard yourself against a pestilent man, for he devises evil things, or else he may bring mockery upon you forever.
reason: ne inducat depends on Attende tibi (guard yourself, lest he bring); "so that he may not" after "he devises" makes the evildoer's scheming aim to avoid mockery

old: Vulgate 'eleemosynas non danti' ("does not give alms") and 'et misertus est poenitentibus' ("and has shown mercy to those who repent") are distinctly Vulgate readings; the Greek speaks of not showing gratitude and lacks the final clause.
new: The closing words 'et misertus est poenitentibus' ("and has shown mercy to those who repent") have no counterpart in the Greek.
reason: the Greek also speaks of one who does not give alms (ἐλεημοσύνην μὴ χαριζομένῳ), not of withholding gratitude; only the final clause is distinctive

old: who reflects on her ways in his heart and has understanding in her secrets, going after her like a tracker and taking his stand in her ways;
new: who reflects on her ways in his heart and has understanding in his own secrets, going after her like a tracker and taking his stand in her ways;
reason: in absconditis suis is reflexive (the man's own), set against vias illius ("her ways") in the same verse; "her secrets" follows the Greek αὐτῆς

old: Clementine Vulgate conversatione here functions as a late-Latin variant of conversione ("turning"), rendering Greek apostrophe ("turning away of the face"), whereas in v. 21 conversationem carries its usual Latin sense of "way of life, conduct."
new: This Latin text's conversatione here functions as a late-Latin variant of conversione ("turning"), rendering Greek apostrophe ("turning away of the face"), whereas in v. 21 conversationem carries its usual Latin sense of "way of life, conduct."
reason: The form conversatione is this Latin text's reading; the note no longer asserts what the printed Clementine Vulgate reads.

old: Vulgate reads suscipient te ("they will take hold of you"), whereas the Greek reads "it will bite you" and adds a line comparing sin's teeth to a lion's teeth.
new: Vulgate reads suscipient te ("they will take hold of you"), whereas the Greek reads "it will bite you"; the Greek's following line on a lion's teeth stands in the Vulgate as a separate line (Dentes leonis dentes ejus, interficientes animas hominum).
reason: the Clementine Vulgate does have the lion's-teeth line (Clem 21:3), so the note must not imply that only the Greek has it

old: Vulgate reads suscipient te ("they will take hold of you"), whereas the Greek reads "it will bite you"; the Greek's following line on a lion's teeth stands in the Vulgate as a separate line (Dentes leonis dentes ejus, interficientes animas hominum).
new: Vulgate reads suscipient te ("they will take hold of you"), whereas the Greek reads "it will bite you"; this Latin text lacks the Greek's following line on a lion's teeth.
reason: The line Dentes leonis… is not in this Latin text (CT 21:2-3), so the note's claim that it stands in the Vulgate is false for the Latin translated here.

old: Tow gathered together is the assembly of those who sin, and their end is a flame of fire.
new: Tow gathered together is the congregation of those who sin, and their end is a flame of fire.
reason: synagoga peccantium is "the congregation of sinners" at 16:6; "assembly" is the edition's rendering of ecclesia (15:5; 21:17)

old: A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely smile quietly.
new: A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely laugh quietly.
reason: ridebit is "will laugh" (answering in risu, "in laughter"); "smile" follows the Greek μειδιάσει

old: Latin sine impensa uses impensa in its architectural sense of "mortar" or "binding material." As transmitted here, the Vulgate preserves only the opening half of the comparison (the concluding clause about a timid heart in the Greek text is absent).
new: Latin sine impensa uses impensa in its architectural sense of "mortar" or "binding material." The comparison is completed in a separate Vulgate line (sic et cor timidum in cogitatione stulti contra impetum timoris non resistet), corresponding to the Greek clause about a timid heart.
reason: the note called the timid-heart conclusion absent from the Vulgate, but the Clementine Vulgate has it (Clem 22:22, sic et cor timidum...)

old: Latin sine impensa uses impensa in its architectural sense of "mortar" or "binding material." The comparison is completed in a separate Vulgate line (sic et cor timidum in cogitatione stulti contra impetum timoris non resistet), corresponding to the Greek clause about a timid heart.
new: Latin sine impensa uses impensa in its architectural sense of "mortar" or "binding material." This Latin text lacks the line completing the comparison (the Greek clause about a timid heart).
reason: The line sic et cor timidum… is not in this Latin text (CT 22:18-19), so the note's claim that it completes the comparison is false for the Latin translated here.

old: One who throws a stone at birds will drive them off; so also one who reviles a friend dissolves friendship.
new: One who throws a stone at birds will bring them down; so also one who reviles a friend dissolves friendship.
reason: dejiciet illa is "will cast them down"; "drive them off" follows the Greek ἀποσοβεῖ

old: Latin primogenita ante omnem creaturam ("firstborn before every creature") is a well-known Vulgate-distinct reading echoing Colossians 1:15, whereas the Greek reads "and like a mist I covered the earth."
new: The Vulgate reads primogenita ante omnem creaturam ("firstborn before every creature"), whereas the Greek reads "and like a mist I covered the earth."
reason: Remove the evaluative "well-known" and the typological link to Colossians 1:15; keep a neutral comparison with the Greek.

old: Then the Creator of all commanded and spoke to me, and He who created me rested in my tent.
new: Then the Creator of all commanded and spoke to me, and He who created me rested in my tabernacle.
reason: tabernaculum of Wisdom's sacred dwelling (cf. habitatione sancta, 24:9) takes the edition's "tabernacle"; "tent" is for ordinary tents.

old: The Vulgate reads requievit in tabernaculo meo ("rested in my tent"), whereas the Greek has the Creator assign a resting place for Wisdom's tent.
new: The Vulgate reads requievit in tabernaculo meo ("rested in my tabernacle"), whereas the Greek has the Creator assign a resting place for Wisdom's tent.
reason: Gloss updated to match the verse rendering of tabernaculo.

old: It is He who fills wisdom like the Pishon, and like the Tigris in the days of new fruits,
new: It is he who fills wisdom like the Pishon, and like the Tigris in the days of new fruits,
reason: Flag: the antecedent of masculine Qui is open (liber vitae or Altissimi in 24:23; the Greek refers to the law), so a capital He should not settle it.

old: The Vulgate omits the negative before perficit ("completes") and reads infirmior ("the weaker one") rather than the Greek "the first man did not finish knowing her, and likewise the last man will not trace her out"; the masculine Qui connects 24:25-28 to God the Most High rather than the Greek masculine noun nomos ("law").
new: The Vulgate omits the negative before perficit ("completes") and reads infirmior ("the weaker one") rather than the Greek "the first man did not finish knowing her, and likewise the last man will not trace her out"; the antecedent of the masculine Qui in 24:25-28 is not stated (the Most High or liber, "book," in 24:23), whereas the Greek refers to the law.
reason: The note asserted that Qui refers to God, but liber ("book") in 24:23 is also masculine; state the antecedent as open.

old: A woman's anger is both shamelessness and great disgrace. If a woman holds supremacy, she is opposed to her husband.
new: A woman's anger, and shamelessness, and great disgrace. If a woman holds supremacy, she is opposed to her husband.
reason: Mulieris ira, et irreverentia, et confusio magna is a list of three nouns; "is both ... and" makes anger the subject equated with the other two.

old: Do not pursue him, because he is far away; for he has escaped like a gazelle from a snare, because his soul has been wounded.
new: Do not pursue him, because he is far away; for he has escaped like a roe deer from a snare, because his soul has been wounded.
reason: Latin caprea is rendered "roe deer", the edition's rendering of caprea (Deut 12:15, 2 Sam 2:18, Song 2:9, Sirach 11:30).

old: Following the added clause at the end of v. 20, the Vulgate negates the opening clause ("you will no longer be able to bind him up," vs. Greek "a wound can be bound up") and omits the closing clause about one who reveals secrets losing hope.
new: Following the added clause at the end of v. 20, this Latin text negates the opening clause ("you will no longer be able to bind him up," vs. Greek "a wound can be bound up") and omits the closing clause about one who reveals secrets losing hope.
reason: The closing clause on revealing secrets is absent from this Latin text (CT 27:21-22), so the note now speaks of "this Latin text" rather than the Vulgate as a whole.

old: The Vulgate omits the second half of Greek v. 6 ("remember corruption and death, and abide in the commandments"), and in v. 7 reads timorem Dei ("the fear of God") without the Greek second clause on the covenant of the Most High.
new: This Latin text lacks the second half of Greek v. 6 ("remember corruption and death, and abide in the commandments"), and in v. 7 reads timorem Dei ("the fear of God") without the Greek second clause on the covenant of the Most High.
reason: The clause is absent from this Latin text (CT 28:6-8); the note no longer asserts what the Vulgate as a whole omits.

old: "A third tongue" (lingua tertia, also in v. 15) is an idiom for a slanderous or meddling tongue intervening as a third party between others. The Vulgate also omits the Greek closing clauses about pulling down strong cities and overturning the houses of great men.
new: "A third tongue" (lingua tertia, also in v. 15) is an idiom for a slanderous or meddling tongue intervening as a third party between others. This Latin text also lacks the Greek closing clauses about pulling down strong cities and overturning the houses of great men.
reason: The clauses are absent from this Latin text (CT 28:14-15); the note no longer asserts what the Vulgate as a whole omits.

old: Therefore his good things have been established in the Lord, and the whole assembly of the saints will recount his alms.
new: Therefore his good things have been established in the Lord, and the whole assembly of the holy ones will recount his alms.
reason: omnis ecclesia sanctorum in the OT: sancti (persons) is "holy ones" in this edition (cf. 24:12).

old: Most wicked presumption, from where were you created to cover the dry land with wickedness and its deceitfulness?
new: O most wicked presumption, from where were you created to cover the dry land with wickedness and its deceitfulness?
reason: The interjection O of the vocative exclamation (O praesumptio nequissima) is not represented.

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads "mittat sudem in terram" ("thrust a stake into the ground," where the Greek has "cast a lot") and breaks off at "et dicat tibi:" without the counselor's quoted words found in the Greek.
new: This Latin text reads "mittat sudem in terram" ("thrust a stake into the ground," where the Greek has "cast a lot") and breaks off at "et dicat tibi:" without the counselor's quoted words found in the Greek.
reason: It is this Latin text (CT 37:9-10) that breaks off at et dicat tibi; the note no longer attributes this to the printed Clementine Vulgate.

old: Unlike the Greek ("do not consult"), the Clementine Vulgate lacks a negative before the imperative "tracta" ("confer"), giving the series an ironic force leading into the contrast of v. 12, and omits several additional examples present in the Greek.
new: Unlike the Greek ("do not consult"), this Latin text lacks a negative before the imperative "tracta" ("confer"), giving the series an ironic force leading into the contrast of v. 12, and lacks several additional examples present in the Greek.
reason: The further examples are absent from this Latin text (CT 37:11-12); the note no longer attributes their absence to the printed Clementine Vulgate.

old: and He Himself will direct his counsel and instruction, and he will reflect on His secrets.
new: and he himself will direct his counsel and instruction, and he will reflect on his secrets.
reason: Flag: ipse is genuinely ambiguous (the note says so; the Greek and Vulgate context make it the wise man), consiliabitur shares the subject of diriget, and reflexive suis follows that subject; capitals should not settle the referent.

old: The Latin pronouns (ipse, ejus, suis) are ambiguous following the Vulgate's shorter transition from 39:6; here ipse is taken as the Lord directing the wise man's counsel while consiliabitur shifts to the wise man reflecting on God's secrets, though a single subject throughout is also possible.
new: The Latin pronouns (ipse, ejus, suis) are ambiguous following the Vulgate's shorter transition from 39:6: ipse may be the Lord directing the wise man's counsel, or the wise man himself, as in the Greek; consiliabitur and the reflexive suis follow the same subject.
reason: Rewritten to match the uncapitalized verse and to state the ambiguity neutrally.

old: Many will praise his wisdom, and it will not be blotted out forever.
new: Many will praise his wisdom, and to eternity it will not be blotted out.
reason: usque in saeculum non delebitur means it will never be blotted out; "will not be blotted out forever" can be misread as "not permanently."

old: He was troubled in the vision of his heart, like one who has escaped on the day of battle; at the time of his deliverance he rose up, even marveling at no fear,
new: He was troubled in the vision of his heart, like one who has escaped on the day of battle; at the time of his deliverance he rose up, and marveling at no fear,
reason: et admirans is simply "and marveling"; "even" adds an intensifier the Latin does not have.

old: Death, how bitter is the memory of you for a man who has peace in his possessions!
new: O death, how bitter is the memory of you for a man who has peace in his possessions!
reason: The Latin opens with the interjection O (O mors), which the edition keeps elsewhere (e.g. "O God"); it was dropped.

old: Death, your judgment is good for a man in need and for one who is diminished in strength.
new: O death, your judgment is good for a man in need and for one who is diminished in strength.
reason: The Latin repeats the interjection O (O mors), parallel to 41:1; it was dropped.

old: The inheritance of the children of sinners will perish, and with their offspring will be continual disgrace.
new: The inheritance of the children of sinners will perish, and with their seed will be continual disgrace.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: All things that are from the earth will return to the earth; so too the ungodly, from a curse to destruction.
new: All things that are from the earth will turn back to the earth; so too the ungodly, from a curse to destruction.
reason: The clause Omnia quæ de terra sunt in terram convertentur is identical to 40:11, where convertentur is "will turn back" (kept distinct from revertentur "will return").

old: Vulgate 'pulchritudo ejus' ('His beauty', continuing the reference to the Lord's glory in 42:26, or possibly 'its beauty', referring to the height) differs from the Greek, which reads 'the expanse of purity'.
new: Vulgate 'pulchritudo ejus' ('His beauty', continuing the reference to the Lord's glory in 42:25, or possibly 'its beauty', referring to the height) differs from the Greek, which reads 'the expanse of purity'.
reason: There is no 42:26 in this text; the reference to His glory (gloriam ejus) is in 42:25.

old: With their offspring good things endure;
new: With their seed good things endure;
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: their descendants are a holy inheritance, and in the covenants their offspring stood;
new: their descendants are a holy inheritance, and in the covenants their seed stood;
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: and for their sake their children remain forever; their offspring and their glory will not be abandoned.
new: and for their sake their children remain forever; their seed and their glory will not be abandoned.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: He made him equal in the glory of the holy ones, and He magnified him in the fear of enemies, and by his words he calmed portents.
new: He made him similar in the glory of the holy ones, and He magnified him in the fear of enemies, and by his words he calmed portents.
reason: similem illum fecit is "made him like/similar"; "equal" (aequalis) overstates similis.

old: First of all, He prepared bread for them to the full; for they will also eat the sacrifices of the Lord, which He gave to him and to his offspring.
new: First of all, He prepared bread for them to the full; for they will also eat the sacrifices of the Lord, which He gave to him and to his seed.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Therefore He established for him a covenant of peace, as ruler of the holy things and of his nation, so that the dignity of the priesthood might belong to him and to his offspring forever.
new: Therefore He established for him a covenant of peace, as ruler of the holy things and of his nation, so that the dignity of the priesthood might belong to him and to his seed forever.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And a covenant for King David, the son of Jesse, from the tribe of Judah, an inheritance for him and for his offspring,
new: And a covenant for King David, the son of Jesse, from the tribe of Judah, an inheritance for him and for his seed,
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And the Lord gave might to Caleb himself, and even into old age strength remained with him, so that he ascended to the high place of the land, and his offspring obtained the inheritance,
new: And the Lord gave might to Caleb himself, and even into old age strength remained with him, so that he ascended to the high place of the land, and his seed obtained the inheritance,
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: You put a blemish on your glory, and profaned your offspring, to bring wrath upon your children and for your folly to be stirred up,
new: You put a blemish on your glory, and profaned your seed, to bring wrath upon your children and for your folly to be stirred up,
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: But God will not abandon His mercy, and He will not ruin nor blot out His works, nor will He destroy from the root the descendants of His chosen one; and He will not ruin the offspring of him who loves the Lord.
new: But God will not abandon His mercy, and He will not ruin nor blot out His works, nor will He destroy from the root the descendants of His chosen one; and He will not ruin the seed of him who loves the Lord.
reason: Latin semen (nepotes "descendants" left) (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And Solomon came to his end with his fathers. And he left behind him from his offspring the folly of the nation, and one lacking in prudence, Rehoboam, who turned the nation away by his counsel;
new: And Solomon came to his end with his fathers. And he left behind him from his seed the folly of the nation, and one lacking in prudence, Rehoboam, who turned the nation away by his counsel;
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Clementine Latin spells the noun pernicem (for perniciem, 'destruction') and adds the clause 'and easily shattered their power,' absent from the standard Greek.
new: This Latin text spells the noun pernicem (for perniciem, 'destruction') and adds the clause 'and easily shattered their power,' absent from the standard Greek.

old: Vulgate reads 'were adorned in your friendship' (decorati sunt, reflecting the Greek variant kekosmenoi) and omits the Greek closing clause 'for we too shall surely live.'
new: Vulgate reads 'were adorned in your friendship' (decorati sunt, reflecting the Greek variant kekosmenoi); this Latin text lacks the Greek closing clause 'for we too shall surely live.'
reason: The closing clause is absent from this Latin text (CT 48:11-12); the note no longer asserts that the Vulgate as a whole omits it.

old: The Clementine Vulgate ends verse 1 after 'the work of a perfumer,' omitting the Greek lines comparing Josiah's memory to honey and banquet music.
new: This Latin text ends verse 1 after 'the work of a perfumer,' omitting the Greek lines comparing Josiah's memory to honey and banquet music.

old: Vulgate Dominum patrem Domini mei ("the Lord, the Father of my Lord") follows the Greek textual tradition rather than the Hebrew ("O LORD, you are my father"), a reading widely noted in Christian exegesis for its messianic resonance.
new: Vulgate Dominum patrem Domini mei ("the Lord, the Father of my Lord") follows the Greek textual tradition rather than the Hebrew ("O Lord, you are my father").
reason: Removes capital LORD and the confessional comment on messianic resonance; keeps the factual textual comparison.

old: Vulgate "talpas et vespertiliones" ("moles and bats") stands in the accusative case, serving as the object of "adoraret" or in apposition to the idols, rather than the dative ("cast ... to the moles and bats") found in translations of the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
new: Vulgate "talpas et vespertiliones" ("moles and bats") stands in the accusative case, serving as the object of "adoraret" or in apposition to the idols, where the Hebrew has "to the moles and to the bats."
reason: Removes a claim about what translations of the Hebrew do; keeps the neutral comparison with the Hebrew itself.

old: Latin 'qui te beatum dicunt' ('those who call you blessed') reflects an alternative vocalization of the Hebrew verb usually rendered 'those who guide you.'
new: Latin 'qui te beatum dicunt' ('those who call you blessed') takes the Hebrew verb in its sense 'call happy' rather than 'guide.'
reason: The Hebrew participle is the same form in both senses, so 'alternative vocalization' is inaccurate, and 'usually rendered' is a claim about translations.

old: Latin 'crinem earum nudabit' ('will lay bare their hair') is a distinctly Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew is usually translated 'foreheads' or 'secret parts.'
new: Latin 'crinem earum nudabit' ('will lay bare their hair') is a distinctly Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew word is variously understood as 'foreheads' or 'secret parts.'
reason: 'usually translated' is a claim about translations; restated as a neutral comment on the Hebrew word.

old: Latin 'ubi invocatus est' ('where He has been invoked') is a distinctly Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew term usually translated 'her assemblies.'
new: Latin 'ubi invocatus est' ('where He has been invoked') is a distinctly Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew term meaning 'her assemblies.'
