old: Latin 'patruelis mei' ('of my cousin') translates a Hebrew kinsman term often rendered 'my beloved,' and 'in cornu filio olei' ('on a horn, the son of oil') preserves the Hebrew idiom for a fertile hilltop.
new: Latin 'patruelis mei' ('of my cousin') takes the Hebrew term for 'my beloved' in its kinship sense ('uncle, kinsman'), and 'in cornu filio olei' ('on a horn, the son of oil') preserves the Hebrew idiom for a fertile hilltop.
reason: 'often rendered' is a claim about translations; restated as a neutral lexical comparison.

old: Therefore hell has enlarged its soul, and has opened its mouth without any limit; and her mighty ones, and her people, and her lofty and glorious ones will go down to it.
new: Therefore the underworld has enlarged its soul, and has opened its mouth without any limit; and her mighty ones, and her people, and her lofty and glorious ones will go down to it.
reason: infernus is rendered 'the underworld' in this edition (as at 7:11, 14:9, 14:15); 'hell' imports a later theological sense.

old: Therefore the fury of the Lord grew angry against His people, and He stretched out His hand over them and struck them; and the mountains were shaken, and their corpses became like dung in the middle of the streets. In all these things His fury has not turned away, but His hand is still stretched out.
new: Therefore the fury of the Lord grew angry against His people, and He stretched out His hand over them and struck them; and the mountains were shaken, and their corpses became like dung in the middle of the streets. In all these things His fury has not been turned away, but His hand is still stretched out.
reason: The same refrain (non est aversus/adversus furor ejus) is rendered 'has not been turned away' at 9:11, 9:16, 9:20 and 10:4.

old: The Clementine Vulgate prints 'adversus' as an orthographic variant for 'aversus' ('turned away').
new: This Latin text reads 'adversus' as an orthographic variant for 'aversus' ('turned away').
reason: adversus is this Latin text's reading (it has aversus at 9:11, 9:16, 9:20, 10:4); the note no longer asserts what the printed Clementine Vulgate prints.

old: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew verb (often translated "I am ruined/undone") from its homonymous root meaning "be silent" (quia tacui, "because I have kept silent").
new: The Vulgate takes the Hebrew verb (which can mean "I am ruined") from its homonymous root meaning "be silent" (quia tacui, "because I have kept silent").
reason: 'often translated' is a claim about translations; restated as a neutral lexical comment.

old: The Vulgate reads "a virgin" (virgo) and the passive "His name will be called" (vocabitur nomen ejus), aligning with the Septuagint and Matthew 1:23 rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's active "she will call."
new: The Vulgate reads "a virgin" (virgo) where the Hebrew has 'almah' and the Septuagint 'parthenos'; its passive "His name will be called" (vocabitur nomen ejus) differs from the Hebrew "she will call" and the Septuagint "you will call."
reason: The old note was inaccurate: the passive vocabitur does not align with the Septuagint (kaleseis, 'you will call') or Matthew 1:23 (kalesousin, 'they will call'); rewritten as a neutral comparison. Flag: the capitals 'His'/'He' in 7:14-15 (and 8:8 'Your land') settle a disputed referent; left as the edition has them, per instructions.

old: The Vulgate reads "has rather adopted" (assumpsit magis) Rezin and the son of Remaliah, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly translated "rejoices in" or "melts in fear before."
new: The Vulgate reads "has rather adopted" (assumpsit magis) Rezin and the son of Remaliah, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "and rejoicing in."
reason: 'commonly translated' is a claim about translations (and 'melts in fear' is an emendation, not the Masoretic Text); restated as a neutral comparison.

old: Sanctify the Lord of hosts Himself; let Him be your dread, and let Him be your terror;
new: Sanctify the Lord of hosts Himself; He is your dread, and He is your terror;
reason: ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester is a verbless clause with emphatic ipse, naturally supplied with 'is'; 'let Him be' imports a jussive the Latin does not express.

old: The Clementine Vulgate prints suscipiet sursum, a traditional orthographic variant for suspiciet sursum ("will look upward"), parallel to "gaze at the earth" in 8:22.
new: This Latin text reads suscipiet sursum, an orthographic variant for suspiciet sursum ("will look upward"), parallel to "gaze at the earth" in 8:22.
reason: suscipiet is this Latin text's reading; the note no longer asserts what the printed Clementine Vulgate prints.

old: Following Hebrew versification (corresponding to English 9:1), the Vulgate renders the Hebrew antithesis literally through passive verbs of weight, "was lightened" (alleviata est) versus "was weighed down" (aggravata est), where the Hebrew is commonly rendered "treated with contempt" versus "made glorious."
new: Following Hebrew versification (corresponding to English 9:1), the Vulgate renders the Hebrew antithesis literally through passive verbs of weight, "was lightened" (alleviata est) versus "was weighed down" (aggravata est); the Hebrew verbs can also mean "treated with contempt" and "made glorious."
reason: 'commonly rendered' is a claim about translations; restated as a neutral lexical comment.

old: Vulgate Isaiah 9:1-20 corresponds to 9:2-21 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most modern English versions, since Vulgate 8:23 corresponds to Hebrew 9:1.
new: The numbering here (8:23; 9:1-20) follows the Hebrew; in the alternative numbering these verses are 9:1-21.
reason: The old note was false: the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the same 8:23 / 9:1-20 numbering as this Latin (the 9:1-21 numbering is the Greek-based/English one); it also made a claim about English versions.

old: Latin 'consummatio abbreviata' ("a shortened completion," echoed in 10:23 'consummationem et abbreviationem') follows the phrasing reflected in Romans 9:28, whereas the Hebrew has "destruction is decreed."
new: Latin 'consummatio abbreviata' ("a shortened completion," echoed in 10:23 'consummationem et abbreviationem') renders the Hebrew words for "destruction" and "decreed" by their root senses "finishing" and "cut short"; compare Romans 9:28.
reason: The claim that the Latin 'follows' Romans 9:28 is unsupported; restated as a neutral lexical comparison with the Hebrew and a cross-reference.

old: And the Lord of hosts will raise up a scourge against him, according to the blow against Midian at the rock of Oreb; and His rod will be over the sea, and He will lift it up in the way of Egypt.
new: And the Lord of hosts will raise up a scourge against him, according to the blow against Midian at the rock of Oreb; and His rod over the sea, and He will lift it up in the way of Egypt.
reason: virgam suam is accusative, still governed by suscitabit; 'will be' supplies a different verb and makes it a subject.

old: Latin 'a facie olei' ("before the face of the oil") renders the Hebrew word for fatness/oil specifically as "oil," a reading traditionally associated with anointing oil in Latin exegesis.
new: Latin 'a facie olei' ("before the face of the oil") renders the Hebrew word for fatness/oil specifically as "oil."
reason: Removes an interpretive remark about anointing in later exegesis, which is not about the Latin itself.

old: Together with 11:3, the Vulgate distinguishes 'pietatis' ("piety") from 'timoris Domini' ("the fear of the Lord," which "will fill Him"), producing the traditional sevenfold enumeration where the Hebrew repeats "fear of the Lord."
new: Together with 11:3, the Vulgate distinguishes 'pietatis' ("piety") from 'timoris Domini' ("the fear of the Lord," which "will fill Him"), giving seven distinct terms where the Hebrew repeats "fear of the Lord."
reason: 'the traditional sevenfold enumeration' alludes to a doctrinal tradition; kept as a neutral count of the Latin terms.

old: Latin 'sepulchrum ejus' ("His tomb") is a celebrated Vulgate-distinct reading where the Hebrew text has "his resting place."
new: Latin 'sepulchrum ejus' ("His tomb") is a Vulgate-distinct reading where the Hebrew text has "his resting place."
reason: 'celebrated' is evaluative; the note should stay neutral and factual.

old: You will not have fellowship, not even with them in burial; for you have destroyed your own land, you have killed your own people; the offspring of the most wicked will not be named forever.
new: You will not have fellowship, not even with them in burial; for you have destroyed your own land, you have killed your own people; the seed of the most wicked will not be named forever.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Do not rejoice, all of you, Philistia, because the rod of the one who struck you has been broken to pieces; for from the root of the serpent a basilisk will come out, and its offspring will swallow up the bird.
new: Do not rejoice, all of you, Philistia, because the rod of the one who struck you has been broken to pieces; for from the root of the serpent a basilisk will come out, and its seed will swallow up the bird.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin "aratra, et segetes" ("plows and grainfields") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering of a difficult Hebrew phrase often translated "wooded heights and summit" (or in the Septuagint, "the Hivites and the Amorites"); in 17:8 "lucos et delubra" ("groves and shrines") renders Hebrew Asherah poles and incense altars.
new: Latin "aratra, et segetes" ("plows and grainfields") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering of a difficult Hebrew phrase understood as "wooded heights and summit" (or in the Septuagint, "the Hivites and the Amorites"); in 17:8 "lucos et delubra" ("groves and shrines") renders Hebrew Asherah poles and incense altars.

old: Latin "cymbalo alarum" ("cymbal of wings") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of a rare Hebrew phrase often translated "whirring wings" or "shadowing wings."
new: Latin "cymbalo alarum" ("cymbal of wings") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of a rare Hebrew phrase also understood as "whirring wings" or "shadowing wings."
reason: 'often translated' is a claim about translations; restated neutrally.

old: The Vulgate renders the difficult Hebrew descriptions of the Ethiopian nation as "uprooted and torn to pieces," "after whom there is no other," and "waiting and trampled down" (repeated in 18:7), where modern translations from the Masoretic Text often read "tall and smooth," "feared near and far," and "mighty and conquering."

old: The Vulgate reads "its irrigated grounds will droop: all who made ponds to catch fish" for a difficult Hebrew verse often translated "her weavers [or pillars] will be crushed, and all who work for wages will be grieved."
new: The Vulgate reads "its irrigated grounds will droop: all who made ponds to catch fish" for a difficult Hebrew verse that may mean "her weavers [or pillars] will be crushed, and all who work for wages will be grieved."
reason: 'often translated' is a claim about translations; restated neutrally.

old: The princes of Tanis have become foolish; the princes of Memphis have languished; they have deceived Egypt, the cornerstone of its peoples.
new: The princes of Tanis have become foolish; the princes of Memphis have languished; they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples.
reason: angulum is simply 'corner'; 'cornerstone' follows the usual English rendering of the Hebrew pinnah.

old: Latin "servient Aegyptii Assur" ("the Egyptians will serve Assyria") follows the Septuagint in taking Assyria as the object of service, whereas many modern translations from Hebrew render it "the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians."
new: Latin "servient Aegyptii Assur" ("the Egyptians will serve Assyria") takes Assyria as the object of service, as the Septuagint does; the Hebrew can also mean "the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians."
reason: Removes a claim about what modern translations do; keeps the neutral comparison with the Greek and Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate connects "of three years" (trium annorum) to the future "sign and wonder" rather than to the duration of Isaiah's walking naked and barefoot, as commonly construed in translations from the Masoretic Text.
new: The Vulgate connects "of three years" (trium annorum) to the future "sign and wonder" rather than to the duration of Isaiah's walking naked and barefoot.

old: For the Lord says this to me: "Within one more year, as in the year of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will be taken away,
new: For this is what the Lord says to me: "Within one more year, as in the year of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will be taken away,

old: And your choicest valleys will be full of chariots, and horsemen will set their stations at the gate.

reason: electæ is positive ('choice, chosen'), not superlative; 'choicest' adds a degree the Latin lacks.

old: The Lord God of hosts says this: "Go, enter to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna, the overseer of the temple, and you will say to him:
new: This is what the Lord God of hosts says: "Go, enter to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna, the overseer of the temple, and you will say to him:

old: Look, the land of the Chaldeans: such a people did not exist; Assyria founded it; they led away its strong men into captivity, they undermined its houses, they turned it into a ruin.

old: Vulgate reads "in teachings" (in doctrinis), interpreting the Hebrew term (often translated "in the east" or "in the regions of light") in the sense of illuminations or doctrines.
new: Vulgate reads "in teachings" (in doctrinis), taking the Hebrew term meaning "in the lights" (understood of the regions of light, the east) in the sense of illuminations or doctrines.

old: Vulgate renders the Hebrew expression often translated "I waste away" as "My secret to me" (Secretum meum mihi), taking the Hebrew root in the sense of "secret" or "mystery."
new: Vulgate reads "My secret to me" (Secretum meum mihi), taking the Hebrew razi-li in the sense of "secret" or "mystery" rather than "leanness" ("I waste away").
reason: Removes a claim about how the expression is usually translated; keeps the factual Latin/Hebrew comparison.

old: Because You have turned the city into a heap, the strong city into a ruin, the house of foreigners, so that it is not a city and will not be built forever.
new: Because You have turned the city into a heap, the strong city into a ruin, the house of foreigners, so that it is not a city and will never be built.
reason: in sempiternum non ædificetur = "will never be built"; "will not be built forever" misreads as "not built to last forever."

old: Let us show mercy to the wicked, and he will not learn righteousness; in the land of the saints he has done unjust things, and he will not see the glory of the Lord.

old: For you have said, "We have struck a covenant with death, and with the underworld we have made a pact; when the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon us, because we have set falsehood as our hope, and by falsehood we have been protected."
new: For you have said, "We have struck a covenant with death, and with the underworld we have made a covenant; when the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon us, because we have set falsehood as our hope, and by falsehood we have been protected."

old: And your covenant with death will be blotted out, and your pact with hell will not stand; when the overflowing scourge passes through, you will be to it for trampling.

old: Bread, however, will be crushed; yet the one threshing will not thresh it forever, nor bruise it with a wagon wheel, nor crush it with his hooves.

reason: neque vexabit eum rota plaustri: rota plaustri is the subject ("nor will the wagon wheel bruise it"), not an instrument of the thresher.

old: The roads have been laid waste, the one passing along the path has ceased; the treaty has been made void, he has cast aside the cities, he has had no regard for men.

old: Vulgate "legis verba ponderans" ("weighing the words of the law") and "doctor parvulorum" ("teacher of little children") are distinctive Latin renderings of Hebrew expressions usually translated as one who weighs tribute and one who counts towers.

old: Look upon Zion, the city of our solemn feast: your eyes will see Jerusalem, a wealthy dwelling, a tent that can by no means be moved; nor will its pegs ever be taken away, and none of its ropes will be broken:

old: Vulgate "et hæc erit vobis directa via" ("and this will be a straight way for you") offers a clear Latin rendering of a difficult Hebrew clause often translated "and it will be for the one who walks on that way."
new: Vulgate "et hæc erit vobis directa via" ("and this will be a straight way for you") gives a clear sense to a difficult Hebrew clause (literally "and it is for them; one walking the way").

old: Latin habitatorem quietis ("inhabitant of rest") reflects Jerome's rendering of Hebrew chadel as "rest" or "cessation," whereas many Hebrew-based translations render it "the world."
new: Latin habitatorem quietis ("inhabitant of rest") reflects Jerome's rendering of Hebrew chadel as "rest" or "cessation."
reason: Removes a claim about what other translations do.

old: The Vulgate pairs passive/middle consolamini with the vocative popule meus ("Take comfort, My people"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly taken transitively ("Comfort my people").
new: The Vulgate pairs passive/middle consolamini with the vocative popule meus ("Take comfort, My people"), whereas the Hebrew has a transitive imperative with "My people" as its object ("Comfort My people").
reason: The Hebrew is not merely "commonly taken" as transitive (ammi is its object); also capitalizes My for God's speech as the edition does.

old: You will seek them and will not find them, the men who rebel against you; the men who wage war against you will be as though they did not exist and like utter destruction.
new: You will seek them and will not find them, the men who rebel against you; the men who wage war against you will be as though they did not exist and like destruction.
reason: veluti consumptio is simply "like destruction/consumption"; "utter" is an added intensifier.

old: Latin malum ("evil"), contrasted here with pacem ("peace"), refers to calamity, adversity, or physical hardship rather than moral evil.

reason: The note settled a theologically disputed sense ("rather than moral evil"); malum is ambiguous, so the note now states the range neutrally.

old: Unlike the Hebrew abstract nouns ("righteousness" and "salvation"), the Vulgate renders justum ("the Righteous One"), Salvatorem ("the Savior"), and eum ("Him") personally, giving this verse its classic messianic form; Latin germinet literally means "sprout" or "bud forth."
new: Unlike the Hebrew abstract nouns ("righteousness" and "salvation"), the Vulgate renders justum ("the Righteous One"), Salvatorem ("the Savior"), and eum ("Him") personally; Latin germinet literally means "sprout" or "bud forth."

old: I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob in vain, 'Seek Me.' I am the Lord, speaking righteousness, declaring what is right.

old: Latin Ergo ("Therefore") and meæ sunt justitiæ et imperium ("my acts of righteousness and dominion") represent a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew reads "Only in the LORD, one shall say of me, are righteousness and strength."
new: Latin Ergo ("Therefore") and meæ sunt justitiæ et imperium ("my acts of righteousness and dominion") represent a distinctly Vulgate reading, where the Hebrew has "only" and says that righteousness and strength are in the Lord.

old: In the Lord all the offspring of Israel will be justified and will be praised.

old: Latin "elegi te in camino paupertatis" literally reads "I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty," preserving the primary sense of the Hebrew verb ("choose") and translating the noun as "poverty," whereas many translations from Hebrew render "tested you in the furnace of affliction."
new: Latin "elegi te in camino paupertatis" literally reads "I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty," taking the Hebrew verb in its usual sense ("choose," though it can also mean "test") and rendering the Hebrew noun for "affliction" as "poverty."
reason: Removed the claim about what "many translations" do; kept the factual Latin/Hebrew comparison.

old: Latin "ex tempore antequam fieret" ("from the time before it came to be") emphasizes the speaker's preexistence before events unfolded, whereas the Hebrew reads "from the time it took place"; Christian interpretation traditionally identifies the speaker sent by "the Lord God ... and His Spirit" as the Messiah.

old: Latin "et Israel non congregabitur" ("and Israel will not be gathered") follows the written Hebrew consonantal text (Ketiv, "not"), whereas most modern versions follow the marginal reading (Qere, "to Him": "that Israel might be gathered to Him").
new: Latin "et Israel non congregabitur" ("and Israel will not be gathered") follows the written Hebrew consonantal text (Ketiv, "not") rather than the marginal reading (Qere, "to Him": "that Israel might be gathered to Him").

old: Can prey be taken from the mighty? Or can what has been captured by the strong be saved?

reason: tolletur is a simple future passive ("will be taken"); only the second question has poterit ("can").

old: Look, all you who kindle a fire, armed with flames: walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have set ablaze; from My hand this has happened to you: in sorrows you will sleep.

old: Your Ruler, the Lord, and your God, who will fight for His people, says this: "Look, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of My indignation; you will not drink it anymore.

new: For this is what the Lord says: "You were sold for nothing, and without silver you will be redeemed."
reason: Latin "hæc dicit Dominus" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: For the Lord God says this: "My people went down into Egypt at the beginning to be a settler there, and Assyria oppressed them without any cause.
