reason: Removed a claim about how the Hebrew is "often rendered" and the interpretive comment identifying the sign-act with God's act.

old: This is what the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, speaks, saying: You and your wives have spoken with your mouth, and with your hands you have fulfilled it, saying, 'Let us perform our vows that we have vowed, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven and to pour out libations to her.' You have fulfilled your vows, and in deed you have carried them out.
new: This is what the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, says: You and your wives have spoken with your mouth, and with your hands you have fulfilled it, saying, 'Let us perform our vows that we have vowed, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven and to pour out libations to her.' You have fulfilled your vows, and in deed you have carried them out.
reason: Latin "Hæc inquit Dominus exercituum, Deus Israël, dicens" is the same formula (inquit = says), rendered "This is what X says"; the pleonastic dicens is carried by the colon.

old: Therefore, look, days are coming, and I will visit judgment upon the carved images of Babylon, and all her land will be put to shame, and all her slaughtered will fall in the midst of her.
new: Therefore, look, days are coming, and I will punish the carved images of Babylon, and all her land will be put to shame, and all her slaughtered will fall in the midst of her.
reason: visitabo super has no word for "judgment"; the edition renders visitabo super "punish" (36:32; 51:13, 29).

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads "of the multitude" (de multitudine) here rather than "of the artisans."
new: The Clementine Vulgate reads "of the multitude" (de multitudine) here, where the Hebrew word may mean "artisans."
reason: "rather than 'of the artisans'" left the comparison unstated (reads as a comment on English versions); made it an explicit Hebrew comparison.

old: Verse 1:14 (found in the Hebrew text) is absent from the Clementine Vulgate, and Latin 'visio' ("vision") in 1:13 reflects a Vulgate-distinct reading for the movement of the fire among the living creatures.
new: Latin 'visio' ("vision") reflects a Vulgate-distinct reading for the movement of the fire among the living creatures.
reason: The claim that 1:14 is absent is false for this Latin: the critical text has 1:14 ('Et animalia ibant et revertebantur, in similitudinem fulguris coruscantis') as an additional verse after 1:13; the accurate part of the note is kept.

old: Latin 'spiritus vitæ' ("the spirit of life," repeated in 1:21) is a Vulgate-distinct reading where the Hebrew phrase is commonly rendered "the spirit of the living creature."
new: Latin 'spiritus vitæ' ("the spirit of life," repeated in 1:21) is a Vulgate-distinct reading where the Hebrew has "the spirit of the living creature."
reason: Removes the claim about how the Hebrew is 'commonly rendered' (a statement about translations); keeps the neutral Latin/Hebrew comparison.

old: The Vulgate opens chapter 2 with 'Hæc visio similitudinis gloriæ Domini' ("This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord"), which the Hebrew text and most modern versions place at the end of 1:28.
new: The Vulgate opens chapter 2 with 'Hæc visio similitudinis gloriæ Domini' ("This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord"), which the Hebrew text places at the end of 1:28.
reason: Removes the claim about 'most modern versions' (a statement about translations).

old: Vulgate reads congregabo ("gather"), reflecting Hebrew "gather" rather than Masoretic "increase/add".
new: Vulgate reads congregabo ("gather"), where the Hebrew has "increase/add".
reason: The note contradicted itself (crediting 'gather' to the Hebrew and then to the Masoretic 'increase/add'); the Hebrew has 'add', the Latin congregabo 'gather'.

old: Vulgate renders Hebrew hammanim ("incense altars" or "sun-pillars") as simulacra ("images") here and in 6:5, and as delubra ("shrines") in 6:6.
new: Vulgate renders Hebrew hammanim ("incense altars" or "sun-pillars") as simulacra ("images") here, and as delubra ("shrines") in 6:6.
reason: In 6:5 simulacrorum stands for the Hebrew word for idols (gillulim), not hammanim, so 'and in 6:5' is inaccurate.

old: And I saw, and look, a likeness like the appearance of fire: from the appearance of His waist downward, fire; and from His waist upward, like the appearance of brightness, as the sight of electrum.
new: And I saw, and look, a likeness like the appearance of fire: from the appearance of His loins downward, fire; and from His loins upward, like the appearance of brightness, as the sight of electrum.
reason: lumborum/lumbis are 'loins', as in the parallel vision at 1:27 ('from His loins and upward'); FLAG: the capitalized 'His' for this fiery figure is kept per edition policy, though whether the figure is God or an angelic being is disputed.

old: And He said to me, "Surely you have seen, son of man. Is this a light thing to the house of Judah, that they should do these abominations which they have done here, because, filling the land with iniquity, they have turned again to provoke Me? And look, they hold the branch to their noses.
new: And He said to me, "Surely you have seen, son of man. Is this a light thing to the house of Judah, that they should do these abominations which they have done here, because, filling the land with iniquity, they have turned to provoke Me? And look, they hold the branch to their noses.
reason: conversi sunt ad irritandum me is 'they have turned to provoke Me'; 'again' follows the Hebrew idiom (wayyashuvu) and has no basis in the Latin.

old: Latin "volubiles" ("Whirling" or "revolving") renders the Hebrew term for the wheelwork ("Galgal"). Verse 10:14 of the Hebrew text (describing the four faces of each cherub) is omitted in the Clementine Vulgate.
new: Latin "volubiles" ("Whirling" or "revolving") renders the Hebrew term for the wheelwork ("Galgal").
reason: The claim that 10:14 is omitted is false for this Latin: the critical text has 10:14 ('Quatuor autem facies habebat unum...') as an additional verse after 10:13. FLAG: in the verse, capitalized 'He' for vocavit decides an open referent (the Hebrew is impersonal); left unchanged per edition policy.

old: And the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the east gate of the house of the Lord, which faces toward the rising of the sun; and look, at the entrance of the gate were twenty-five men, and I saw in the midst of them Jaazaniah son of Azzur, and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, leaders of the people.
new: And the Spirit lifted me up and brought me to the east gate of the house of the Lord, which faces toward the rising of the sun; and look, at the entrance of the gate were twenty-five men, and I saw in the midst of them Jaazaniah son of Azzur, and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, leaders of the people.
reason: introduxit me ad portam ... orientalem is 'to the east gate'; the prophet is then at its entrance (in introitu portæ), not inside it.

old: Latin "Nonne dudum aedificatae sunt domus?" ("Were not the houses built recently?") frames the leaders' boast as a confident question, whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered "The time is not near to build houses."
new: Latin "Nonne dudum aedificatae sunt domus?" ("Were not the houses built recently?") frames the leaders' boast as a confident question, whereas the Hebrew reads "The time is not near to build houses."
reason: Removes the claim about how the Hebrew is 'commonly rendered' (a statement about translations).

old: For this reason, speak to them and you will say to them, 'The Lord God says this: Each and every man from the house of Israel who places his impurities in his heart, and sets up the stumbling block of his iniquity in front of his face, and comes to a prophet inquiring of Me through him—I, the Lord, will answer him in the multitude of his impurities,
new: For this reason, speak to them and you will say to them, 'This is what the Lord God says: Each and every man from the house of Israel who places his impurities in his heart, and sets up the stumbling block of his iniquity in front of his face, and comes to a prophet inquiring of Me through him—I, the Lord, will answer him in the multitude of his impurities,
reason: Latin "Hæc dicit" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: Therefore say to the house of Israel, 'The Lord God says this: Turn back and depart from your idols, and turn your faces away from all your defilements.
new: Therefore say to the house of Israel, 'This is what the Lord God says: Turn back and depart from your idols, and turn your faces away from all your defilements.
reason: Latin "Hæc dicit" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads "Dominus exercituum" ("the Lord of hosts") here and in 14:14, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Lord GOD" (Adonai YHWH).
new: The Clementine Vulgate reads "Dominus exercituum" ("the Lord of hosts") here and in 14:14, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Lord God."
reason: Capital 'GOD' and the divine-name transliteration are excluded from notes by house style.

old: For the Lord God says this: Even if I send My four worst judgments—sword, and famine, and evil beasts, and pestilence—into Jerusalem to kill man and livestock from it,
new: For this is what the Lord God says: Even if I send My four worst judgments—sword, and famine, and evil beasts, and pestilence—into Jerusalem to kill man and livestock from it,
reason: Latin "Quoniam hæc dicit Dominus Deus" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: Therefore, the Lord God says this: Just as the wood of the vine among the trees of the forests, which I have given to the fire to be devoured, so I will hand over the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
new: Therefore, this is what the Lord God says: Just as the wood of the vine among the trees of the forests, which I have given to the fire to be devoured, so I will hand over the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
reason: Latin "Propterea hæc dicit Dominus Deus" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: And having confidence in your beauty, you committed fornication on account of your name, and you offered your fornication to every passerby, so that you might become his.
new: And having confidence in your beauty, you committed fornication in your name, and you offered your fornication to every passerby, so that you might become his.
reason: fornicata es in nomine tuo is 'in your name'; 'on account of' follows the Hebrew ('al shemekh) rather than the Latin preposition.

old: Latin aes tuum ("your bronze") takes the underlying Hebrew noun from the root for bronze/copper, whereas translations from the Hebrew commonly render it as "your lust" or "your filthiness."
new: Latin aes tuum ("your bronze") takes the underlying Hebrew noun from the root for bronze/copper, whereas the Hebrew is usually understood here as "your lust" or "your filthiness."
reason: Removes the claim about what translations do; keeps the neutral Latin/Hebrew comparison.

old: Latin et non feci juxta scelera tua ("and I have not acted according to your wicked deeds") preserves a first-person reading, whereas most translations from the Hebrew follow a second-person reading ("Have you not committed lewdness...").
new: Latin et non feci juxta scelera tua ("and I have not acted according to your wicked deeds") preserves a first-person reading, whereas the Hebrew is usually read in the second person ("Have you not committed lewdness...").
reason: Removes the claim about 'most translations'; keeps the neutral comparison of readings.

old: Vulgate "in superficie" ("on the surface") reflects a distinct understanding of the obscure Hebrew word "tsaftsafah" (often rendered "like a willow" from the Masoretic Text).
new: Vulgate "in superficie" ("on the surface") reflects a distinct understanding of the obscure Hebrew word "tsaftsafah" (usually understood as "like a willow").
reason: Removes the claim about how the word is 'often rendered' (a statement about translations).

old: so that the kingdom may be lowly and not be lifted up, but may keep his pact and observe it.
new: so that the kingdom may be lowly and not be lifted up, but may keep his covenant and observe it.
reason: pactum is 'covenant' in this edition (2:3, 16:8, 16:59-62) and the same agreement is fœdus 'covenant' in 17:13, 18, 19 of this passage.

old: Yet he, withdrawing from him, sent messengers to Egypt, so that it might give him horses and many people. Will the one who did these things prosper, or obtain safety? And he who broke the pact, will he escape?
new: Yet he, withdrawing from him, sent messengers to Egypt, so that it might give him horses and many people. Will the one who did these things prosper, or obtain safety? And he who broke the covenant, will he escape?
reason: pactum is 'covenant' in this edition, as in 17:13-14 and 17:18-19 for the same agreement.

old: As I live, says the Lord God, surely in the place of the king who appointed him king, whose oath he made void, and he broke the pact that he had with him, in the midst of Babylon he will die.
new: As I live, says the Lord God, surely in the place of the king who appointed him king, whose oath he made void, and he broke the covenant that he had with him, in the midst of Babylon he will die.
reason: pactum is 'covenant' in this edition, as in 17:13-14 and 17:18-19 for the same agreement.

old: Vulgate "egerit poenitentiam" (and "agite poenitentiam" in 18:30) renders the Hebrew verb "turn" explicitly with the Latin idiom for repentance ("repent" or "do penance").
new: Vulgate "egerit poenitentiam" (and "agite poenitentiam" in 18:30) renders the Hebrew verb "turn" explicitly with the Latin idiom for repentance ("repent").
reason: pœnitentiam agere is rendered 'repent' in this edition; the alternative 'do penance' imports confessional vocabulary into the note.

old: And the children of Israel say, 'The way of the Lord is not fair!' Are My ways not fair, house of Israel, and are your ways not rather crooked?
new: And the sons of Israel say, 'The way of the Lord is not fair!' Are My ways not fair, house of Israel, and are your ways not rather crooked?
reason: filii Israël is 'sons of Israel' throughout this edition (e.g. 2:3, 4:13 in this book).

old: Vulgate "in sanguine tuo" ("in your blood") translates the difficult Hebrew phrase literally, where many modern versions emend or render "in your vineyard" or "in your likeness."
new: Vulgate "in sanguine tuo" ("in your blood") translates the difficult Hebrew phrase literally.
reason: Removes the claim about what 'many modern versions' do; keeps the neutral statement about the Latin.

old: And it happened in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth of the month, that men from the elders of Israel came to inquire of the Lord, and they sat before me.
new: And it happened in the seventh year, in the fifth, on the tenth of the month, that men from the elders of Israel came to inquire of the Lord, and they sat before me.
reason: in quinto has no 'mense'; the edition renders the identical construction literally at 1:1 ('in the fourth, on the fifth of the month').

old: Therefore I brought them out of the land of Egypt, and I led them out into the desert.
new: Therefore I cast them out of the land of Egypt, and I led them out into the desert.
reason: ejeci is 'I cast out', distinct from eduxi ('I led out') in the same verse; the edition renders ejicio 'cast out' (4:13, 11:9).

old: and I acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from which I brought them out in their sight.
new: and I acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their sight.
reason: de quibus ejeci eos: ejeci is 'I cast out' (as in 20:10, 20:22), not 'brought out'.

old: But I turned away My hand and acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from which I brought them out before their eyes.
new: But I turned away My hand and acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out before their eyes.
reason: de quibus ejeci eos: ejeci is 'I cast out' (as in 20:10, 20:14), not 'brought out'.

old: And I will subject you to My scepter, and I will bring you into the bonds of the covenant.
new: And I will subject you to My scepter, and I will bring you in the bonds of the covenant.
reason: in vinculis fœderis is ablative ("in the bonds"), not motion "into" them; "into" follows the Hebrew.

old: Vulgate chapter 21 begins five verses earlier than the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most modern English Bibles (Vulgate 21:1-5 corresponds to MT 20:45-49, and Vulgate 21:6-37 to MT 21:1-32).
new: The Vulgate's chapter division here agrees with the Hebrew Masoretic Text; in the alternative numbering, Vulgate 21:1-5 is 20:45-49 and Vulgate 21:6-37 is 21:1-32.
reason: The Masoretic Text also begins chapter 21 here (MT 21:1-37 = Vulgate 21:1-37), so the stated difference from the MT is false; also removes the claim about English Bibles.

old: "Son of man, set your face toward the way of the south, and let words drop toward the southwest, and prophesy to the forest of the southern field.
new: "Son of man, set your face against the way of the south, and let words drop toward the southwest, and prophesy to the forest of the southern field.
reason: Latin has contra ("against"), rendered "against" in the same formula at 25:2, 28:21, 29:2; "toward" follows the Hebrew.

old: You will lay out a road so that the sword may come to Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, and to Judah, into strongly fortified Jerusalem.
new: You will lay out a road so that the sword may come to Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, and to Judah, into very strongly fortified Jerusalem.
reason: munitissimam is superlative ("most/very strongly fortified"); the superlative was lost.

old: Her priests have despised My law, and they have defiled My sanctuaries; they have kept no distinction between the holy and the profane, and they have not discerned between the defiled and the clean; and they have turned their eyes away from My Sabbaths, and I was profaned in their midst.
new: Her priests have despised My law, and they have defiled My sanctuaries; they have kept no distinction between the holy and the profane, and they have not discerned between the defiled and the clean; and they have turned their eyes away from My Sabbaths, and I was defiled in their midst.
reason: coinquinabar is "I was defiled" (coinquino = defile, pollute); "profaned" follows the Hebrew.

old: The Vulgate renders "came from the desert" (veniebant de deserto) where the Hebrew contains a disputed term often translated "drunkards" or "Sabeans," and uses the masculine pronoun (eorum) for "their hands" and "their heads."
new: The Vulgate renders "came from the desert" (veniebant de deserto) where the Hebrew contains a disputed term (read either as "drunkards" or as "Sabeans"), and uses the masculine pronoun (eorum) for "their hands" and "their heads."
reason: Removes a claim about how the term is usually translated; keeps the neutral Latin/Hebrew comparison.

old: And I said of her who was worn out in adulteries: 'Now even this one will commit fornication in her fornication.'
new: And I said to her who was worn out in adulteries: 'Now even this one will commit fornication in her fornication.'
reason: dixi ei is "I said to her" (dative); "of her" follows the Hebrew.

old: Latin strues ossium ("piles of bones", echoed by ossa in v. 10) translates the Hebrew consonants literally as bones used for fuel, whereas many modern versions emend the Hebrew to "wood" or "logs." The Vulgate also renders the second half of the verse with perfect indicatives ("has boiled up... have been boiled thoroughly") rather than imperatives.
new: Latin strues ossium ("piles of bones", echoed by ossa in v. 10) follows the Hebrew "bones" literally, as bones used for fuel. The Vulgate also renders the second half of the verse with perfect indicatives ("has boiled up... have been boiled thoroughly") rather than imperatives.
reason: Removes a claim about what modern versions do.

old: 'Speak to the house of Israel, "This is what the Lord God says: Look, I will profane My sanctuary, the pride of your dominion, and the delight of your eyes, and that over which your soul is in dread; your sons and your daughters whom you left behind will fall by the sword.
new: 'Speak to the house of Israel, "This is what the Lord God says: Look, I will defile My sanctuary, the pride of your dominion, and the delight of your eyes, and that over which your soul is in dread; your sons and your daughters whom you left behind will fall by the sword.
reason: polluam is "I will defile", as polluo sanctuarium is rendered elsewhere (22:26; 23:38 "defiled My sanctuary"); "profane" follows the Hebrew.

old: And you shall say to the sons of Ammon, 'Hear the word of the Lord God. This is what the Lord God says: Because you said, "Aha, aha!" over My sanctuary, because it was profaned, and over the land of Israel, because it was made desolate, and over the house of Judah, because they were led into captivity,
new: And you shall say to the sons of Ammon, 'Hear the word of the Lord God. This is what the Lord God says: Because you said, "Aha, aha!" over My sanctuary, because it was defiled, and over the land of Israel, because it was made desolate, and over the house of Judah, because they were led into captivity,
reason: pollutum est is "was defiled" (polluo rendered "defile" throughout); "profaned" follows the Hebrew.

old: Vulgate super repentino casu tuo ("at your sudden fall") takes the Hebrew phrase usually rendered "every moment" (lirga'im) in the sense of suddenness.
new: Vulgate super repentino casu tuo ("at your sudden fall") takes the Hebrew phrase meaning "every moment" (lirga'im) in the sense of suddenness.
reason: Removes a claim about how translations render the Hebrew; restated neutrally.

old: Syria was your merchant because of the abundance of your works; they displayed gems, and purple, and checkered cloth, and fine linen, and silk, and chodchod in your market.
new: The Syrian was your merchant because of the abundance of your works; they displayed gems, and purple, and checkered cloth, and fine linen, and silk, and chodchod in your market.
reason: Syrus is the gentilic "the Syrian", not the country name.

old: Damascus was your merchant in the abundance of your works, in the abundance of diverse wealth, in rich wine, in wool of the finest color.
new: The Damascene was your merchant in the abundance of your works, in the abundance of diverse wealth, in rich wine, in wool of the finest color.
reason: Damascenus is the gentilic "the Damascene", not the city name.

old: And the message of the Lord came to me, saying:
new: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:
reason: sermo Domini is rendered "the word of the Lord" in every other occurrence of this formula.

old: "Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, 'This is what the Lord God says: Because your heart has been lifted up, and you have said, "I am God, and I have sat in the seat of God in the heart of the sea," although you are a man and not God, and you have set your heart like the heart of God;
new: "Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, 'This is what the Lord God says: Because your heart has been lifted up, and you have said, "I am God, and I have sat in the seat of God in the heart of the sea," although you are a man and not a god, and you have set your heart like the heart of God;
reason: The critical text has lowercase non deus ("not a god") against Deus/Dei in the same verse; capital "God" erases the distinction.

old: Therefore, this is what the Lord God says: Because your heart has been lifted up like the heart of God,
new: Therefore, this is what the Lord God says: Because your heart has been lifted up like the heart of a god,
reason: The critical text reads lowercase quasi cor dei here (contrast cor Dei in v. 2), i.e. "the heart of a god".

old: Will you really speak, saying, "I am God," before those who kill you, although you are a man and not God, in the hand of those who strike you down?
new: Will you really speak, saying, "I am God," before those who kill you, although you are a man and not a god, in the hand of those who strike you down?
reason: The critical text has lowercase non deus ("not a god") in contrast to Deus ego sum.

old: And the message of the Lord came to me, saying: "Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre,
new: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: "Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre,
reason: sermo Domini is rendered "the word of the Lord" in every other occurrence of this formula.

old: Vulgate has singular "your sanctification" (sanctificationem tuam, the Vulgate's standard rendering of Hebrew miqdash, "sanctuary"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has plural "your sanctuaries."
new: Vulgate has singular "your sanctification" (sanctificationem tuam), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has plural "your sanctuaries."
reason: sanctificatio is not the Vulgate's standard rendering of miqdash (normally sanctuarium, as in 24:21 and 25:3); the false claim is removed.

old: And the message of the Lord came to me, saying:
new: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:
reason: sermo Domini is rendered "the word of the Lord" in every other occurrence of this formula.

old: Among the other kingdoms it will be the lowliest, and it will no longer be lifted up above the nations; and I will diminish them so that they will not rule over the peoples.
new: Among the other kingdoms it will be the lowliest, and it will no longer be lifted up above the nations; and I will diminish them so that they will not rule over the nations.
reason: gentibus is "nations" per the edition's rendering of gentes; "peoples" is used for populi.

old: Therefore the Lord God says this: "I will spread My net over you in a multitude of many peoples, and I will draw you out in My dragnet.
new: Therefore this is what the Lord God says: "I will spread My net over you in a multitude of many peoples, and I will draw you out in My dragnet.
reason: Latin "Propterea hæc dicit Dominus Deus" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: All the lights of the sky I will make mourn over you, and I will set darkness over your land, says the Lord God, when your wounded have fallen in the midst of the land, declares the Lord God.
new: All the lights of the sky I will make mourn over you, and I will set darkness over your land, says the Lord God, when your wounded have fallen in the midst of the land, says the Lord God.
reason: ait Dominus Deus is rendered "says the Lord God" throughout the edition (e.g. 20:40, 26:5, 30:6); "declares" is the Hebrew ne'um formula.

old: The final clause ('when your wounded have fallen in the midst of the land, declares the Lord God') is distinctive to the Clementine Vulgate and absent from the Masoretic Text; 'moerere' ('mourn') also translates a Hebrew verb meaning both 'darken' and 'mourn.'
new: The final clause ('when your wounded have fallen in the midst of the land, says the Lord God') is absent from the Masoretic Text; 'moerere' ('mourn') also translates a Hebrew verb meaning both 'darken' and 'mourn.'
reason: Matches the verse wording; drops the unsupported claim that the clause is peculiar to the Clementine edition.

old: For the Lord God says this: "The sword of the king of Babylon will come to you.
new: For this is what the Lord God says: "The sword of the king of Babylon will come to you.
reason: Latin "Quia hæc dicit Dominus Deus" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: And I will destroy all its livestock that were beside abundant waters; and the foot of man will no longer stir them up, nor will the hoof of livestock disturb them.
new: And I will destroy all its livestock that were beside very many waters; and the foot of man will no longer stir them up, nor will the hoof of livestock disturb them.
reason: aquas plurimas is superlative ("very many waters"; cf. 31:6 gentium plurimarum "very many nations").

old: Then I will make their waters most pure, and I will lead their rivers like oil, declares the Lord God,
new: Then I will make their waters most pure, and I will lead their rivers like oil, says the Lord God,
reason: ait Dominus Deus is rendered "says the Lord God" throughout the edition.

old: It is a lamentation, and they will lament it; the daughters of the nations will lament it; over Egypt and over its multitude they will lament it, declares the Lord God."
new: It is a lamentation, and they will lament it; the daughters of the nations will lament it; over Egypt and over its multitude they will lament it, says the Lord God."
reason: ait Dominus Deus is rendered "says the Lord God" throughout the edition.

old: The Clementine Vulgate omits verse 19 (found in the Masoretic Text and modern editions), moving directly from verse 18 to verse 20.
reason: False for this Latin: the critical text has 32:19 (Quo pulchrior es? descende, et dormi cum incircumcisis), carried as an additional verse after 32:18.

old: Edom is there, and its kings, and all its leaders, who were placed with their army, with those killed by the sword, and who slept with the uncircumcised and with those who go down into the pit.
new: Idumea is there, and its kings, and all its leaders, who were placed with their army, with those killed by the sword, and who slept with the uncircumcised and with those who go down into the pit.
reason: Latin has Idumæa, which the edition renders "Idumea" (25:12-14, 35:15, 36:5); "Edom" follows the Hebrew.

old: Pharaoh saw them and was comforted over all his multitude that was killed by the sword: Pharaoh and all his army, declares the Lord God.
new: Pharaoh saw them and was comforted over all his multitude that was killed by the sword: Pharaoh and all his army, says the Lord God.
reason: ait Dominus Deus is rendered "says the Lord God" throughout the edition.

old: For I have put My terror in the land of the living, and he has slept in the midst of the uncircumcised with those killed by the sword: Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord God."
new: For I have put My terror in the land of the living, and he has slept in the midst of the uncircumcised with those killed by the sword: Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God."
reason: ait Dominus Deus is rendered "says the Lord God" throughout the edition.

old: Vulgate 'egerit poenitentiam' (lit. 'does penance / repents') renders a Hebrew verb meaning simply 'turns back'; similarly in v. 16, 'non imputabuntur' ('will not be imputed') corresponds to 'will not be remembered' in the Masoretic Text.
new: Vulgate 'egerit poenitentiam' ('repents') renders a Hebrew verb meaning 'turns back'; similarly in v. 16, 'non imputabuntur' ('will not be imputed') corresponds to 'will not be remembered' in the Masoretic Text.
reason: Drops the confessional gloss "does penance" and the evaluative "simply"; keeps the neutral lexical comparison.

old: The Clementine Vulgate omits verse 26 (found in the Masoretic Text and modern editions), moving directly from verse 25 to verse 27.
reason: False for this Latin: the critical text has 33:26 (stetistis in gladiis vestris...), carried as an additional verse after 33:25.

old: Therefore you will say to them: 'The Lord God says this: "You who eat with blood, and lift up your eyes to your uncleannesses, and shed blood, will you indeed possess the land by inheritance?"'
new: Therefore you will say to them: 'This is what the Lord God says: "You who eat with blood, and lift up your eyes to your uncleannesses, and shed blood, will you indeed possess the land by inheritance?"'
reason: Latin "Hæc dicit" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: Latin germen nominatum ("a renowned shoot") renders the Hebrew "planting of renown" with germen ("shoot/sprout"), echoing the messianic title used in the Vulgate of Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15.
new: Latin germen nominatum ("a renowned shoot") renders the Hebrew "planting of renown" with germen ("shoot/sprout"), the same noun the Vulgate uses in Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15.
reason: Removes the doctrinal label "messianic title"; keeps the factual lexical cross-reference.

old: And they will know that I, the Lord their God, am with them, and that they themselves are My people, the house of Israel, declares the Lord God.
new: And they will know that I, the Lord their God, am with them, and that they themselves are My people, the house of Israel, says the Lord God.
reason: ait Dominus Deus is rendered "says the Lord God" throughout the edition.

old: And I will strike a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting pact for them. And I will establish them and multiply them, and I will place My sanctification in their midst forever.
new: And I will strike a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant for them. And I will establish them and multiply them, and I will place My sanctification in their midst forever.
reason: pactum (like fœdus earlier in the verse) is rendered "covenant" in this edition.

old: And I will make My holy name known in the midst of My people Israel, and I will not profane My holy name any longer; and the nations will know that I am the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.
new: And I will make My holy name known in the midst of My people Israel, and I will not defile My holy name any longer; and the nations will know that I am the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.
reason: polluo is rendered "defile" throughout (36:17-23, 37:23, 43:7-8); "profane" breaks the series.

old: Vulgate 'non polluam' is first-person active ("I will not profane"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered permissively ("I will not let My holy name be profaned").
new: Vulgate 'non polluam' is first-person active ("I will not defile"), where the Hebrew can be read permissively ("I will not let My holy name be profaned").
reason: Match the verse's "defile" and drop the claim about how the Hebrew is "commonly rendered".

old: And oblique windows in the chambers and in their fronts, which were inside the gate on every side all around; and likewise there were also windows in the vestibules all around on the inside, and before the fronts a depiction of palm trees.
new: And slanted windows in the chambers and in their fronts, which were inside the gate on every side all around; and likewise there were also windows in the vestibules all around on the inside, and before the fronts a depiction of palm trees.
reason: fenestræ obliquæ is "slanted windows" in 41:16 and 41:26; keep one rendering within the vision.

old: Verse 30, which in the Hebrew Masoretic Text adds a separate vestibule measurement, is absent from the Clementine Vulgate (as also from the Septuagint), so the numbering moves directly from 40:29 to 40:31.
reason: False for this Latin: the critical text has 40:30 (Et vestibulum per gyrum...), shown as an additional verse after 40:29.

old: And in the vestibule of the gate, two tables on this side and two tables on that side, so that the burnt offering may be sacrificed on them, and the offering for sin and for offense.
new: And in the vestibule of the gate, two tables on this side and two tables on that side, so that the burnt offering may be sacrificed on them, and the offering for sin and for guilt.
reason: pro delicto is "for guilt" in 44:29, 46:20 and Leviticus; "offense" here and "trespass" in 42:13 are outliers.

old: Latin "labia" ("rims" or "lips") reflects a Vulgate-distinct rendering of a difficult Hebrew architectural term often translated "hooks" in Masoretic-based versions.
new: Latin labia ("rims," literally "lips") renders a rare Hebrew term of uncertain meaning.
reason: Remove the claim about what "Masoretic-based versions" translate; keep only the lexical point.

old: And between the chambers was a width of twenty cubits all around the house on every side,
new: And between the treasury chambers was a width of twenty cubits all around the house on every side,
reason: gazophylacia is "treasury chambers" in 40:17-46, 45:5, 46:19 and is kept distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: And he led me out into the outer court by the way leading to the north, and he brought me into the chamber that was opposite the separated building and opposite the edifice facing toward the north.
new: And he led me out into the outer court by the way leading to the north, and he brought me into the treasury chamber that was opposite the separated building and opposite the edifice facing toward the north.
reason: gazophylacium = "treasury chamber" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalamus ("chamber").

old: And before the chambers was a walkway ten cubits in width, facing toward the interior, a way of one cubit. And their doors were toward the north,
new: And before the treasury chambers was a walkway ten cubits in width, facing toward the interior, a way of one cubit. And their doors were toward the north,
reason: gazophylacia = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: where the chambers in the upper parts were lower, because they supported the porticoes that projected out from them, from the lower and from the middle parts of the building.
new: where the treasury chambers in the upper parts were lower, because they supported the porticoes that projected out from them, from the lower and from the middle parts of the building.
reason: gazophylacia = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: And the outer enclosure wall alongside the chambers that were on the way of the outer court before the chambers: its length was fifty cubits,
new: And the outer enclosure wall alongside the treasury chambers that were on the way of the outer court before the treasury chambers: its length was fifty cubits,
reason: gazophylacia (twice) = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: because the length of the chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits, and the length before the face of the temple was one hundred cubits.
new: because the length of the treasury chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits, and the length before the face of the temple was one hundred cubits.
reason: gazophylaciorum = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: And beneath these chambers was an entrance from the east for those entering into them from the outer court.
new: And beneath these treasury chambers was an entrance from the east for those entering into them from the outer court.
reason: gazophylacia = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: In the width of the enclosure wall of the court that was opposite the eastern way, facing the separated building, there were also chambers before the building.
new: In the width of the enclosure wall of the court that was opposite the eastern way, facing the separated building, there were also treasury chambers before the building.
reason: gazophylacia = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: And there was a way before their face, according to the likeness of the chambers that were on the way of the north: according to their length, so also was their width, and every entrance of theirs, and the likenesses, and their doors.
new: And there was a way before their face, according to the likeness of the treasury chambers that were on the way of the north: according to their length, so also was their width, and every entrance of theirs, and the likenesses, and their doors.
reason: gazophylaciorum = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: According to the doors of the chambers that were on the way facing the south, there was a door at the head of the way, the way that was before the separated vestibule for those entering by the eastern way.
new: According to the doors of the treasury chambers that were on the way facing the south, there was a door at the head of the way, the way that was before the separated vestibule for those entering by the eastern way.
reason: gazophylaciorum = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46, distinct from thalami ("chambers").

old: And he said to me, "The chambers of the north and the chambers of the south, which are before the separated building, these are the holy chambers, in which the priests who draw near to the Lord into the Holy of Holies eat; there they will place the most holy things and the offering for sin and for trespass, for the place is holy.
new: And he said to me, "The treasury chambers of the north and the treasury chambers of the south, which are before the separated building, these are the holy treasury chambers, in which the priests who draw near to the Lord into the Holy of Holies eat; there they will place the most holy things and the offering for sin and for guilt, for the place is holy.
reason: gazophylacia (three times) = "treasury chambers" as in 40:17-46; pro delicto = "for guilt" as in 44:29, 46:20.

old: Latin Sancta sanctorum appears twice: first spatially with in ('into the Holy of Holies') modifying the priests who draw near to the Lord, and second as the object of ponent ('the most holy things', i.e., sacred offerings). The Vulgate also joins the offerings as oblationem pro peccato et pro delicto ('the offering for sin and for trespass').
new: Latin Sancta sanctorum appears twice: first spatially with in ('into the Holy of Holies') modifying the priests who draw near to the Lord, and second as the object of ponent ('the most holy things', i.e., sacred offerings). The Vulgate also joins the offerings as oblationem pro peccato et pro delicto ('the offering for sin and for guilt').
reason: Keep the note in step with the verse (pro delicto = "for guilt").

old: And you shall grant to the priests and the Levites who are of the offspring of Zadok, who approach Me,' says the Lord God, 'to offer to Me a young bull from the herd for sin.
new: And you shall grant to the priests and the Levites who are of the seed of Zadok, who approach Me,' says the Lord God, 'to offer to Me a young bull from the herd for sin.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And when they go out into the outer court to the people, they shall take off their garments in which they had ministered and lay them away in the treasury of the sanctuary; and they shall clothe themselves with other garments, and they shall not sanctify the people with their garments.
new: And when they go out into the outer court to the people, they shall take off their garments in which they had ministered and lay them away in the treasury chamber of the sanctuary; and they shall clothe themselves with other garments, and they shall not sanctify the people with their garments.
reason: gazophylacium = "treasury chamber" throughout the vision (40:17-46, 42:1-13, 45:5, 46:19).

old: The Vulgate renders the priestly rooms as the singular 'treasury of the sanctuary' (Latin in gazophylacio sanctuarii), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'the holy chambers.'
new: The Vulgate renders the priestly rooms as the singular 'treasury chamber of the sanctuary' (Latin in gazophylacio sanctuarii), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'the holy chambers.'
reason: Keep the note in step with the verse.

old: And they shall not take as wives a widow or a divorced woman, but virgins of the offspring of the house of Israel; yet they may also take a widow who has been a widow of a priest.
new: And they shall not take as wives a widow or a divorced woman, but virgins of the seed of the house of Israel; yet they may also take a widow who has been a widow of a priest.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And on every side there shall be a sanctified portion of five hundred by five hundred, square all around, and fifty cubits for its surrounding grounds around its perimeter.
new: And on every side there shall be a sanctified portion of five hundred by five hundred, square all around, and fifty cubits for its outskirts around its perimeter.
reason: suburbana is "outskirts" in 48:15 and 48:17; keep one rendering within the vision.

old: When the man who had a line in his hand went out toward the east, he measured a thousand cubits, and led me through the water up to the ankles.
new: When the man who had a cord in his hand went out toward the east, he measured a thousand cubits, and led me through the water up to the ankles.
reason: funiculus (the measuring man's cord) is "cord" in 40:3.

old: Vulgate Metiemini etiam plagam orientalem ("You shall also measure the eastern side") reflects a verbal reading of the Hebrew consonants normally rendered "this is the eastern side"; in v. 19, Vulgate also translates Hebrew Meriboth literally as aquas contradictionis ("the waters of contradiction").
new: Vulgate Metiemini etiam plagam orientalem ("You shall also measure the eastern side") takes the Hebrew verb "you shall measure" together with the following words "and the eastern side"; in v. 19, Vulgate also translates Hebrew Meriboth literally as aquas contradictionis ("the waters of contradiction").
reason: The Hebrew itself has the verb "you shall measure" here; drop the inaccurate "verbal reading" claim and the reference to how it is "normally rendered".

old: Vulgate reads sanctuarium ("the sanctuary"), taking the underlying Hebrew form as the noun "sanctuary" rather than the participle "consecrated" applied to the priests in Hebrew-based translations.
new: Vulgate reads sanctuarium ("the sanctuary"), taking the underlying Hebrew form as the noun "sanctuary" rather than as the participle "consecrated" applied to the priests.
reason: Remove the claim about "Hebrew-based translations".

old: Vulgate Dominus ibidem renders the symbolic Hebrew name YHWH Shammah ("the Lord is there"), with Latin ibidem carrying the emphatic nuance "in that very place."
new: Latin Dominus ibidem (literally "the Lord in that very place") renders the Hebrew name meaning "the Lord is there."
reason: Remove "YHWH" (the edition avoids the divine name in notes) and the interpretive "symbolic"; keep the lexical point.

old: And the king told Ashpenaz, the overseer of the eunuchs, to bring in from the sons of Israel, and from the royal offspring and that of the rulers,
new: And the king told Ashpenaz, the overseer of the eunuchs, to bring in from the sons of Israel, and from the royal seed and that of the rulers,
reason: Latin semine (regio) (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And in every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king questioned them, he found in them tenfold above all the diviners and magicians who were in his entire kingdom.
new: And in every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king questioned them, he found in them tenfold above all the soothsayers and magicians who were in his entire kingdom.
reason: ariolus is rendered "soothsayer" in 2:2, 2:10, 2:27 (where "diviners" renders aruspices in the same list); keep the two Latin terms distinct.

old: Latin invenit in eis decuplum super ('he found in them tenfold above') reflects a distinctive Vulgate phrasing without the Hebrew comparative 'better', while ariolos et magos literally denotes 'diviners and magicians'.
new: Latin invenit in eis decuplum super literally reads 'he found in them tenfold above'.
reason: The Hebrew has no word 'better' here ('ten hands above'), so the comparison is inaccurate; the ariolos gloss is dropped to match the verse's "soothsayers".

old: And once he was removed, he ordered the other one to come and said to him, "Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you, and lust has perverted your heart."
new: And once he was removed, he ordered the other one to come and said to him, "Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you, and lust has perverted your heart."
reason: Latin semen (vocative Semen Chanaan) (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And He Himself changes times and ages; He removes kingdoms and establishes them; He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who understand instruction.
new: And He Himself changes times and ages; He transfers kingdoms and establishes them; He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who understand instruction.
reason: transfert regna means "transfers kingdoms"; "removes" follows the Aramaic "removes kings" rather than the Latin.

old: Latin favillam literally means "fine ash/dust" rather than "chaff."
new: Latin favillam literally means "fine ash/dust"; the Aramaic has "chaff."
reason: Make the contrast a neutral comparison with the Aramaic rather than an implied comment on other renderings.

old: Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face and paid homage to Daniel, and commanded that they offer sacrifices and incense to him.
new: Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face and worshiped Daniel, and commanded that they offer sacrifices and incense to him.
reason: adoravit is the verb rendered "worship" throughout (3:5-18, 6:11, 1:24-25 add.); "paid homage" softens it here, though the sacrifices and incense show the same sense.

old: And Daniel requested of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon; but Daniel himself remained at the doors of the king.
new: And Daniel requested of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon; but Daniel himself was at the doors of the king.
reason: erat in foribus regis is simply "was at the doors"; "remained" adds a sense of continuation the Latin does not state.

old: Unlike the Aramaic Masoretic Text, which begins conditionally, the Vulgate follows the Greek Theodotion reading with a direct affirmation: 'Ecce enim' ('For look').
new: Latin 'Ecce enim' ('For look') is a direct affirmation, whereas the Aramaic Masoretic Text begins conditionally ('if').
reason: Keep the factual contrast but drop the unsupported claim that the Vulgate 'follows' Theodotion here (Ecce reflects the Aramaic particle read as 'behold').

old: Verses 3:24-90 preserve the deuterocanonical Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men, translated in the Vulgate from the Greek Theodotion text and absent from the Aramaic Masoretic Text.
new: Verses 3:24-90 preserve the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men, translated in the Vulgate from the Greek Theodotion text and absent from the Aramaic Masoretic Text.
reason: "deuterocanonical" is a confessional canon classification, not information about the Latin; the rest of the note is factual.

old: to whom You spoke, promising that You would multiply their offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea;
new: to whom You spoke, promising that You would multiply their seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea;
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin 'infernus' translates Greek 'Hades' (Hebrew 'Sheol'), denoting the underworld or realm of the dead, as reflected in the parallel phrase 'from the hand of death.'
new: Latin 'infernus' translates Greek 'Hades', denoting the underworld or realm of the dead, as reflected in the parallel phrase 'from the hand of death.'
reason: This passage has no extant Hebrew text, so the parenthetical '(Hebrew Sheol)' is inaccurate.

old: Bless the Lord, God of gods, all devout ones; praise and give thanks to Him, for His mercy is for all ages."
new: Bless the Lord God of gods, all devout ones; praise and give thanks to Him, for His mercy is for all ages."
reason: Domino Deo deorum is the dative object ("the Lord God of gods"); the comma made "God of gods" read as a second vocative alongside omnes religiosi.

old: Following the Greek Theodotion text, the Vulgate reads the singular 'filio Dei' ('a son of God', also renderable 'the Son of God'), whereas the Aramaic Masoretic Text has the plural 'bar elahin' ('a son of the gods').
new: Latin 'filio Dei' has the singular 'Dei' ('a son of God'), as does the Greek Theodotion text, whereas the Aramaic Masoretic Text has the plural 'bar elahin' ('a son of the gods').
reason: Keep the neutral textual comparison but drop the steer toward 'the Son of God', which decides a disputed referent that the verse deliberately leaves lowercase and open.

old: Belteshazzar, chief of the diviners, since I know that you have the spirit of the holy gods in you, and no mystery is impossible for you, relate the visions of my dreams, which I saw, and their explanation.
new: Belteshazzar, chief of the soothsayers, since I know that you have the spirit of the holy gods in you, and no secret is impossible for you, relate the visions of my dreams, which I saw, and their explanation.
reason: ariolorum is rendered "soothsayers" elsewhere (2:2, 2:10, 2:27; "diviners" is used for aruspices), and sacramentum is "secret" as distinct from mysterium "mystery" (2:18, 2:30, 2:47).

old: Vulgate eleemosynis redime ("redeem with almsgiving") and forsitan ignoscet delictis tuis ("perhaps He will forgive your offenses") reflect the traditional Greek and Latin rendering, where the Aramaic reads "break off your sins by righteousness" and "perhaps there may be a lengthening of your prosperity."
new: Vulgate eleemosynis redime ("redeem with almsgiving") and forsitan ignoscet delictis tuis ("perhaps He will forgive your offenses") differ from the Aramaic, which has "by righteousness" and "perhaps there may be a lengthening of your prosperity."
reason: Remove the characterization of a 'traditional rendering' and the one-sided gloss of the disputed Aramaic verb (break off/redeem); keep the factual contrast.

old: In this Latin text, 4:37 opens with Nebuchadnezzar's proclamation and praise (corresponding to Vulgate 3:98-100 / English 4:1-3) before concluding with the king's final doxology.
new: This verse renders the Latin 3:98-100 (Nebuchadnezzar's proclamation and praise, English 4:1-3) followed by the Latin 4:37 (the king's final praise).
reason: In the critical text the proclamation is numbered 3:98-100, not part of 4:37, so the note's claim about 'this Latin text' is false.

old: For this reason, the part of the hand that wrote what has been inscribed was sent from Him.
new: For this reason, the joint of the hand that wrote what has been inscribed was sent from Him.
reason: articulus manus is the same term rendered "the joints of the hand" in 5:5 (and glossed "joint" in this verse's note); "part" is vaguer than the Latin.

old: Vulgate 'cibi' ('food') renders the obscure Aramaic term often translated 'diversions' or 'entertainment,' and 'dormivit incoenatus' literally says the king went to sleep without supper before sleep departed from him.
new: Vulgate 'cibi' ('food') renders an obscure Aramaic term, and 'dormivit incoenatus' literally says the king went to sleep without supper before sleep departed from him.
reason: Remove the claim about how the term is 'often translated'; notes should not describe other translations.

old: But the saints of the Most High God will receive the kingdom, and they will possess the kingdom forever, and for ages of ages.'
new: But the holy ones of the Most High God will receive the kingdom, and they will possess the kingdom forever, and for ages of ages.'
reason: OT sancti (persons) is rendered "holy ones" in this edition, as in Daniel 4:17, 8:13 and 8:24 (populum sanctorum "the people of the holy ones").

old: I was watching, and look, that horn was making war against the saints and prevailing over them,
new: I was watching, and look, that horn was making war against the holy ones and prevailing over them,
reason: OT sancti (persons) is rendered "holy ones" (cf. 4:17, 8:13, 8:24).

old: until the Ancient of Days came and gave judgment to the saints of the Exalted One, and the time arrived, and the saints took possession of the kingdom.
new: until the Ancient of Days came and gave judgment to the holy ones of the Exalted One, and the time arrived, and the holy ones took possession of the kingdom.
reason: OT sancti (persons) is rendered "holy ones" (cf. 4:17, 8:13, 8:24).

old: And he will speak words against the Exalted One, and he will crush the saints of the Most High; and he will think that he can change times and laws, and they will be handed over into his hand until a time, and times, and half a time.
new: And he will speak words against the Exalted One, and he will crush the holy ones of the Most High; and he will think that he can change times and laws, and they will be handed over into his hand until a time, and times, and half a time.
reason: OT sancti (persons) is rendered "holy ones" (cf. 4:17, 8:13, 8:24).

old: And let the kingdom, and the authority, and the greatness of the kingdom that is beneath the whole heaven, be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings will serve Him and obey.'
new: And let the kingdom, and the authority, and the greatness of the kingdom that is beneath the whole heaven, be given to the people of the holy ones of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings will serve Him and obey.'
reason: populo sanctorum matches 8:24 populum sanctorum, rendered "the people of the holy ones". (Flag, not changed: capital "Him" decides whether ei/cujus refers to the people or to the Most High; the Latin is ambiguous.)

old: The Vulgate reads abbreviatae sunt ("have been shortened") where the Hebrew verb is commonly rendered "decreed," and masculine capitalized Sanctus sanctorum ("the Holy One of holies") rather than a neuter "most holy place."
new: The Vulgate reads abbreviatae sunt ("have been shortened"), where the Hebrew verb means "decreed" (literally "cut"), and the masculine Sanctus sanctorum ("the Holy One of holies"), not the neuter sanctum sanctorum used elsewhere for the most holy place.
reason: Remove the claim about how the Hebrew is 'commonly rendered' and the appeal to capitalization; state the Latin's grammatical contrast factually. (Flag, not changed: the verse's capitalized "Holy One of holies" decides a disputed referent.)

old: Latin dissolutae sunt compages meae ("my joints have been loosened") is a distinctly Vulgate reading corresponding to the Hebrew clause usually rendered "pains/anguish turned upon me."
new: Latin dissolutae sunt compages meae ("my joints have been loosened") is a distinctly Vulgate reading, where the Hebrew has "my pangs have turned upon me."
reason: Replace the claim about how the Hebrew is 'usually rendered' with a direct statement of what the Hebrew says.

old: Latin Cum ego egrederer, apparuit princeps Graecorum veniens uses past tenses ("When I was going out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming"), whereas the Hebrew is normally rendered as future.
new: Latin Cum ego egrederer, apparuit princeps Graecorum veniens uses past tenses ("When I was going out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming"), whereas the Hebrew uses participles ("I am going out, and the prince of Greece is coming").
reason: Replace the claim about how the Hebrew is 'normally rendered' with a factual description of the Hebrew forms.

old: And after the end of years they will make an alliance; and the daughter of the king of the south will come to the king of the north to make friendship, and she will not retain the strength of the arm, nor will her offspring stand; and she herself will be handed over, and her young men who brought her, and those who were strengthening her in the times.
new: And after the end of years they will make an alliance; and the daughter of the king of the south will come to the king of the north to make friendship, and she will not retain the strength of the arm, nor will her seed stand; and she herself will be handed over, and her young men who brought her, and those who were strengthening her in the times.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And arms from him will stand, and they will defile the sanctuary of strength, and take away the continual sacrifice; and they will place the abomination for desolation.
new: And arms from him will stand, and they will defile the sanctuary of strength, and take away the perpetual sacrifice; and they will place the abomination for desolation.
reason: juge sacrificium is rendered "perpetual sacrifice" in 8:11, 8:12, 8:13; use the same here.

old: And from the time when the continual sacrifice has been taken away and the abomination has been set up for desolation, there will be one thousand two hundred ninety days.
new: And from the time when the perpetual sacrifice has been taken away and the abomination has been set up for desolation, there will be one thousand two hundred ninety days.
reason: juge sacrificium is rendered "perpetual sacrifice" in 8:11, 8:12, 8:13; use the same here.

old: The Vulgate translates the children's symbolic names into Latin ("Absque misericordia", "Without Mercy"; "Non populus meus", "Not My People" in 1:9) rather than transliterating the Hebrew. Its closing clause "oblivione obliviscar eorum" ("in forgetfulness I will forget them") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew is commonly rendered as refusing forgiveness or carrying away.
new: The Vulgate translates the children's symbolic names into Latin ("Absque misericordia", "Without Mercy"; "Non populus meus", "Not My People" in 1:9) rather than transliterating the Hebrew. Its closing clause "oblivione obliviscar eorum" ("in forgetfulness I will forget them") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew is read as refusing forgiveness or as carrying away.
reason: "commonly rendered" is a claim about how translations render the Hebrew; restated as a neutral comparison with the Hebrew.
