new: Latin ambulantes ("those who walk") takes the Hebrew term as a plural participle (persons walking) rather than as a noun meaning "goings" or "access."
reason: Removes the claim about what translations do and the interpretive "angelic attendants"; keeps the grammatical point about ambulantes.

old: Listen, Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are foreshadowing men: for look, I will bring My servant, the Dawn.
new: Listen, Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are foreshadowing men: for look, I will bring My servant, the Rising.
reason: Oriens is rendered "Rising" at 6:12 (where it plays on orietur "will rise"); the same name should get the same English. Capitalization left as the edition has it (disputed figure, flagged).

old: Latin Orientem ("the Dawn" or "the Rising") follows the Septuagint Anatole as a messianic title for Hebrew Tsemach ("the Branch"); viri portendentes ("foreshadowing men") literally means men who serve as a prophetic portent.
new: Latin Orientem ("the Rising," also "the Dawn" or "the East") follows the Septuagint anatole where the Hebrew has tsemach ("Branch" or "Sprout"); viri portendentes ("foreshadowing men") means men who serve as a portent.
reason: Removes the doctrinal label "messianic title" and the added "prophetic"; aligns the gloss with the verse.

old: For look, the stone that I have placed before Joshua: on one stone are seven eyes; look, I will carve its engraving, declares the Lord of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.
new: For look, the stone that I have placed before Joshua: on one stone are seven eyes; look, I will carve its engraving, says the Lord of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.
reason: Latin "ait Dominus exercituum" is rendered "says the Lord of hosts", the edition's majority for this formula, not "declares".

old: Latin "in me" literally translates the Hebrew preposition denoting interior prophetic speech, often rendered "with me" in modern versions.
reason: Claim about what modern versions do; the point about in me is already made in the note at 1:9.

old: And he said, "These are the two sons of oil who stand beside the Ruler of the whole earth."
new: And he said, "These are the two sons of oil who stand beside the Sovereign of the whole earth."
reason: Dominator (of God) is "the Sovereign" elsewhere in this edition (Isa 3:1; 10:16, 33; Dan 5:23; Sir 15:10; Mal 3:1).

old: And the angel answered and said to me, "These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand before the Ruler of all the earth."
new: And the angel answered and said to me, "These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand before the Sovereign of all the earth."
reason: Dominator is "the Sovereign" elsewhere in this edition (e.g. Dan 5:23 "the Sovereign of heaven", Mal 3:1).

old: and you will speak to him, saying, 'This is what the Lord of hosts declares, saying: Look, a man, Rising is His name, and beneath Him He will rise, and He will build the temple for the Lord.
new: and you will speak to him, saying, 'This is what the Lord of hosts says: Look, a man, Rising is His name, and beneath Him He will rise, and He will build the temple for the Lord.
reason: Latin "Hæc ait Dominus exercituum, dicens" is the same formula (ait = says, not "declares"), rendered "This is what X says"; the pleonastic dicens is carried by the colon.

old: Latin "et erit sacerdos super solio suo" may be read either as "He will be a priest upon His throne" (uniting royal and priestly offices in the Messiah) or "a priest will be upon his throne" (pointing to the two figures in "between those two").
new: Latin "et erit sacerdos super solio suo" may be read either as "He will be a priest upon His throne" (one figure holding both offices) or "a priest will be upon his throne" (pointing to the two figures in "between those two").
reason: Removes the doctrinal identification "in the Messiah"; the grammatical ambiguity is kept. Verse capitalization left as the edition has it (disputed figure, flagged).

old: "This is what the Lord of hosts declares, saying, 'Render true judgment, and practice mercy and compassions, each one with his brother.
new: "This is what the Lord of hosts says: 'Render true judgment, and practice mercy and compassions, each one with his brother.
reason: Latin "Hæc ait Dominus exercituum, dicens" is the same formula (ait = says, not "declares"), rendered "This is what X says"; the pleonastic dicens is carried by the colon.

old: The Vulgate includes exercituum ("of hosts") in the opening formula (where the Hebrew has only "the LORD") and renders the final title as mons sanctificatus ("the sanctified mountain") rather than "the mountain of holiness."
new: The Vulgate includes exercituum ("of hosts") in the opening formula (where the Hebrew has only "the Lord") and renders the final title as mons sanctificatus ("the sanctified mountain") rather than "the mountain of holiness."
reason: House style: never capital LORD in notes.

old: The Vulgate reads salvator ("a savior," active, matching the Septuagint) rather than the passive Hebrew "saved/victorious," translates "afflicted/humble" as pauper ("poor"), and makes both donkeys feminine (asinam ... asinae), aligning with Matthew 21:5.
new: The Vulgate reads salvator ("a savior," active, matching the Septuagint) rather than the passive Hebrew "saved/victorious," translates "afflicted/humble" as pauper ("poor"), and reads the feminine asinam ("a female donkey") where the Hebrew has the masculine "donkey."
reason: False for the Latin: the colt (pullum filium) is masculine, only asinam and its dam asinæ are feminine; the Matthew alignment is removed. Verse capitalization of the king left as is (disputed figure, flagged).

old: Whereas the Hebrew shifts to the first person ("I have set your prisoners free"), the Vulgate uses the second-person verb emisisti ("You have released"), which traditional Latin exegesis often reads as addressed to the Messianic King of verses 9-10 releasing captives by the blood of His covenant (testamenti).
new: Whereas the Hebrew has the first person ("I have set your prisoners free"), the Vulgate uses the second-person verb emisisti ("you have released"); the Latin does not name the one addressed.
reason: Removes the doctrinal exegesis ("Messianic King"). Flag: the verse's capitalized "You/Your" settles a disputed addressee (Zion is addressed in 9:9, 9:12 tibi, 9:13); left unchanged per instructions.

old: From him the cornerstone, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle, from him every exactor will go out together.
new: From him the corner, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle, from him every exactor will go out together.
reason: angulus is "corner" (as in caput anguli, Ps 117:22 "head of the corner"); "stone" is not in the Latin and adds an interpretive image.

old: Vulgate "non erit lux, sed frigus et gelu" ("there will not be light, but cold and frost") follows the Septuagint in resolving a difficult Hebrew phrase often translated "the bright ones will congeal" or "dwindle."
new: Vulgate "non erit lux, sed frigus et gelu" ("there will not be light, but cold and frost") agrees with the Septuagint in reading a difficult Hebrew phrase as "cold and frost."
reason: Removes the claim about how the Hebrew is "often translated"; keeps the neutral Latin/Greek comparison.

old: And if Edom says, "We have been destroyed, yet returning we will rebuild what has been destroyed," the Lord of hosts says this: "They will build, and I will destroy; and they will be called the borders of wickedness, and the people with whom the Lord is angry forever."
new: And if Edom says, "We have been destroyed, yet returning we will rebuild what has been destroyed," this is what the Lord of hosts says: "They will build, and I will destroy; and they will be called the borders of wickedness, and the people with whom the Lord is angry forever."
reason: Latin "hæc dicit Dominus exercituum" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

old: Vulgate renders the difficult Hebrew idiom (often translated "him who wakes and him who answers") as "master and disciple" (magistrum et discipulum).
new: Vulgate renders the difficult Hebrew idiom (literally "one who wakes and one who answers") as "master and disciple" (magistrum et discipulum).
reason: Removes the claim about how the Hebrew is "often translated"; states the literal Hebrew neutrally.

old: Vulgate reads a second-person directive ("When you hate her, send her away," cf. Deut 24:1) followed by the warning that "iniquity will cover his garment," whereas many translations of the Hebrew render the opening clause as "I hate divorce."
new: Vulgate reads a second-person directive ("When you hate her, send her away," cf. Deut 24:1) followed by the warning that "iniquity will cover his garment"; the Hebrew opening clause can also be read as "he hates sending away."
reason: Removes the claim about what "many translations" do; keeps a neutral comparison with the Hebrew.

old: This Latin text continues chapter 3 through 3:24 rather than beginning a fourth chapter (English Protestant Bibles number 3:19-24 as 4:1-6).
new: This Latin text continues chapter 3 through 3:24 rather than beginning a fourth chapter (3:19-24 are numbered 4:1-6 in some editions).
reason: Removes the confessional claim about English Protestant Bibles; keeps the neutral numbering fact.

old: Latin "Pœnitentiam agite" literally means "do penance" (or "practice repentance"), the standard Vulgate idiom for "repent" and lexically linked to "pœnitentia" ("repentance") in vv. 8 and 11.
new: Latin "Pœnitentiam agite" literally means "do repentance," the standard Vulgate idiom for "repent" and lexically linked to "pœnitentia" ("repentance") in vv. 8 and 11.
reason: Note no longer glosses pœnitentiam agere as "do penance"; the edition renders it "repent" (literal "do repentance").

old: Latin "in quo mihi complacui" (literally "in whom I have pleased Myself / taken delight") uses the reflexive dative and perfect tense to express the Father's full delight in His Son.
new: Latin "in quo mihi complacui" (literally "in whom I have pleased Myself") uses the perfect tense with the reflexive dative "mihi."
reason: The closing clause ("to express the Father's full delight in His Son") is interpretive comment, not explanation of the Latin.

old: Latin poenitentiam agite literally means "do penance" or "practice repentance," the Vulgate idiom for Greek metanoeite; it is rendered "Repent" here, as in 3:2, where the Latin is identical.
new: Latin poenitentiam agite literally means "do repentance," the Vulgate idiom for Greek metanoeite; it is rendered "Repent" here, as in 3:2, where the Latin is identical.
reason: Note no longer glosses pœnitentiam agere as "do penance"; the edition renders it "repent" (literal "do repentance").

old: And while praying, do not speak much, like the pagans, for they think that through their much speaking they will be heard.
new: And while praying, do not speak much, like the Gentiles, for they think that through their much speaking they will be heard.
reason: ethnici is rendered "Gentiles" at 5:47; the same term in the same sense should get the same English.

old: So then, seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you besides.
new: So then, seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.
reason: adjicientur vobis is simply "will be added to you"; "besides" has no Latin basis.

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads the exclamation Quam ("How narrow...!") following the Greek variant ti, whereas many manuscripts and modern translations read causal hoti ("For/Because the gate is narrow").
new: The Vulgate reads the exclamation Quam ("How narrow...!"), corresponding to the Greek variant ti, where many Greek manuscripts read causal hoti ("For/Because the gate is narrow").
reason: Notes should not make claims about what modern translations do; keep only the neutral Latin/Greek comparison.

old: And then I will declare openly to them, 'I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice iniquity.'
new: And then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice iniquity.'
reason: confitebor illis is "I will declare/acknowledge to them"; "openly" has no Latin basis.

old: but the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and grinding of teeth."
new: but the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth."
reason: The identical formula ibi erit fletus et stridor dentium is rendered "weeping and gnashing of teeth" at 13:42 and 13:50.

old: And Jesus was going about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and proclaiming the Gospel of the kingdom, and curing every sickness and every infirmity.
new: And Jesus was going about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and curing every sickness and every infirmity.
reason: The identical phrase prædicans Evangelium regni is rendered "preaching the gospel of the kingdom" (lowercase) at 4:23.

old: Amen, I tell you, among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen; yet whoever is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he is.
new: Amen, I tell you, among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen; yet whoever is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he is.
reason: qui minor est is comparative ("lesser"), not superlative ("least"), and the rendering should not narrow its sense.

old: The Vulgate phrase "pœnitentiam agere" (here and in 11:21) literally means "to perform repentance" or "do penance," and serves as the regular Latin equivalent for "repent."
new: The Vulgate phrase "pœnitentiam agere" (here and in 11:21) literally means "to perform repentance" and serves as the regular Latin equivalent for "repent."
reason: Note no longer glosses pœnitentiam agere as "do penance"; the edition renders it "repent" (literal "do repentance").

old: But if you knew what this means, 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice,' you would never have condemned the innocent.
new: But if you knew what this means, 'Mercy I desire, and not sacrifice,' you would never have condemned the innocent.
reason: The identical quotation Misericordiam volo, et non sacrificium is rendered "Mercy I desire, and not sacrifice" at 9:13.

old: "Here is My servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul is thoroughly pleased. I will place My Spirit upon Him, and He will announce judgment to the nations.
new: "Here is My servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul is well pleased. I will place My Spirit upon Him, and He will announce judgment to the nations.
reason: bene complacuit is "is well pleased"; "thoroughly" overstates bene.

old: The Latin idiom poenitentiam egerunt (literally "did penance" or "practiced repentance") is Jerome's standard rendering of the Greek verb metanoeo ("repent").
new: The Latin idiom poenitentiam egerunt (literally "did repentance") is Jerome's standard rendering of the Greek verb metanoeo ("repent").
reason: Note no longer glosses pœnitentiam agere as "do penance"; the edition renders it "repent" (literal "do repentance").

old: and they will throw them into the furnace of fire. In that place will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
new: and they will throw them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
reason: Ibi erit is rendered "there will be" in the identical formula at 8:12; "In that place will be" is also awkward English.

old: and they will throw them into the furnace of fire; in that place will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
new: and they will throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
reason: ibi erit is rendered "there will be" in the identical formula at 8:12; "in that place will be" is also awkward English.

old: And coming into His own homeland, He was teaching them in their synagogues, so that they were astonished and said, "From where does this Man have this wisdom and mighty works?
new: And coming into His own homeland, He was teaching them in their synagogues, so that they were astonished and said, "From where does this man have this wisdom and mighty works?
reason: huic is just a pronoun ("this one"). Where the edition supplies "this man" for hic in the crowd's words (9:3, 12:23, 12:24), "man" is lowercase.

old: Now in the fourth watch of the night, He came to them walking on the sea.
new: For in the fourth watch of the night, He came to them walking on the sea.
reason: Quarta enim vigilia: enim is causal "for"; "Now" drops the connective (and follows the Greek de).

old: The Vulgate renders the elliptical Greek clause as a complete statement, "Whatever gift is from me will benefit you" (Latin Munus, quodcumque est ex me, tibi proderit), whereas Greek-based translations usually read "What you would have gained from me is an offering [to God]." In 15:6, the Clementine Vulgate also includes "or his mother" and reads "commandment" (mandatum) rather than "word."
new: The Vulgate renders the elliptical Greek clause as a complete statement, "Whatever gift is from me will benefit you" (Latin Munus, quodcumque est ex me, tibi proderit). In 15:6, the Clementine Vulgate also includes "or his mother" and reads "commandment" (mandatum) where critical Greek editions read "word."
reason: Removes a claim about what translations usually read; keeps the factual Latin/Greek comparison.

old: The Latin preserves the wordplay between Petrus ("Peter") and petram ("rock"). Inferi (genitive singular of inferus) literally denotes the underworld or realm of the dead (rendering Greek Hades), distinct from gehenna, though traditionally often translated "hell."
new: The Latin preserves the wordplay between Petrus ("Peter") and petram ("rock"). Inferi denotes the underworld or realm of the dead (rendering Greek Hades), distinct from gehenna.
reason: Removes the claim about traditional English translation and the uncertain grammatical label; keeps the lexical explanation.

old: And to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven also, and whatever you unbind on earth will be unbound in heaven also."
new: And to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven also, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven also."
reason: solveris/solutum is rendered "loose/loosed" in the parallel 18:18 (solveritis/soluta); same term, same sense.

old: Across 16:25-26, the Latin uses the single noun anima four times, spanning both earthly "life" (16:25) and one's eternal "soul" (16:26).
new: Across 16:25-26, the Latin uses the single noun anima four times, rendered "life" in 16:25 and "soul" in 16:26.
reason: "earthly" and "eternal" are interpretive glosses not in the Latin; the note should simply state the lexical fact.

old: Then the disciples approached Jesus privately and said, "Why were we not able to cast it out?"
new: Then the disciples approached Jesus privately and said, "Why were we not able to cast him out?"
reason: ejicere illum: illum is masculine "him" (as illum in 17:18); neuter "it" follows the Greek auto.

old: In that hour the disciples approached Jesus, saying, "Who, do you think, is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?"
new: In that hour the disciples approached Jesus, saying, "Who, do You think, is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?"
reason: putas is addressed to Jesus; the edition capitalizes pronouns referring to Jesus.

old: Looking steadily, Jesus said to them, "With human beings this is impossible; with God, however, everything is possible."
new: Looking at them, Jesus said to them, "With human beings this is impossible; with God, however, everything is possible."
reason: Aspiciens is simply "looking (at)"; "steadily" is an intensifier with no Latin basis (from the Greek emblepsas).

old: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached Him with her sons, paying homage and asking something from Him.
new: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached Him with her sons, worshiping and asking something from Him.
reason: adorans is the same verb rendered "worshiped" at 14:33 and 15:25 (adoraverunt/adoravit eum); "paying homage" alone here is an interpretive variation.

old: saying, "Teacher, Moses said that if anyone dies without having a son, his brother should marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.
new: saying, "Teacher, Moses said that if anyone dies without having a son, his brother should marry his wife and raise up seed for his brother.

old: Now there were seven brothers among us; and the first, having taken a wife, died, and having no offspring, left his wife to his brother.
new: Now there were seven brothers among us; and the first, having taken a wife, died, and having no seed, left his wife to his brother.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: The Vulgate shifts from "from" (ex) with the heart to "in" (in) with the soul and mind, echoing the Latin of Deuteronomy 6:5 rather than repeating a single preposition as in the Greek text.
new: The Vulgate shifts from "from" (ex) with the heart to "in" (in) with the soul and mind, whereas the Greek text repeats a single preposition.
reason: The Vulgate of Deuteronomy 6:5 has ex toto ... ex tota ... ex tota, so the claimed echo is false; the Greek comparison is kept.

old: but the one who perseveres to the very end, this one will be saved.
new: but the one who perseveres to the end, this one will be saved.
reason: usque in finem is "to the end"; "very" is an intensifier with no Latin basis.

old: Following the Latin and Byzantine textual tradition, the Clementine Vulgate omits "nor the Son," reading only neque angeli caelorum, nisi solus Pater ("not even the angels of the heavens, except the Father alone").
new: The Clementine Vulgate reads only neque angeli caelorum, nisi solus Pater ("not even the angels of the heavens, except the Father alone"), without "nor the Son," agreeing with the Byzantine Greek manuscripts; critical Greek editions include it.
reason: Many Old Latin witnesses do read neque filius, so "following the Latin tradition" is inaccurate; restated as a neutral comparison.

old: The prudent ones answered, saying, 'Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go instead to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.'
new: The prudent ones answered, saying, 'In case there is not enough for us and for you, go instead to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.'
reason: Ne forte non sufficiat is a negative purpose clause ("lest perhaps") motivating the command, not an independent statement of possibility.

old: The Vulgate places 'immediately' (statim) at the end of v. 15 modifying the master's departure, whereas many modern Greek editions and translations attach the adverb to the first servant's departure at the start of v. 16.
new: The Vulgate places 'immediately' (statim) at the end of v. 15 modifying the master's departure, whereas many modern Greek editions attach the adverb to the first servant's departure at the start of v. 16.
reason: Removes a claim about what translations do; the Greek-edition comparison is kept.

old: Then Jesus said to them, "All of you will suffer stumbling because of Me on this very night. For it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be dispersed.'
new: Then Jesus said to them, "All of you will suffer stumbling because of Me on this night. For it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be dispersed.'
reason: in ista nocte is simply "on this night" (as hac nocte in v. 34); "very" is an intensifier with no Latin basis.

old: The Vulgate translates the ambiguous Greek clause ep' ho parei clearly as a direct question, ad quid venisti? ("for what purpose have you come?"), whereas many translations from the Greek render it as a command ("do what you have come for").
new: The Vulgate renders the elliptical Greek clause eph' ho parei as a direct question, ad quid venisti? ("for what purpose have you come?").
reason: Removes a claim about what other translations do and corrects the transliteration (eph' ho); keeps the neutral Latin/Greek comparison.

old: Then when Judas, who had handed Him over, saw that He had been condemned, he was moved by remorse and brought back the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and the elders,
new: Then when Judas, who had handed Him over, saw that He had been condemned, he was moved by repentance and brought back the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and the elders,
reason: pœnitentia ductus: the edition renders pœnitentia as "repentance"; "remorse" narrows the Latin term interpretively.

old: and said to him, "See that you tell no one; but go, show yourself to the chief priest, and offer for your cleansing the things that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them."
new: and said to him, "See that you tell no one; but go, show yourself to the high priest, and offer for your cleansing the things that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them."
reason: Singular princeps sacerdotum is rendered "high priest" throughout this edition (e.g. Matt 26:3, 26:57; Mark 2:26); "chief priest" is reserved for plural principes sacerdotum.

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads "principi sacerdotum" ("to the chief priest," or "high priest"), whereas Greek manuscripts read simply "to the priest."
new: The Clementine Vulgate reads "principi sacerdotum" ("to the high priest"), whereas Greek manuscripts read simply "to the priest."
reason: Aligns the note with the corrected verse rendering of principi sacerdotum.

old: And Jesus said to them, "Can the sons of the wedding fast as long as the bridegroom is with them? For as long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.
new: And Jesus said to them, "Can the sons of the wedding fast as long as the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.
reason: Quanto tempore habent secum sponsum, non possunt jejunare has no connective; "For" adds a causal link not in the Latin.

old: The Vulgate distinctively reads 'cæcitate cordis eorum' ("the blindness of their heart") rather than "hardness of heart" as in most Greek-based translations.
new: The Vulgate distinctively reads 'cæcitate cordis eorum' ("the blindness of their heart"), where most Greek manuscripts read "hardness of heart."
reason: Replaces a claim about what translations do with a neutral comparison to the Greek.

old: and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed Him.
new: and Judas Iscariot, who also handed Him over.
reason: tradidit (of Judas) is rendered "handed Him over" throughout this edition (e.g. Matt 26:25, 27:3); "betrayed" is inconsistent.

old: Latin faber denotes a craftsman or artisan (traditionally rendered "carpenter"). The Vulgate reads Joseph (matching certain ancient manuscripts), whereas many Greek texts read "Joses."
new: Latin faber denotes a craftsman or artisan. The Vulgate reads Joseph (matching certain ancient manuscripts), whereas many Greek texts read "Joses."
reason: Removes a claim about how English translations traditionally render the word; keeps the lexical and textual information.

old: And He called the Twelve, and began to send them out two by two, and He was giving them authority over unclean spirits.
new: And He called the twelve, and began to send them out two by two, and He was giving them authority over unclean spirits.
reason: duodecim is lowercase "the twelve" elsewhere in this edition (Matt 26:14, 26:47; Mark 4:10).

old: And answering, He said to them, "You give them something to eat." And they said to Him, "Should we go and buy loaves for two hundred denarii and give them something to eat?"
new: And answering, He said to them, "You give them something to eat." And they said to Him, "Let us go and buy loaves for two hundred denarii, and we will give them something to eat."
reason: Euntes emamus ... et dabimus is a hortatory statement ("let us buy ... and we will give"), not a question; the question form follows the Greek.

old: And immediately He compelled His disciples to board the boat, so that they would go ahead of Him across the water to Bethsaida, while He Himself dismissed the people.
new: And immediately He compelled His disciples to board the boat, so that they would go ahead of Him across the strait to Bethsaida, while He Himself dismissed the people.

old: and running through that entire region, they began to carry around on mats those who were ill, wherever they heard He was.

reason: grabatum is rendered "cot" in this edition (Mark 2:4, 2:9, 2:11, 2:12).

old: The Clementine Vulgate joins "doctrines and precepts of men" with et ("and"), whereas the Greek lacks "and" and is commonly rendered "teaching as doctrines the commandments of men."
new: The Clementine Vulgate joins "doctrines and precepts of men" with et ("and"), whereas the Greek lacks "and" and reads "teaching as doctrines the commandments of men."
reason: Removes a claim about how the Greek is commonly translated; keeps the neutral comparison.

old: Latin communicant (also in vv. 18, 20, 23) literally means "make common," a biblical Latin calque for ritual defilement corresponding to "common hands" in vv. 2 and 5. The Clementine Vulgate omits v. 16.
new: Latin communicant (also in vv. 18, 20, 23) literally means "make common," a biblical Latin calque for ritual defilement corresponding to "common hands" in vv. 2 and 5.
reason: The claim that the Vulgate omits v. 16 is false for this Latin, which has Mark 7:16 (Si quis habet aures audiendi, audiat) as an additional verse.

old: In the Clementine Vulgate, "cleansing all foods?" (purgans omnes escas?) stands within Jesus's question rather than as a parenthetical narrator comment (as in many modern translations of the Greek masculine participle katharizon).
new: In the Clementine Vulgate, "cleansing all foods?" (purgans omnes escas?) stands within Jesus's question rather than as a parenthetical narrator comment.
reason: Removes a claim about what modern translations do; the Latin observation stands.

old: Latin anima, rendered "life" here and "soul" in verses 36-37, encompasses both earthly life and the enduring soul.
new: Latin anima can mean both "life" and "soul"; it is rendered "life" here and "soul" in verses 36-37.
reason: "enduring soul" is a theological gloss; the note should only explain the range of anima.

old: And He, answering, said to them, "Elijah, when he comes first, will restore all things; and how is it written concerning the Son of Man that He should suffer many things and be despised?
new: And He, answering, said to them, "Elijah, when he comes first, will restore all things; and as it is written concerning the Son of Man, that He should suffer many things and be despised.
reason: The Latin is a statement ending in a period, with quomodo meaning "as"; making it a question follows the Greek.

old: The Clementine Vulgate ends this verse with a period rather than a question mark, though "et quomodo" ("and how") renders the Greek interrogative and contrasts with "sicut" ("just as") in 9:13.
new: The Latin punctuates this as a statement, with quomodo in its sense "as"; the Greek is commonly read as a question ("and how is it written...?").
reason: The note now explains the Latin as translated instead of justifying the Greek interrogative.

old: But I tell you that Elijah has indeed come (and they did to him whatever they wished), just as it is written about him."
new: But I tell you that Elijah has also come (and they did to him whatever they wished), just as it is written about him."
reason: quia et Elias venit: et means "also/too", not the intensifier "indeed".

old: And He, answering them, said, "Unbelieving generation, how long will I be with you? How long will I bear with you? Bring him to Me."
new: And He, answering them, said, "O unbelieving generation, how long will I be with you? How long will I bear with you? Bring him to Me."
reason: The vocative interjection O (O generatio incredula) was not represented.

old: Following the broader Latin and Byzantine tradition, the Vulgate includes "et jejunio" ("and fasting") alongside prayer; likewise, it retains "credere" ("to believe") in 9:23, "in vitam æternam" ("into eternal life") and "ignis inextinguibilis" ("of unquenchable fire") in 9:45, and "et omnis victima sale salietur" ("and every sacrifice will be salted with salt") in 9:49.
new: Following the broader Latin and Byzantine tradition, the Vulgate includes "et jejunio" ("and fasting") alongside prayer; likewise, it retains "credere" ("to believe") in 9:23, "ignis inextinguibilis" ("of unquenchable fire") in 9:45, and "et omnis victima sale salietur" ("and every sacrifice will be salted with salt") in 9:49.
reason: "in vitam æternam" in 9:45 is not a Byzantine reading (the Greek has only "into life"), so listing it here is inaccurate.

old: The Clementine Vulgate places "do not commit adultery" (ne adulteres) before "do not kill" (ne occidas), reversing the order found in most Greek manuscripts of Mark.
new: The Clementine Vulgate places "do not commit adultery" (ne adulteres) before "do not kill" (ne occidas), as does the Byzantine Greek text; critical Greek editions have the reverse order.
reason: The majority (Byzantine) Greek text has the same order as the Vulgate, so "reversing the order found in most Greek manuscripts" is inaccurate.

old: For indeed, the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give His life as a redemption for many."
new: For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give His life as a redemption for many."
reason: Nam et Filius hominis: et means "even", not the intensifier "indeed".

old: Therefore, still having one dearest son, he sent him also to them last, saying, 'They will respect my son.'
new: Therefore, still having one most beloved son, he sent him also to them last, saying, 'They will respect my son.'
reason: carissimum is rendered "most beloved" for the same word in 9:7; keep the same rendering here.

old: "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if anyone's brother dies and leaves behind a wife, and leaves no children, his brother should take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.
new: "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if anyone's brother dies and leaves behind a wife, and leaves no children, his brother should take his wife and raise up seed for his brother.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: There were, then, seven brothers; and the first took a wife, and died leaving no offspring.
new: There were, then, seven brothers; and the first took a wife, and died leaving no seed.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And the second took her and died, and neither did he leave offspring. And the third likewise.
new: And the second took her and died, and neither did he leave seed. And the third likewise.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And the seven took her likewise, and left no offspring. Last of all, the woman also died.
new: And the seven took her likewise, and left no seed. Last of all, the woman also died.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And among all nations the gospel must first be proclaimed.
new: And among all nations the Gospel must first be proclaimed.
reason: Evangelium is capitalized "Gospel" everywhere else in Mark (8:35, 10:29, 14:9, 16:15).

old: so you also, when you see these things happening, know that He is near, at the doors.
new: so you also, when you see these things happening, know that it is near, at the doors.
reason: in proximo sit has no expressed subject and parallels in proximo sit æstas in 13:28; the capitalized "He" settles a disputed referent.

old: Latin sit has no expressed subject; it is rendered "He is near" (referring to the Son of Man of verse 26), though it may also be understood impersonally as "it is near" (referring to the end or fulfillment).
new: Latin sit has no expressed subject; it may be understood impersonally ("it is near") or as referring to the Son of Man of verse 26 ("He is near").
reason: The note is updated to match the neutral rendering of the verse.

old: And He took Peter and James and John along with Him, and began to feel dread and deep distress.
new: And He took Peter and James and John along with Him, and began to feel dread and to be weary.
reason: tædere means "to be weary/loathing"; "deep distress" follows the Greek ademonein and adds an intensifier.

old: And answering, Jesus said to them, "Have you come out as against a bandit with swords and clubs to apprehend Me?
new: And answering, Jesus said to them, "Have you come out as against a robber with swords and clubs to apprehend Me?
reason: latro is rendered "robber" in 11:17 and 15:27; use the same English here.

old: Verse 28 ("And the Scripture was fulfilled which says, 'He was numbered with the transgressors'") is absent from the Clementine Vulgate, so the verse numbering passes directly from 15:27 to 15:29.
reason: False for this text: the Latin has 15:28 (Et impleta est Scriptura...), given as an additional verse, so the claim about the Vulgate and its numbering is wrong.

old: And looking up, they saw the stone rolled back. For indeed it was very large.
new: And looking, they saw the stone rolled back. For indeed it was very large.
reason: respicientes means "looking (back/at)"; "looking up" follows the Greek anablepsasai.

old: Vulgate uses the present tense sedet ("sits") rather than the Greek aorist ("sat down"), emphasizing Christ's ongoing session at the right hand of God.
new: The Vulgate uses the present tense sedet ("sits") where the Greek has the aorist ("sat down").
reason: Remove the theological gloss "emphasizing Christ's ongoing session"; keep the factual tense comparison.

old: to a virgin engaged to a man whose name was Joseph, from the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary.
new: to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, from the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary.
reason: desponsatam here and desponsata in 2:5 are the same term; 2:5 renders it "betrothed", so use the same English here

old: The Vulgate reads 'cognoverunt' ("they came to know"), reflecting the variant 'egnosan', whereas most Greek editions read 'egnorisan' ("they made known").
new: The Vulgate reads cognoverunt ("they came to know"), where the Greek reads 'they made known.'
reason: the claim that cognoverunt reflects a Greek variant 'egnosan' is unsupported; keep only the neutral factual comparison

old: a light for the revelation of the nations, and the glory of Your people Israel."
new: a light for the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of Your people Israel."
reason: gentium is set in contrast to plebis tuæ Israël, which is where the edition uses "Gentiles" for gentes

old: And He went down with them and came to Nazareth, and remained subject to them. And His mother was keeping all these words in her heart.
new: And He went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. And His mother was keeping all these words in her heart.
reason: erat subditus is simply "was subject"; "remained" adds a nuance the Latin does not have

old: The Clementine Vulgate uniquely adds 'et diem retributionis' ("and the day of retribution") from Isaiah 61:2.
new: The Clementine Vulgate adds 'et diem retributionis' ("and the day of retribution") from Isaiah 61:2, which the Greek text of Luke lacks here.
reason: "uniquely" is an unsupported claim; state the plain textual fact instead

old: And He said to them, "Certainly you will say this proverb to Me: 'Physician, heal yourself! All the things we have heard were done in Capernaum, do here also in Your homeland.'"
new: And He said to them, "Certainly you will say this proverb to Me: 'Physician, heal Yourself! All the things we have heard were done in Capernaum, do here also in Your homeland.'"
reason: teipsum is addressed to Jesus, like tua in the same quoted saying ("Your homeland"); capitalize consistently per house style

old: And Jesus rebuked it, saying, "Be silent, and come out of him." And when the demon had thrown him into the middle, it came out of him and did not harm him at all.
new: And Jesus rebuked him, saying, "Be silent, and come out of him." And when the demon had thrown him into the middle, it came out of him and did not harm him at all.
reason: the Latin has masculine illum (not neuter, as dæmonium would be), so "it" follows the Greek neuter; "him" keeps the Latin as it stands

old: And if you love those who love you, what credit do you have? For even sinners love those who love them.
new: And if you love those who love you, what thanks do you have? For even sinners love those who love them.
reason: quæ vobis est gratia: gratia in this sense is rendered "thanks" in the edition; "credit" is a published translation's wording

old: And if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit do you have? For indeed, even sinners do this.
new: And if you do good to those who do good to you, what thanks do you have? For indeed, even sinners do this.
reason: quæ vobis est gratia: same term and rendering as 6:32 ("thanks")

old: And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive back, what credit do you have? For even sinners lend to sinners so that they may receive back an equal amount.
new: And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive back, what thanks do you have? For even sinners lend to sinners so that they may receive back an equal amount.
reason: quæ gratia est vobis: same term and rendering as 6:32-33 ("thanks")

old: And all the people who heard, and the tax collectors, vindicated God, having been baptized with the baptism of John.
new: And all the people who heard, and the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John.
reason: justificaverunt is rendered "justify" in the edition; "vindicated" interprets

old: And wisdom has been vindicated by all her children."
new: And wisdom has been justified by all her children."
reason: justificata est, the same verb as 7:29; the edition renders justificare as "justify"

old: Then He said to her, "Your sins are forgiven you."
new: Then He said to her, "Sins are forgiven you."
reason: Remittuntur tibi peccata has no tua; "Your sins" follows the Greek (cf. the edition's own handling of the same wording at 5:23)

old: Now when a very large crowd was gathering and people were hurrying to Him from the cities, He spoke through a comparison:
new: Now when a very large crowd was gathering and people were hurrying to Him from the cities, He spoke through a parable:
reason: similitudo (of a parable story) is "parable" at 5:36 and 6:39, and the same story is called parabola in 8:9

old: While He was still speaking, someone came to the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him, "Because your daughter has died, do not trouble Him."
new: While He was still speaking, someone came to the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him, "Your daughter has died; do not trouble Him."
reason: Quia after dicens ei introduces direct speech (recitative), as the edition treats it elsewhere (e.g. 1:61, 4:21, 7:16); "Because" makes it causal

old: But He, sternly warning them, ordered them not to tell this to anyone,
new: But He, rebuking them, ordered them not to tell this to anyone,
reason: increpans is "rebuking" (increpare is "rebuke" in 4:35, 4:41, 8:24, 9:42); "sternly warning" paraphrases

old: And answering, Jesus said, "Unbelieving and perverse generation, how long will I be with you and endure you? Bring your son here."
new: And answering, Jesus said, "O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long will I be with you and endure you? Bring your son here."
reason: the Latin has the interjection O (O generatio infidelis), which is not represented

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads simply 'that clung to us' (qui adhaesit nobis), without the phrase 'to our feet' found in Greek manuscripts, and also omits 'to you' after 'the kingdom of God has drawn near.'
new: The Clementine Vulgate reads simply 'that clung to us' (qui adhaesit nobis), without the phrase 'to our feet' found in Greek manuscripts.
reason: The critical Greek also lacks 'to you' after 'has drawn near' in this verse (only later manuscripts add it), so presenting it as a Vulgate omission is misleading.

old: And you, Capernaum, exalted up to heaven, will be plunged down to hell.
new: And you, Capernaum, exalted up to heaven, will be plunged down to the underworld.
reason: infernus is rendered "the underworld" in this edition; "hell" decides the sense.

old: Unlike Greek editions that punctuate the first clause as a rhetorical question, the Vulgate uses a declarative participle ('exalted up to heaven,' exaltata) followed by 'plunged down to hell' (usque ad infernum demergeris).
new: Where critical Greek editions read a question ('will you be exalted to heaven?'), the Vulgate has the participle exaltata ('exalted up to heaven'), followed by 'plunged down to the underworld' (usque ad infernum demergeris).
reason: The Greek difference is a variant reading, not just punctuation; also align infernus with the edition's "the underworld".

old: And I too tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened for you.
new: And I tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened for you.
reason: Et ego dico vobis is simply "And I tell you"; the sentence-initial et is the connective, so "too" adds.

old: Vulgate reads et quid volo nisi ut accendatur? ("and what do I want except that it be kindled?"), whereas the Greek text is usually rendered "and how I wish it were already kindled!"
new: Vulgate reads et quid volo nisi ut accendatur? ("and what do I want except that it be kindled?"), whereas the Greek can be read as an exclamation, "and how I wish it were already kindled!"
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Greek.

old: Vulgate places "the sky and the earth" (cæli et terræ) in that order and omits "know how to" in the second clause (quomodo non probatis?), differing from the Greek order ("earth and sky") and repeated verb.
new: Vulgate places "the sky and the earth" (cæli et terræ) in that order, whereas the Greek has "the earth and the sky."
reason: The critical Greek also reads simply "how do you not discern" in the second clause (the repeated "know how to" is a later reading), so that contrast is inaccurate.

old: The Vulgate shifts from poenitentiam habueritis ("have repentance") here to poenitentiam non egeritis ("do not practice repentance," traditionally "do penance") in verse 5, varying its rendering of the Greek verb for repenting.
new: The Vulgate shifts from poenitentiam habueritis ("have repentance") here to poenitentiam non egeritis ("do not repent," literally "do not do repentance") in verse 5, varying its rendering of the Greek verb for repenting.
reason: Remove the appeal to traditional English renderings ("do penance") and align with the edition's poenitentiam agere = "repent".

old: No, I tell you; but if you do not practice repentance, you will all perish in the same way."
new: No, I tell you; but if you do not repent, you will all perish in the same way."
reason: pœnitentiam agere is rendered "repent" in this edition (cf. 11:32, 17:3); "practice repentance" is non-standard.

old: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, and yourselves being driven outside.
new: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves being driven outside.
reason: vos autem expelli foras sets the hearers in contrast with those in the kingdom; autem = "but", not a plain "and".

old: The Vulgate reads Dico autem vobis ("And I tell you," plural) rather than the Greek explanatory "For I tell you"; while continuing the host's declaration about "my dinner," the plural pronoun also reaches Jesus's own hearers.
new: The Vulgate reads Dico autem vobis ("And I tell you") where the Greek has "For I tell you."
reason: The Greek also has the plural pronoun, so "plural" is not a Vulgate distinctive, and the remark about whom it reaches is interpretive comment.

old: Latin ita ... quam preserves an elliptical comparative without an explicit "more." Poenitentiam agente (literally "doing penance," also in 15:10 and 16:30) is the Vulgate idiom for repentance and is rendered "repents" in keeping with the other Gospel occurrences.
new: Latin ita ... quam preserves an elliptical comparative without an explicit "more." Poenitentiam agente (literally "doing repentance," also in 15:10 and 16:30) is the Vulgate idiom for repentance and is rendered "repents" in keeping with the other Gospel occurrences.
reason: The literal sense of poenitentiam agere is "do repentance"; "doing penance" imports a confessional technical term.

old: And he called him and said to him, 'What is this that I hear about you? Render an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer act as steward.'
new: And he called him and said to him, 'What is this that I hear about you? Render an account of your stewardship, for you will no longer be able to act as steward.'
reason: non poteris is future ("you will not be able"); the present "can" follows the Greek dynē.

old: The clause "et nemo illi dabat" ("and no one gave him any") is a distinctive Vulgate reading echoing 15:16 and is absent from Greek manuscripts.
new: The clause "et nemo illi dabat" ("and no one gave him any") is a distinctive Vulgate reading echoing 15:16 and is absent from most Greek manuscripts.
reason: A few Greek witnesses (e.g. family 13) do have the clause, so "absent from Greek manuscripts" overstates.

old: Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom. And the rich man also died and was buried in hell.
new: Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom. And the rich man also died and was buried in the underworld.
reason: in inferno: infernus is rendered "the underworld" in this edition; "hell" decides the sense.

old: The Clementine Vulgate attaches "in inferno" ("in hell," rendering Greek hades, the underworld or realm of the dead) to "was buried" at the end of verse 22, whereas the Greek text places it at the beginning of verse 23.
new: The Clementine Vulgate attaches "in inferno" ("in the underworld," rendering Greek hades) to "was buried" at the end of verse 22, whereas the Greek text places it at the beginning of verse 23.
reason: Align the note with the verse's "the underworld" for infernus.

old: But the Lord said, "If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mulberry tree, 'Be uprooted and be transplanted into the sea,' and it will obey you.
new: But the Lord said, "If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mulberry tree, 'Be uprooted and be transplanted into the sea,' and it will obey you.
reason: granum sinapis = "a grain of mustard seed" (so rendered at 13:19); granum was not represented.

old: and would not say to him, 'Prepare what I may dine on, and fasten your belt, and serve me while I eat and drink, and after these things you will eat and drink'?
new: and would not say to him, 'Prepare what I may dine on, and gird yourself, and serve me while I eat and drink, and after these things you will eat and drink'?
reason: præcinge te is "gird yourself", as præcinget se is "he will gird himself" at 12:37.

old: Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will keep it alive.
new: Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will give it life.
reason: vivificabit means "will make alive / give life to"; "keep it alive" follows the Greek zōogonēsei rather than the Latin.

old: But Jesus, answering, said to them, "I too will ask you one question. Answer Me:
new: But Jesus, answering, said to them, "I too will ask you one thing. Answer Me:
reason: unum verbum is "one word/thing" (verbum → "word" or "thing" in this edition); "question" interprets.

old: He will come and destroy those tenant farmers, and give the vineyard to others." Upon hearing this, they said to Him, "May that never happen!"
new: He will come and destroy those tenant farmers, and give the vineyard to others." Upon hearing this, they said to Him, "Far from it!"
reason: Latin bare "Absit." is rendered "Far from it", the edition's majority rendering (Romans 3:3, 6:2, 9:14; 1 Cor 6:15; Gal 2:17, 3:21).

old: But He, looking closely at them, said, "What then is this that is written: 'The stone that the builders rejected, this one has become the head of the corner'?
new: But He, looking at them, said, "What then is this that is written: 'The stone that the builders rejected, this one has become the head of the corner'?
reason: aspiciens eos is simply "looking at them"; "closely" has no basis in the Latin (it reflects the Greek emblepsas).

old: saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if anyone's brother dies having a wife, and this man is without children, his brother should take her as his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.
new: saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if anyone's brother dies having a wife, and this man is without children, his brother should take her as his wife and raise up seed for his brother.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And the third took her, and likewise all seven as well, and they left no offspring and died.
new: And the third took her, and likewise all seven as well, and they left no seed and died.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: And they questioned Him, saying, "Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when they begin to take place?"
new: And they questioned Him, saying, "Master, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when they begin to take place?"
reason: The Latin reads Præceptor (rendered "Master" elsewhere in Luke, e.g. 5:5, 8:24, 9:33), not Magister; "Teacher" follows the Greek didaskale.

old: And one of them struck the slave of the high priest and severed his right ear.
new: And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and severed his right ear.
reason: servum principis sacerdotum: servus is rendered "servant" by default (no slave/free contrast here), as in the parallel Matthew 26:51.

old: Latin "Sinite usque huc" ("Allow it this far") is concise and can be understood either as telling the disciples to stop resisting or as asking the arresting party to permit Him to heal the wounded slave.
new: Latin "Sinite usque huc" ("Allow it this far") is concise and can be understood either as telling the disciples to stop resisting or as asking the arresting party to permit Him to heal the wounded servant.
reason: Keep the note in line with "servant" for servum in v. 50.

old: Then Jesus said to those who had come to Him, the chief priests and the magistrates of the temple and the elders, "As if against a bandit, have you come out with swords and clubs?
new: Then Jesus said to those who had come to Him, the chief priests and the magistrates of the temple and the elders, "As if against a robber, have you come out with swords and clubs?
reason: latro is rendered "robber" in Luke 23:33, 39 (latrones) and in Matthew 26:55; use the same word here.

old: And they began to accuse Him, saying, "We found this man subverting our nation, and forbidding taxes to be given to Caesar, and saying that He is the Christ, a king."
new: And they began to accuse Him, saying, "We found this man subverting our nation, and forbidding tribute to be given to Caesar, and saying that He is the Christ, a king."
reason: prohibentem tributa dare Cæsari repeats the wording of 20:22 (tributum dare Cæsari = "pay tribute to Caesar"); keep "tribute".

old: But the other, answering, was rebuking him, saying, "Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation?
new: But the other, answering, was rebuking him, saying, "You do not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation.
reason: The Latin (Neque tu times Deum, quod in eadem damnatione es.) is punctuated as a statement, not a question; follow it.

old: In the beginning the Word existed, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
new: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
reason: erat is simply "was"; "existed" interprets (the brief's own example), and the Latin order In principio erat Verbum is natural in English.

old: Latin Verbum renders Greek Logos ("Word," denoting speech, expression, or divine reason); erat ("was/existed") is existential in the opening clause.
new: Latin Verbum renders Greek Logos ("Word").
reason: Remove the claim that erat means "existed"/is existential, which no longer matches the verse and interprets the Latin; drop the interpretive gloss "divine reason".

old: who were born not from bloodlines, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a husband, but from God.
new: who were born not from bloodlines, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God.
reason: viri (vir) means "man" as well as "husband"; "husband" narrows the Latin, "a man" keeps its range.

old: John bears witness about Him and cries out, saying, "This was the One of whom I said, 'The One who is going to come after me has been placed ahead of me, because He existed before me.'"
new: John bears witness about Him and cries out, saying, "This was the One of whom I said, 'The One who is going to come after me has been placed ahead of me, because He was before me.'"
reason: prior me erat: erat is "was", not "existed".

old: And from His fullness all of us have received, even grace in place of grace;
new: And from His fullness all of us have received, even grace for grace;
reason: gratiam pro gratia: pro is open ("for", "in return for", "instead of"); "in place of" decides a disputed interpretation the Latin leaves open.

old: This is the One about whom I said, 'After me comes a man who has been placed ahead of me, because He existed before me.'
new: This is the One about whom I said, 'After me comes a man who has been placed ahead of me, because He was before me.'
reason: quia prior me erat: erat is "was", not "existed" (same wording as 1:15).

old: Latin "Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier?" ("What is it to Me and to you, woman?") renders a Semitic idiom distancing the speaker from the interlocutor's concern, with "woman" used as a respectful form of address.
new: Latin "Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier?" renders a Semitic idiom, literally "What is it to Me and to you, woman?"
reason: The note asserts an interpretation ("distancing", "respectful") the Latin does not state; keep it to the idiom itself.

old: I am not able to do anything on My own. Just as I hear, so I judge; and My judgment is righteous, because I do not seek My will, but the will of the One who sent Me.
new: I am not able to do anything on My own. Just as I hear, so I judge; and My judgment is just, because I do not seek My will, but the will of the One who sent Me.
reason: judicium meum justum est concerns judicial fairness, where this edition uses "just"/"justice" rather than "righteous".

old: After these things, Jesus was walking about in Galilee, for He did not want to walk about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill Him.
new: Now after these things, Jesus was walking about in Galilee, for He did not want to walk about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill Him.
reason: Post hæc autem: the connective autem is unrepresented; "Now" renders it, as the edition does elsewhere for transitional autem.

old: Now in the Law Moses commanded us to stone such women. What therefore do You say?"
new: Now in the law Moses commanded us to stone such women. What therefore do You say?"
reason: lex is lowercase "the law" everywhere else in this section (7:19, 7:23, 7:49, 7:51, 8:17, 10:34, 12:34); capital "Law" here is an outlier.

old: Vulgate Principium, qui et loquor vobis ("The Beginning, who also speak to you") takes the difficult Greek phrase ten archen as a Christological title rather than an adverbial expression ("from the beginning").
new: Principium can be nominative or accusative; it is rendered here as a noun ("The Beginning, who also speak to you"), as the first-person qui et loquor vobis suggests, whereas the corresponding Greek ten archen is usually taken adverbially.
reason: "Christological title" is a theological characterization, and the note hides that neuter Principium is formally ambiguous (nominative/accusative); rewritten as a neutral grammatical note.

old: They answered Him, "We are Abraham's offspring, and we have never been slaves to anyone; how do You say, 'You will be free'?"
new: They answered Him, "We are Abraham's seed, and we have never been slaves to anyone; how do You say, 'You will be free'?"
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: For as long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world."
new: As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world."
reason: quamdiu sum in mundo has no causal connective; "For" adds a logical link not in the Latin.

old: If He called them gods, to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken,
new: If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken,
reason: Si illos dixit deos has no expressed subject (God as speaker of the quoted psalm, or the law/Scripture of v. 34 are both read); capital "He" settles a disputed referent, so lowercase keeps the Latin's ambiguity (flagged for editorial decision).

old: Martha told Him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the final day."
new: Martha told Him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day."
reason: in novissimo die is rendered "on the last day" everywhere else in John (6:39, 6:40, 6:44, 6:54, 12:48).

old: And now, You, Father, glorify Me with Yourself, with the glory that I had with You before the world existed.
new: And now, You, Father, glorify Me with Yourself, with the glory that I had with You before the world was.
reason: priusquam mundus esset is simply "before the world was"; "existed" interprets the verb esse.

old: Latin Ego sum literally means "I am" without an expressed predicate "he," serving both to identify Jesus to the arresting party and to echo the divine self-designation of Exodus 3:14 and John 8:58 (likewise in 18:6 and 18:8).
new: Latin Ego sum literally means "I am" without an expressed predicate "he" (likewise in 18:6 and 18:8).
reason: The claim about echoing a divine self-designation is theological interpretation, not explanation of the Latin; keep only the grammatical point.

old: Pilate said to Him, "What is truth?" And when he had said this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them, "I find no fault in Him.
new: Pilate said to Him, "What is truth?" And when he had said this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them, "I find no grounds for a charge in Him.
reason: The same Latin nullam invenio in eo causam is rendered "no grounds for a charge in Him" in 19:4 (and non invenio in eo causam in 19:6); use the same English here.

old: So when the chief priests and the attendants saw Him, they were shouting, saying, "Crucify, crucify Him!" Pilate said to them, "Take Him yourselves and crucify Him, for I myself find no grounds for a charge in Him."
new: So when the chief priests and the officers saw Him, they were shouting, saying, "Crucify, crucify Him!" Pilate said to them, "Take Him yourselves and crucify Him, for I myself find no grounds for a charge in Him."
reason: ministri here are the same temple officers rendered "officers" in 18:3, 18:12, 18:18 and 18:22.

old: And he entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus, "Where are You from?" But Jesus did not give him a reply.
new: And he entered the Praetorium again and said to Jesus, "Where are You from?" But Jesus did not give him a reply.
reason: prætorium is capitalized "Praetorium" in 18:28 and 18:33.

old: Latin "Noli me tangere" literally means "Do not touch Me" (whereas the Greek present imperative is often rendered "Do not cling to Me"). The Clementine Vulgate also reads "to My Father" (ad Patrem meum) in the first clause, where the critical Greek text has "to the Father."
new: Latin "Noli me tangere" literally means "Do not touch Me." The Clementine Vulgate also reads "to My Father" (ad Patrem meum) in the first clause, where the critical Greek text has "to the Father."
reason: Remove the claim about how the Greek is commonly rendered in English translations; keep the facts about the Latin.

old: Simon Peter went aboard and pulled the net onto the land, full of large fish, one hundred fifty-three; and even though there were so many, the net was not torn.
new: Simon Peter went up and pulled the net onto the land, full of large fish, one hundred fifty-three; and even though there were so many, the net was not torn.
reason: Ascendit is simply "went up"; "went aboard" decides where he went, which the Latin leaves unstated.

old: And when they had entered, they went up into the upper room where Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, and Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James were staying.
new: And when they had entered into the upper room, they went up to where Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, and Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James were staying.
reason: In the Latin in cœnaculum goes with cum introissent, and ascenderunt ubi manebant follows; the English followed the Greek word grouping instead.

old: The Vulgate reads 'doloribus inferni' ("pains of the underworld," where Latin 'infernus' denotes the realm of the dead/hell), differing from the Greek text's "pangs of death."
new: The Vulgate reads 'doloribus inferni' ("pains of the underworld," where Latin 'infernus' denotes the realm of the dead), differing from the Greek text's "pangs of death."
reason: Note gloss aligned with the edition's rendering of infernus as "the underworld"; the "hell" gloss (a claim about traditional English renderings) is removed.

old: The Vulgate reads masculine 'hunc, quem' ("this One, whom"), referring personally to the Holy Spirit, whereas the Greek text uses the neuter "this which."
new: The Vulgate reads masculine 'hunc, quem' ("this One, whom"), agreeing with the masculine noun Spiritus, whereas the Greek text uses the neuter "this which."
reason: The masculine is grammatical agreement with Spiritus; "referring personally" is a doctrinal inference, not a fact about the Latin.

old: Here and in 3:26, the Vulgate renders the Greek title pais ("servant/child") as filius ("Son"), emphasizing Jesus' divine sonship.
new: Here and in 3:26, the Vulgate renders the Greek title pais ("servant/child") as filius ("Son").
reason: "emphasizing Jesus' divine sonship" is a doctrinal assertion; keep only the textual fact.

old: The Latin salus ("salvation") and salvos fieri ("be saved") directly echo salvus factus est ("has been made well") in 4:9, linking physical restoration and spiritual salvation.
new: The Latin salus ("salvation") and salvos fieri ("be saved") share the root of salvus factus est ("has been made well") in 4:9.
reason: Keep the lexical connection; "linking physical restoration and spiritual salvation" is theological comment.

old: saying, "What shall we do with these men? For indeed a notable sign has been done through them; it is evident to all who live in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.
new: saying, "What shall we do with these men? For indeed a sign known to all who live in Jerusalem has been done through them; it is evident, and we cannot deny it.
reason: In the Latin omnibus habitantibus Jerusalem goes with notum signum factum est ("a sign known to all who live in Jerusalem"), and manifestum est stands alone; the English followed the Greek grouping with "evident."

old: Vulgate renders Greek "prosēlyton" with the Latin calque "advenam" (lit. "newcomer" or "stranger"), the standard Vulgate biblical term for a Gentile convert or proselyte.
new: Vulgate renders Greek "prosēlyton" with "advenam" (lit. "newcomer" or "stranger"); elsewhere it keeps the loanword proselytus (e.g. 2:11).
reason: The claim that advena is the standard Vulgate term for a proselyte is false for this text, which has Proselyti at Acts 2:11.

old: for we have heard him saying that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the traditions that Moses handed down to us."
new: for we have heard him saying that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and will change the traditions that Moses handed down to us."
reason: Jesus Nazarenus is rendered "Jesus the Nazarene" elsewhere in this edition (John 18:5, 19:19; Acts 2:22, 3:6, 4:10).

old: And He did not give him an inheritance in it, not even a foot's step; but He promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his offspring after him, although he had no son.
new: And He did not give him an inheritance in it, not even a foot's step; but He promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his seed after him, although he had no son.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Now God spoke to him, that his offspring would be a resident alien in a foreign land, and they would subject them to servitude and mistreat them for four hundred years.
new: Now God spoke to him, that his seed would be a resident alien in a foreign land, and they would subject them to servitude and mistreat them for four hundred years.
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: This is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received words of life to give to us.
new: This is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, the one who received words of life to give to us.
reason: The singular qui accepit refers to Moses (hic), but "our fathers, who received" makes the fathers the receivers.

old: The tabernacle of testimony was with our fathers in the desert, just as God ordained for them, speaking to Moses, that he should make it according to the pattern that he had seen.
new: The tabernacle of the testimony was with our fathers in the desert, just as God ordained for them, speaking to Moses, that he should make it according to the pattern that he had seen.
reason: Tabernaculum testimonii has the established rendering "tabernacle of the testimony".

old: Where the Greek reads "the Lord," the Clementine Vulgate reads Deum ("God"); poenitentiam ... age is the standard Latin idiom for "repent" (historically also rendered "do penance").
new: Where the Greek reads "the Lord," the Clementine Vulgate reads Deum ("God"); poenitentiam ... age is the standard Latin idiom for "repent."
reason: Removes a comment about how English translations have rendered the phrase.

old: Now an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, "Rise and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This road is deserted.
new: Now an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, "Rise and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is deserted.
reason: Hæc est deserta has only a pronoun, which could refer to the road or to Gaza; supplying "road" settles the referent.

old: The Clementine Vulgate encloses this verse in parentheses and omits "in a vision" (found in many Greek manuscripts). The Latin present subjunctive "recipiat" follows primary direct-speech sequence after "orat" in verse 11, indicating that the Lord's speech continues through this verse.
new: The Clementine Vulgate encloses this verse in parentheses and omits "in a vision" (found in many Greek manuscripts). The present subjunctive "recipiat" (primary sequence) suits reading "vidit" as "has seen," continuing the Lord's speech.
reason: The sequence of recipiat depends on vidit in its own clause, not on orat in verse 11; the grammatical claim is corrected.

old: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord, because I have never eaten anything common and unclean."
new: But Peter said, "Far from it, Lord, because I have never eaten anything common and unclean."
reason: Latin "Absit, Domine" is rendered "Far from it", the edition's majority rendering of bare Absit (Romans 3:3, 6:2, 9:14; 1 Cor 6:15; Gal 2:17, 3:21).

old: Now when much debate had taken place, Peter rose up and said to them, "Men and brothers, you know that from early days God chose among us that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe.
new: Now when much debate was taking place, Peter rose up and said to them, "Men, brothers, you know that from early days God chose among us that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe.
reason: Cum ... fieret is imperfect (debate still going on), not the Greek aorist "after much debate"; viri fratres is rendered "Men, brothers" elsewhere in Acts (13:15, 13:26, 13:38) with no "and" in the Latin.

old: And after they became silent, James answered, saying, "Men and brothers, listen to me.
new: And after they became silent, James answered, saying, "Men, brothers, listen to me.
reason: Viri fratres has no "and" and is rendered "Men, brothers" elsewhere in Acts (13:15, 13:26, 13:38).

old: The Latin text omits verse 34 (present in some manuscripts and editions, stating that Silas decided to remain in Antioch), proceeding directly to verse 35.
new: Verse 34 (Silas's decision to remain in Antioch) is present in this Latin text and is shown as an additional verse after 15:33, since the Saints numbering has no slot for it.
reason: The note said the Latin omits 15:34, but the critical text has it (Visum est autem Silæ ibi remanere), carried as an additional verse.

old: Latin seminiverbius (literally "word-sower") is Jerome's coinage rendering Greek spermologos ("seed-picker" or "babbler"); the Vulgate also reads novorum daemoniorum ("new divinities") where Greek has "foreign divinities."
new: Latin seminiverbius (literally "word-sower") renders Greek spermologos ("seed-picker" or "babbler"); the Vulgate also reads novorum daemoniorum ("new divinities") where Greek has "foreign divinities."
reason: Drops the unsupported claim that the word was Jerome's coinage (the Vulgate text of Acts is not generally attributed to Jerome).

old: Vulgate 'Cum apparuissemus autem Cypro' literally reads 'when we had appeared to Cyprus,' a passive nautical idiom for coming into view of land corresponding to the Greek variant 'anaphanentes' rather than active 'anaphanantes' ('having sighted').
new: Vulgate 'Cum apparuissemus autem Cypro' literally reads 'when we had appeared to Cyprus,' a nautical idiom for coming into view of land, corresponding to the Greek variant 'anaphanentes' ('having been shown') rather than 'anaphanantes' ('having sighted').
reason: apparuissemus is an active (intransitive) form, not passive; the note's description of the Latin as 'passive' is inaccurate.

old: And the chief priest Ananias commanded those standing beside him to strike his mouth.
new: And the high priest Ananias commanded those standing beside him to strike his mouth.
reason: Singular princeps sacerdotum is rendered "high priest" elsewhere in Acts (4:6; 5:17, 21, 27; 7:1; 9:1; 22:5); "chief priest" is used for plural principes sacerdotum.

old: And Paul said, "I did not know, brothers, that he is the chief priest. For it is written, 'You shall not curse the ruler of your people.'"
new: And Paul said, "I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest. For it is written, 'You shall not curse the ruler of your people.'"
reason: Singular princeps sacerdotum is rendered "high priest" throughout Acts (e.g. 22:5); keeps the same office named in 23:2 and 23:4.

old: Now after five days, the chief priest Ananias came down with certain elders and a certain orator, Tertullus, and they appeared before the governor against Paul.
new: Now after five days, the high priest Ananias came down with certain elders and a certain orator, Tertullus, and they appeared before the governor against Paul.
reason: Singular princeps sacerdotum is rendered "high priest" elsewhere in Acts (4:6; 5:17; 7:1; 9:1; 22:5).

old: The Clementine Vulgate omits verse 7 (which in the longer text tradition recounts the tribune Lysias taking Paul away by force), leaving the participle "ordering" (jubens) at the start of verse 8 syntactically attached to verse 6.
new: Verse 7 (which in the longer tradition recounts the tribune Lysias taking Paul away by force) is absent from the main Latin text here, leaving the participle "ordering" (jubens) at the start of verse 8 syntactically attached to verse 6.
reason: The printed Clementine Vulgate does contain v. 7 (Superveniens autem tribunus Lysias...), which this edition carries only as an additional verse; the note should describe the main Latin text rather than claim the Clementine omits it.

old: to which our twelve tribes, zealously serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I am accused by the Jews, king.
new: to which our twelve tribes, serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I am accused by the Jews, king.
reason: The Latin has only nocte ac die deservientes; "zealously" reflects the Greek adverbial phrase (en ekteneia), which this Latin lacks (deservio is "serve" in 24:14 and 27:23).

old: Latin si ... si ("whether ... whether," mirroring Greek ei ... ei) introduces the debated prophetic propositions (often smoothed as "that ... that"), and passibilis literally means "capable of" or "subject to suffering."
new: Latin si ... si ("whether ... whether," mirroring Greek ei ... ei) introduces the two propositions, and passibilis literally means "capable of" or "subject to suffering."
reason: Removes the claim about how translations commonly render the clause; keeps the neutral Latin/Greek explanation.

old: we boarded a ship of Adramyttium, about to sail around the places of Asia, and weighed anchor, with Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, remaining with us.
new: we boarded a ship of Adramyttium and, beginning to sail around the places of Asia, weighed anchor, with Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, remaining with us.
reason: incipientes is nominative plural agreeing with the subject of sustulimus ("we"), not with navem; "a ship ... about to sail" follows the Greek participle, which modifies the ship.

old: The Clementine Vulgate names the harbor Boniportus ("Good Harbors," commonly rendered "Fair Havens") and the nearby city Thalassa, where most Greek manuscripts read Lasea.
new: The Clementine Vulgate names the harbor Boniportus ("Good Harbors") and the nearby city Thalassa, where most Greek manuscripts read Lasea.
