reason: Removes a claim about how English translations commonly render the name; the note should explain the Latin only.

old: Latin "Deo odibiles" uses a passive adjective with the dative ("hateful to God"), whereas the Greek "theostygeis" is often rendered actively as "haters of God."
new: Latin "Deo odibiles" uses a passive adjective with the dative ("hateful to God"), whereas the Greek "theostygeis" can also be taken actively ("haters of God").
reason: Removes the claim about how the Greek is usually rendered by translators; keeps the neutral Latin/Greek comparison.

old: foolish, disorderly, without affection, without fidelity, without mercy.
new: foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy.
reason: absque fœdere: fœdus is rendered "covenant" edition-wide (the previous "without fidelity" also matched the Douay-Rheims wording).

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads "Si autem" ("But if"), matching the Byzantine Greek tradition, whereas modern critical Greek editions read "Ide" ("See"); the Vulgate treats verses 19-20 as the concluding clause of the sentence.
new: The Clementine Vulgate reads "Si autem" ("But if"), matching the Greek "Ei de" of modern critical editions, whereas the Byzantine tradition reads "Ide" ("See"); the Vulgate treats verses 19-20 as the concluding clause of the sentence.
reason: The note reverses the Greek evidence: critical editions read Ei de (= Si autem) and the Byzantine text reads Ide.

old: namely, the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, to all and upon all who believe in Him; for there is no distinction,
new: namely, the righteousness of God through the faith of Jesus Christ, to all and upon all who believe in Him; for there is no distinction,
reason: per fidem Jesu Christi is a bare genitive that the note itself calls ambiguous (objective or subjective); "faith in" decides it, while "the faith of" keeps the Latin's ambiguity and matches ex fide ... Abrahæ = "of the faith of Abraham" in 4:16.

old: in the forbearance of God, for the demonstration of His righteousness at this time, so that He Himself may be righteous and may justify him who is of faith in Jesus Christ.
new: in the forbearance of God, for the demonstration of His righteousness at this time, so that He Himself may be righteous and may justify him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ.
reason: ex fide Jesu Christi is a bare genitive (cf. ex fide ... Abrahæ, "of the faith of Abraham," 4:16); "faith in" resolves an ambiguity the Latin leaves open.

old: For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring, that he would be heir of the world, was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.
new: For the promise to Abraham or to his seed, that he would be heir of the world, was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Therefore it is by faith, so that according to grace the promise may be firm to all the offspring, not only to the one who is of the law, but also to the one who is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all
new: Therefore it is by faith, so that according to grace the promise may be firm to all the seed, not only to the one who is of the law, but also to the one who is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all
reason: Latin semini (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Against hope, he believed in hope, so that he might become the father of many nations, according to what had been spoken to him: "So will your offspring be."
new: Against hope, he believed in hope, so that he might become the father of many nations, according to what had been spoken to him: "So will your seed be."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: Latin 'habeamus' is a hortatory subjunctive ('let us have'), whereas many modern translations from the Greek adopt the indicative ('we have').
new: Latin 'habeamus' is a hortatory subjunctive ('let us have'); the standard Greek text reads the indicative ('we have'), though many Greek manuscripts have the subjunctive.
reason: Notes must not make claims about what English translations do; restated as a neutral textual comparison.

old: and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.
new: and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.
reason: diffusa est is perfect passive, parallel to datus est ('has been given'): 'has been poured out'.

old: For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; yet for a good person someone might perhaps dare to die.
new: For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; for someone might perhaps dare to die for a good person.
reason: nam is explanatory 'for', not adversative 'yet'.

old: Latin 'in quo' ('in whom', masculine singular referring back to Adam) and 'in hunc mundum' ('into this world') are famous Vulgate readings; the underlying Greek expression is often translated 'because'.
new: Latin 'in quo' may be masculine ('in whom', referring back to the one man) or neuter ('in which'); the underlying Greek expression is often taken as 'because'. The Vulgate also reads 'in hunc mundum' ('into this world').
reason: quo is ablative masculine or neuter; the note asserted only the masculine and used evaluative 'famous'.

old: Latin 'justificatus est' literally reads 'has been justified' from sin, retaining the same legal verb used in 5:1 and 5:9 rather than 'freed'.
new: Latin 'justificatus est' ('has been justified') is the same verb used in 5:1 and 5:9.
reason: Removed the implicit comparison with English renderings ('rather than freed') and the interpretive label 'legal'.

old: Latin 'Gratia' translates Greek 'charisma' ('free gift') with the standard term 'grace', contrasting unmerited grace with 'stipendia' ('pay' or military wages).
new: Latin 'gratia' ('grace') renders Greek 'charisma' ('free gift'); 'stipendia' is the word for a soldier's pay.
reason: Removed theological commentary ('unmerited grace'); kept the lexical facts.

old: For what was impossible for the Law, in that it was weakened through the flesh—God, by sending His own Son in the likeness of the flesh of sin and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh,
new: For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh—God, by sending His own Son in the likeness of the flesh of sin and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh,
reason: lex is 'the law' (lowercase) throughout Romans 5-8 in this edition; the capital is inconsistent.

old: so that the righteous requirement of the Law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.
new: so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.
reason: legis is 'the law' (lowercase) as elsewhere in Romans.

old: Latin justificatio legis literally means "the justification/righteous requirement of the Law."
new: Latin justificatio legis literally means "the justification/righteous requirement of the law."
reason: Matches the lowercase 'law' used in the verse and throughout Romans.

old: For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory that will be revealed in us.
new: For I reckon that the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory that will be revealed in us.
reason: hujus temporis is 'of this time'; 'present' reflects the Greek 'the now time', not the Latin.

old: For the eager expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God.
new: For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God.
reason: exspectatio is simply 'expectation'; 'eager' imports the Greek apokaradokia.

old: And we know that for those who love God, all things work together toward good, for those who according to His purpose have been called as saints.
new: And we know that for those who love God, all things work together toward good, for those who according to the purpose have been called as saints.
reason: secundum propositum has no possessive; 'His' decides whose purpose is meant, which the Latin leaves open.

old: Two distinctive Vulgate features: omnia ("all things") is the subject of cooperantur ("work together"), and vocati sunt sancti adds sancti ("called as saints"). "His" is implied by secundum propositum ("according to the purpose").
new: Latin omnia ("all things") is the subject of cooperantur ("work together"), and vocati sunt sancti adds sancti ("called as saints"), which the Greek lacks; secundum propositum ("according to the purpose") has no possessive.
reason: omnia as subject is also the standard Greek reading, so it is not a distinctive Vulgate feature; the note's 'His is implied' no longer matches the verse.

old: nor are those who are the offspring of Abraham all sons; rather, "In Isaac your offspring will be called."
new: nor are those who are the seed of Abraham all sons; rather, "In Isaac your seed will be called."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: That is, it is not those who are sons of the flesh who are sons of God, but those who are sons of the promise are reckoned as offspring.
new: That is, it is not those who are sons of the flesh who are sons of God, but those who are sons of the promise are reckoned as seed.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: What then will we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not!
new: What then will we say? Is there injustice with God? Far from it.
reason: Absit is rendered 'Far from it.' throughout Romans in this edition (6:2, 6:15, 7:7, 11:1, 11:11).

old: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: "Even if the number of the sons of Israel is like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.
new: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: "If the number of the sons of Israel is like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.
reason: Si fuerit is a plain condition 'If'; 'Even' adds a concessive nuance not in the Latin.

old: And as Isaiah foretold: "If the Lord Sabaoth had not left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been similar to Gomorrah."
new: And as Isaiah foretold: "If the Lord Sabaoth had not left us seed, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been similar to Gomorrah."
reason: Latin semen (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: just as it is written: "God has given them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they may not see, and ears so that they may not hear, down to this very day."
new: just as it is written: "God has given them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they may not see, and ears so that they may not hear, down to this day."
reason: usque in hodiernum diem is 'until this day'; 'very' is an intensifier with no Latin basis.

old: And do not be conformed to this age, but be reformed in the newness of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is: what is good, and well-pleasing, and perfect.
new: And do not be conformed to this age, but be reformed in the newness of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is: good, and well-pleasing, and perfect.
reason: bona, beneplacens, perfecta are adjectives agreeing with voluntas; 'what is good' turns them into separate substantives.

old: loving one another with brotherly affection, outdoing one another in showing honor;
new: loving one another with brotherly love, outdoing one another in showing honor;
reason: caritate fraternitatis uses caritas, rendered 'love' in this edition; 'affection' follows the Greek philostorgoi.

old: being of the same mind toward one another; not setting your mind on lofty things, but associating with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own estimation;
new: being of the same mind toward one another; not setting your mind on lofty things, but agreeing with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own estimation;
reason: humilibus consentientes means 'agreeing/being in accord with the lowly'; 'associating with' reflects the Greek synapagomenoi.

old: repaying no one evil for evil; taking care for what is honorable not only before God, but also before all people.
new: repaying no one evil for evil; taking care for what is good not only before God, but also before all people.
reason: providentes bona is 'good things'; 'honorable' reflects the Greek kala.

old: Yet we do speak wisdom among the mature, though a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed;
new: Yet we do speak wisdom among the perfect, though a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed;
reason: inter perfectos is 'among the perfect' (cf. perfecti 'perfected' at 1:10); 'mature' reflects the Greek teleioi.

old: The Vulgate preserves fuller divine titles across vv. 4-5 ("Jesus Christ" in v. 4a, "our Lord Jesus" in v. 4b, and "our Lord Jesus Christ" in v. 5) where the critical Greek text has shorter forms, notably simply "the day of the Lord" in v. 5.
new: The Vulgate has fuller titles in v. 4a ("our Lord Jesus Christ") and v. 5 ("the day of our Lord Jesus Christ") where the critical Greek text has shorter forms (in v. 5 simply "the day of the Lord").
reason: Domini nostri Jesu in v. 4b matches the critical Greek, so it is not a fuller form; also dropped the theological label 'divine'.

old: For those who are outside, God will judge. Remove the evil person from among yourselves.
new: For those who are outside, God will judge. Remove the evil from among yourselves.
reason: malum may be masculine or neuter; 'the evil person' follows the Greek masculine and settles what the Latin leaves open.

old: The Vulgate reads the future tense judicabit ("will judge"); malum can grammatically be masculine ("the evil person") or neuter ("the evil"), with v. 2 pointing to the offending individual.
new: The Vulgate reads the future tense judicabit ("will judge"); malum can grammatically be masculine ("the evil person") or neuter ("the evil").
reason: Matches the verse, which now keeps the Latin ambiguity, and removes the interpretive steer.

old: Or do you not know that the saints will judge this world? And if the world will be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the very smallest matters?
new: Or do you not know that the saints will judge this world? And if the world will be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?
reason: de minimis is a plain superlative 'the smallest (things)'; 'very' adds an intensifier.

old: The Vulgate renders the verb as an unambiguous (ironic) imperative, constituite ("appoint"), whereas modern translations from Greek frequently take it as an indicative question.
new: Latin constituite ("appoint") is an imperative; the Greek form kathizete can be read either as an imperative or as an indicative.
reason: Notes must not describe what translations do or add interpretation ('ironic'); restated as a neutral grammatical comparison.

old: The Vulgate translates "possess" (possidebunt) rather than "inherit" in vv. 9-10 and places the verse break before neque molles; in v. 10, molles ("effeminate/soft") and masculorum concubitores ("those who lie with males") denote passive and active male homosexual partners respectively.
new: Latin possidebunt ("will possess") renders the Greek verb for "inherit" in vv. 9-10, and the Latin verse break falls before neque molles; in v. 10, molles literally means "soft ones" and masculorum concubitores "those who lie with males."
reason: Kept the lexical facts and removed an interpretive claim about what the terms denote, which goes beyond the Latin.

old: Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Taking the members of Christ, then, shall I make them members of a prostitute? By no means!
new: Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Taking the members of Christ, then, shall I make them members of a prostitute? Far from it.
reason: Absit is rendered 'Far from it.' elsewhere in this edition (e.g. Romans 6:2, 6:15, 7:7, 11:1).

old: Yet because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.
new: Yet because of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.
reason: fornicatio is rendered 'sexual immorality' in the surrounding verses (5:1, 6:13, 6:18).

old: Literally "authority on her head" (potestatem supra caput), traditionally understood as a veil signifying authority; "because of the angels" (propter angelos) is variously interpreted as referring to heavenly witnesses of Christian worship or guardians of created order.
new: Latin potestatem supra caput is literally "authority over the head"; "her" is supplied in English.
reason: The note gives interpretive commentary (veil symbolism, identity of the angels) rather than explaining the Latin; it is reduced to the lexical point.

old: And if one member suffers anything, all the members suffer with it; or if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it.
new: And if one member suffers anything, all the members suffer with it; or if one member glories, all the members rejoice with it.
reason: gloriatur is the deponent gloriari, active in sense ("glories"); the passive "is glorified" follows the Greek doxazetai rather than the Latin.

old: If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write to you are the Lord's commands.
new: If anyone seems to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write to you are the Lord's commands.
reason: videtur is "seems" (as rendered at 11:16, si quis videtur contentiosus esse); "thinks himself" follows the Greek dokei.

old: The Vulgate reads de tantis periculis ("from such great perils") and adds the present verb et eruit ("and delivers [us]"), whereas most Greek witnesses read "from so great a death" without the present verb.
new: The Vulgate reads de tantis periculis ("from such great perils") where most Greek witnesses read "from so great a death"; et eruit ("and delivers") corresponds to a second Greek verb that many witnesses give in the future ("and will rescue").
reason: The Greek also has a second verb here (future in most witnesses, present in others), so saying the Vulgate "adds" et eruit is misleading; the bracket in the gloss is also removed.

old: who also made us qualified ministers of a new testament, not by the letter, but by the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit makes alive.
new: who also made us qualified ministers of a new covenant, not by the letter, but by the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit makes alive.
reason: testamentum is rendered "covenant" in this edition except where a will is meant (cf. 1 Cor 11:25 novum testamentum = "new covenant"); no will is in view here.

old: Latin novi testamenti ("of a new testament") renders Greek kaines diathekes ("of a new covenant"). Notice also that non littera, sed Spiritu uses ablatives ("not by the letter, but by the Spirit") rather than Greek genitives.
new: Latin non littera, sed Spiritu uses ablatives ("not by the letter, but by the Spirit") where the Greek has genitives.
reason: With novi testamenti now rendered "new covenant", the first sentence no longer applies; the remaining grammatical point is kept in neutral wording.

old: but their minds were dulled. For to this present day that same veil remains unlifted in the reading of the old testament (because in Christ it is done away with),
new: but their minds were dulled. For to this present day that same veil remains unlifted in the reading of the old covenant (because in Christ it is done away with),
reason: veteris testamenti: testamentum = "covenant" in this edition ("testament" only for a will), matching "new covenant" in 3:6.

old: The Clementine Vulgate prints Deus ("God") with a capital letter, reflecting an ancient patristic reading that joins "of this age" to "unbelievers" ("God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age"), though the more common grammatical reading takes Deus hujus sæculi as "the god of this age" (Satan).
new: The critical text capitalizes Deus; some ancient Latin interpreters joined hujus sæculi to infidelium ("God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age"), while others read Deus hujus sæculi as "the god of this age."
reason: The note now states both construals neutrally, without ranking them or settling the referent.

old: For indeed we who are in this tent groan, weighed down, because we do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be absorbed by life.
new: For indeed we who are in this tent groan, weighed down, because we do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
reason: absorbeatur is the same verb rendered "swallowed up" at 1 Cor 15:54 (absorpta est mors) and 2 Cor 2:7 (absorbeatur).

old: Latin species literally denotes "visible appearance" or "form" (often translated "sight"), contrasting outward visible reality with faith.
new: Latin species literally denotes "visible appearance" or "form" (Greek eidos), contrasting outward visible reality with faith.
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Greek.

old: For the sorrow that is according to God produces steadfast repentance to salvation, but the sorrow of the world produces death.
new: For the sorrow that is according to God produces repentance to salvation that is steadfast, but the sorrow of the world produces death.
reason: In pœnitentiam in salutem stabilem the adjective stands after salutem and can go with either noun (as the note says); moving it onto "repentance" follows the Greek ametameleton and settles the ambiguity, so the Latin order is restored.

old: For if the willingness is ready, it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.
new: For if the willingness is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.
reason: accepta est is the perfect passive participle "is accepted"; "acceptable" follows the Greek euprosdektos.

old: Latin renders Greek paraphronon ("speaking like a madman") more softly as ut minus sapiens ("as one less wise"), and places in carceribus ("in prisons") before in plagis ("in beatings").
new: Latin renders Greek paraphronon ("speaking like a madman") more softly as ut minus sapiens ("as one less wise").
reason: The claimed contrast in order is not accurate for the critical Greek, which also has prisons before beatings; the second clause is removed.

old: Latin non egerunt poenitentiam literally means "have not done penance" or "have not practiced repentance," the standard Vulgate idiom for Greek metanoeo ("repent").
new: Latin non egerunt poenitentiam literally means "have not done repentance," the standard Vulgate idiom for Greek metanoeo ("repent").
reason: Note no longer glosses pœnitentiam agere as "do penance"; the edition renders it "repent" (literal "do repentance").

old: Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Or do you not know yourselves, that Christ Jesus is in you, unless perhaps you are unapproved?
new: Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Or do you not know yourselves, that Christ Jesus is in you? Unless perhaps you are unapproved.
reason: The Latin question ends at "in vobis est?"; "nisi forte reprobi estis" is a separate statement, not part of the question.

old: For am I now trying to persuade men, or God? Or am I seeking to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a slave of Christ.
new: For am I now trying to persuade men, or God? Or am I seeking to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ.
reason: Christi servus with no slave/free contrast takes the edition's standard "servant" (as Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

old: and I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my own people, being far more exceedingly zealous for my ancestral traditions.
new: and I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my own people, being more exceedingly zealous for my ancestral traditions.
reason: abundantius is a simple comparative ("more abundantly/exceedingly"); "far" is an added intensifier.

old: Yet knowing that a man is not justified by works of the law, except through faith in Jesus Christ, we also believe in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified.
new: Yet knowing that a man is not justified by works of the law, except through the faith of Jesus Christ, we also believe in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by the faith of Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified.
reason: per fidem Jesu Christi / ex fide Christi are bare genitives (as the note says); "faith in" settles a debated genitive, whereas "the faith of" keeps the Latin's ambiguity and matches this edition at 3:22.

old: Following the Clementine Vulgate verse division, Christo confixus sum cruci ("I have been nailed to the cross with Christ") concludes verse 19 rather than beginning verse 20 as in most modern English editions.
new: In the Clementine Vulgate verse division, Christo confixus sum cruci ("I have been nailed to the cross with Christ") concludes verse 19 rather than beginning verse 20.
reason: Notes should not make claims about what English editions do; the factual point about the Latin verse division is kept.

old: And I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me. And what I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed Himself over for me.
new: And I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me. And what I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and handed Himself over for me.
reason: in fide vivo Filii Dei has a bare genitive ("faith of the Son of God"); "faith in" decides a debated genitive the Latin leaves open (cf. 2:16, 3:22).

old: Vulgate instruite literally means "instruct" or "set in order," rendering the Greek verb often translated "restore." The Latin also shifts directly from plural ("you who are spiritual") to singular ("examining yourself, so that you too may not be tempted").
new: Vulgate instruite literally means "instruct" or "set in order," rendering the Greek verb katartizo ("restore," "mend"). The Latin also shifts directly from plural ("you who are spiritual") to singular ("examining yourself, so that you too may not be tempted").
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Greek.

old: that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may grant you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the full knowledge of Him,
new: that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may grant you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him,
reason: agnitio is simply "knowledge" (so rendered at 4:13); "full" reflects Greek epignosis, not the Latin.

old: Latin adimpletur is passive ("is filled"), conveying the sense of Christ being brought to full completion in His body, the church; the Vulgate also includes "and" (et) before "the fullness."
new: Latin adimpletur is passive in form ("is filled"); the Vulgate also includes "and" (et) before "the fullness."
reason: The clause about Christ being brought to completion in the church is theological interpretation, not a statement about the Latin.

old: Latin praefinitionem saeculorum literally means "predetermination of the ages" (often rendered "eternal purpose").
new: Latin praefinitionem saeculorum literally means "predetermination of the ages."
reason: Notes should not describe how translations usually render a phrase; the parenthesis is removed.

old: But sexual immorality and all impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints,
new: But fornication and all impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints,
reason: fornicatio is rendered "fornication" in this edition at Gal 5:19 and 2 Cor 12:21; the literal term is kept here too.

old: For know this, understanding that no sexually immoral, or impure, or greedy person, which is the service of idols, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
new: For know this, understanding that no fornicator, or impure, or greedy person, which is the service of idols, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
reason: fornicator matches fornicatio ("fornication") in 5:3 and Gal 5:19; keeps the Latin term consistent.

old: This sacrament is great; I, however, speak in Christ and in the church.
new: This mystery is great; I, however, speak in Christ and in the church.
reason: sacramentum is the Vulgate's regular word for Greek mysterion and is rendered "mystery" in this edition at 1:9, 3:3, 3:9 (also 1 Tim 3:16, Rev 1:20); singling out "sacrament" here imports a technical sense the Latin does not require.

old: The Vulgate translates Greek mysterion ("mystery") as sacramentum ("sacrament"), a landmark Latin reading; "in Christ and in the church" literally renders in Christo et in Ecclesia, meaning with reference to Christ and the church.
new: Latin sacramentum, the Vulgate's usual equivalent of Greek mysterion, is rendered "mystery" here as in 1:9, 3:3 and 3:9; "in Christ and in the church" literally renders in Christo et in Ecclesia, meaning with reference to Christ and the church.
reason: Note updated to match the verse change and drop the evaluative "landmark Latin reading" while still naming the Latin word.

old: For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish for His good will.
new: For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish for good will.
reason: pro bona voluntate has no possessive; "His" is supplied and decides whose good will is meant

old: Yet I deemed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and coworker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need,
new: Yet I deemed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and coworker and fellow soldier, and your apostle and minister to my need,
reason: vestrum autem apostolum is "your apostle"; the edition renders apostolus as "apostle" (cf. 2 Cor 8:23 "apostles of the churches")

old: to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this sacrament among the Gentiles, which is Christ, in you the hope of glory,
new: to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ, in you the hope of glory,
reason: sacramentum here means a hidden divine plan and the edition renders it "mystery" (Eph 1:9; 3:3, 9; Rev 17:7); "sacrament" imports a liturgical technical sense

old: Put to death, therefore, your members that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is servitude to idols.
new: Put to death, therefore, your members that are on the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is servitude to idols.
reason: fornicationem is rendered "fornication" elsewhere in the edition (1 Thess 4:3; Gal 5:19; 2 Cor 12:21)

old: Tychicus, the dearly loved brother, faithful minister, and fellow slave in the Lord, will make known to you all things concerning me,
new: Tychicus, the dearly loved brother, faithful minister, and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you all things concerning me,
reason: conservus is "fellow servant" in the edition (Col 1:7; Matt 18:28-33); no slave/free contrast here

old: Epaphras, who is one of you, a slave of Christ Jesus, greets you, always earnestly concerned for you in prayers, so that you may stand perfect and full in all the will of God.
new: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always earnestly concerned for you in prayers, so that you may stand perfect and full in all the will of God.
reason: servus Christi Jesu is "servant" per the edition's standard (Phil 1:1 servi Jesu Christi = "servants"); no slave/free contrast

old: since indeed it is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you,
new: if indeed it is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you,
reason: si tamen is conditional, "if indeed" (as at Col 1:23); "since" turns it into a causal statement

old: Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, honor and glory for the ages of ages. Amen.
new: Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
reason: in sæcula sæculorum is rendered "forever and ever" throughout the edition (e.g. Phil 4:20)

old: And manifestly great is the sacred mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, was justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory.
new: And manifestly great is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, was justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory.
reason: sacramentum is rendered "mystery" elsewhere in the edition (Eph 1:9; 3:3, 9); "sacred" is an added qualifier

old: By setting these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of the faith and of the good teaching that you have followed.
new: By setting these things before the brothers, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of the faith and of the good teaching that you have followed.
reason: minister is "minister" in the edition (Col 1:7, 23; 4:7); "servant" is reserved for servus

old: Let no one look down on your youth; instead, be an example for the believers in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
new: Let no one look down on your youth; instead, be an example for the believers in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, in chastity.
reason: castitas is "chastity" in 1 Tim 2:2 and 3:4 (and 2 Cor 6:6) in this edition

old: elderly women as mothers, young women as sisters, in complete purity.
new: elderly women as mothers, young women as sisters, in all chastity.
reason: in omni castitate: castitas is "chastity" in 1 Tim 2:2 and 3:4 ("with all chastity")

old: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household and to make a return in kind to her parents, for this is pleasing before God.
new: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household and to make a return in kind to her parents, for this is acceptable before God.
reason: acceptum est coram Deo is the same phrase rendered "acceptable before God" at 1 Tim 2:3

old: May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day. And how much he served me in Ephesus, you yourself know very well.
new: May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day. And how much he served me in Ephesus, you yourself know better.
reason: melius is the comparative "better" (tu melius nosti, "you know better"); "very well" loses the comparison.

old: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of the elect of God and the knowledge of the truth which is according to piety,
new: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of the elect of God and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness,
reason: secundum pietatem is rendered "according to godliness" elsewhere in this edition (1 Tim 6:3; pietas = "godliness" in 2 Tim 3:5).

old: Latin ante tempora saecularia literally means "before secular/age-long times," rendering the Greek expression for "before eternal times."
new: Latin ante tempora saecularia, literally "before the times of the ages," renders the Greek expression for "before eternal times."
reason: "secular" is a misleading gloss of sæcularia ("of the ages"), which the verse itself renders "of the ages."

old: training us so that, renouncing impiety and worldly desires, we may live soberly, righteously, and piously in this age,
new: training us so that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live soberly, righteously, and in a godly manner in this age,
reason: impietas/pie are rendered "ungodliness"/"in a godly manner" elsewhere in this edition (2 Tim 2:16; 3:12).

old: Both regenerationis and renovationis are Latin genitives, so "renewal of the Holy Spirit" may depend either on "the washing" or directly on the preposition "through."
new: Both genitives, regenerationis and renovationis, depend on lavacrum ("washing"), the accusative object of per: "the washing of regeneration and of renewal of the Holy Spirit."
reason: per governs the accusative, so the genitive renovationis cannot depend on "through" as the note claimed; it can only depend on lavacrum.

old: The Clementine Vulgate reads second-person cum sis talis ('since you are such a one'), whereas the Greek text and critical Vulgate editions read first-person ('since I am such a one,' cum sim talis).
new: The Clementine Vulgate reads second-person cum sis talis ('since you are such a one'), whereas the Greek participle refers to Paul himself ('being such a one').
reason: The claim that critical Vulgate editions read cum sim talis is doubtful (the Stuttgart text also has cum sis); the note is reduced to the verifiable contrast with the Greek.

old: The Vulgate uses the pluperfect relative clause "qui ... adduxerat" ("who had brought"), unambiguously making God the subject, and singular "per passionem" ("through suffering"), where the Greek is plural.
new: The Vulgate uses the pluperfect relative clause "qui ... adduxerat" ("who had brought") and singular "per passionem" ("through suffering"), where the Greek is plural.
reason: The nominative relative qui does not grammatically settle its antecedent (eum or auctorem), so "unambiguously making God the subject" overstates the Latin.

old: The Vulgate renders Greek "ou depou" ("surely not") literally as "Nusquam" ("nowhere"); "apprehendit" ("takes hold of") denotes laying hold of someone to give aid or take up their nature.
new: The Vulgate renders Greek "ou depou" ("surely not") as "Nusquam" ("nowhere"); "apprehendit" means "takes hold of."
reason: Nusquam is not a literal rendering of ou depou, and the gloss "take up their nature" is a theological interpretation, not lexis.

old: just as I swore in My wrath, 'They will never enter into My rest.'"
new: just as I swore in My wrath, 'They will not enter into My rest.'"
reason: The same oath formula Si introibunt is rendered "They will not enter" in 4:3, 4:5 and Ps 94:11; "never" adds an intensifier.

old: See to it, brothers, that there does not happen to be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God;
new: See to it, brothers, that there does not happen to be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, of departing from the living God;
reason: discedendi is a genitive gerund parallel to incredulitatis ("a heart of unbelief, of departing"), not "in departing."

old: The Vulgate adds "ejus" in "initium substantiae ejus" ("the beginning of His substance," matching "substantiae ejus" in 1:3), whereas the Greek lacks "his" and "hypostasis" is often translated "confidence" or "assurance."
new: The Vulgate adds "ejus" in "initium substantiae ejus" ("the beginning of His substance," matching "substantiae ejus" in 1:3), whereas the Greek lacks "his."
reason: Removed the claim about how hypostasis is "often translated" (a statement about English versions, not the Latin).

old: In this way Christ also did not glorify Himself to become a high priest, but He who spoke to Him: "You are My Son; today I have begotten You."
new: In this way Christ also did not glorify Himself to become a high priest, but He who spoke to Him: "You are My Son; today I have fathered You."
reason: Identical Latin ego hodie genui te is rendered "today I have fathered You" in 1:5 and Acts 13:33.

old: Concerning this we have a great discourse, and one difficult to explain in words, because you have become weak in hearing.
new: Concerning this we have a great discourse, and one that cannot be explained in words, because you have become weak in hearing.
reason: ininterpretabilis means "that cannot be explained/interpreted"; "difficult to explain" follows the Greek dysermeneutos.

old: For this reason, setting aside the introductory word about Christ, let us move forward to more mature things, not again laying a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God,
new: For this reason, setting aside the introductory word about Christ, let us be carried forward to more mature things, not again laying a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God,
reason: feramur is passive ("let us be carried/borne"); "let us move forward" makes it active.

old: But Christ, having appeared as a high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands, that is, not of this creation,
new: But Christ, being present as a high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands, that is, not of this creation,
reason: assistens is a present participle, "standing by/being present"; "having appeared" follows the Greek aorist paragenomenos.

old: Now where there is remission of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.
new: Now where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.
reason: remissio is rendered "forgiveness" in 9:22 and generally in this edition's NT.

old: Therefore, brothers, having confidence in the entrance to the sanctuary by the blood of Christ,
new: Therefore, brothers, having confidence in the entrance to the holy places by the blood of Christ,
reason: sanctorum (the holy places) is rendered "the holy places" in 8:2; 9:8, 12, 24, 25.

old: Latin sperandarum substantia rerum, argumentum non apparentium uses the gerundive sperandarum ("things to be hoped for"), substantia ("substance"), and argumentum ("proof"), where Greek-based versions often render hypostasis and elenchos as "assurance" and "conviction."
new: Latin sperandarum substantia rerum, argumentum non apparentium uses the gerundive sperandarum ("things to be hoped for"), substantia ("substance"), and argumentum ("proof"), rendering Greek hypostasis and elenchos.
reason: Removed the claim about how "Greek-based versions" render the terms (a statement about other translations).

old: By faith Sarah herself also, though barren, received power for the conception of seed even past the time of life, since she believed Him who had promised to be faithful.
new: By faith Sarah herself also, though barren, received power for the conception of seed even past the time of life, since she believed that He who had promised was faithful.
reason: fidelem credidit esse eum qui repromiserat = she believed that the one who had promised was faithful; the English read as if He had promised to be faithful.

old: For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought for sin into the Sanctuary through the high priest are burned outside the camp.
new: For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought for sin into the holy places through the high priest are burned outside the camp.
reason: in Sancta is rendered "into the holy places" in 9:12, 9:24, 9:25; "the Sanctuary" (capitalized) is inconsistent.

old: The extent of the speaker's quotation is debated and may continue to the end of the verse. The Vulgate also reads sine operibus ('without works') with the Byzantine Greek tradition rather than the Alexandrian reading 'by works.'
new: The extent of the speaker's quotation is debated and may continue to the end of the verse. The Vulgate's sine operibus ('without works') agrees with the critical Greek text, whereas the Byzantine Greek tradition reads 'by your works.'
reason: The note reverses the Greek evidence: the critical (Alexandrian) text reads choris ('without'), and the Byzantine text reads ek ('by').

old: And the tongue is a fire, a universe of iniquity. The tongue is established among our members, which stains the whole body and inflames the wheel of our birth, itself inflamed by hell.
new: And the tongue is a fire, a universe of iniquity. The tongue is established among our members, which stains the whole body and inflames the wheel of our birth, itself inflamed by Gehenna.
reason: The Latin has a gehenna, which this edition renders "Gehenna"; "hell" blurs it with infernus.

old: The Vulgate renders Greek "logikon" (often translated "spiritual" or "of the word") as "rationabile" ("reasonable"); in 2:3, "dulcis" ("sweet") corresponds to Greek "chrestos" ("good/kind").
new: The Vulgate renders Greek "logikon" ("rational," "spiritual," or "of the word") as "rationabile" ("reasonable"); in 2:3, "dulcis" ("sweet") corresponds to Greek "chrestos" ("good/kind").
reason: Notes do not report what other translations do; the point is restated directly against the Greek.

old: seeing that all things of His divine power that are for life and godliness have been granted to us through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and virtue,
new: as all things of His divine power that are for life and godliness have been granted to us through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and virtue,
reason: Quomodo means "how/as", not causal "seeing that"; "as" keeps the Latin's open relation to v. 2.

old: The Vulgate reads "through whom" (per quem, masculine singular, referring to Christ), whereas modern critical Greek editions read "through which" (referring to God's glory and virtue).
new: The Vulgate reads "through whom" (per quem, masculine singular, referring back to the one who called us in 1:3), whereas the Greek reads "through which" (plural, referring to glory and virtue).
reason: The antecedent of per quem is ejus qui vocavit nos (1:3), which the Latin does not identify as Christ rather than God; the Greek di' hon is not just a modern critical reading.

old: The Vulgate reads "with ropes of hell" (rudentibus inferni) and adds "to be tormented" (cruciandos), whereas modern critical Greek editions read "chains" or "pits of gloom" without the added phrase.
new: The Vulgate reads "with ropes of the underworld" (rudentibus inferni) and adds "to be tormented" (cruciandos), whereas modern critical Greek editions read "chains" or "pits of gloom" without the added phrase.
reason: Infernus is "the underworld" in this edition and in the verse itself; the note's "hell" contradicts both.

old: The Vulgate includes the clause ut gaudeatis ('so that you may rejoice') and reads gaudium vestrum ('your joy'), whereas many Greek manuscripts omit the first clause and read 'our joy.'
new: The Vulgate includes the clause ut gaudeatis ('so that you may rejoice'), which the Greek text lacks, and reads gaudium vestrum ('your joy') with part of the Greek tradition, whereas other Greek manuscripts read 'our joy.'
reason: The Greek tradition is not divided on ut gaudeatis, which it lacks, but it is divided on 'your'/'our joy' (Byzantine 'your', critical text 'our'); the old wording mixed the two up.

old: Dearest ones, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see if they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
new: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see if they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
reason: Carissimi is "Beloved" elsewhere in 1 John (2:7, 3:2, 3:21) and in 1-2 Peter.

old: Dearest ones, let us love one another, because love is from God. And everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.

reason: Carissimi is "Beloved" elsewhere in 1 John (2:7, 3:2, 3:21) and in 1-2 Peter.

old: Dearest ones, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
new: Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
reason: Carissimi is "Beloved" elsewhere in 1 John (2:7, 3:2, 3:21) and in 1-2 Peter.

old: The Vulgate uses the hortatory subjunctive 'diligamus' ('let us love') with explicit 'Deum' ('God') and 'Deus' ('God'), whereas most Greek manuscripts read indicative 'we love' and 'he' without explicit nouns.
new: The Vulgate uses the hortatory subjunctive 'diligamus' ('let us love') with explicit 'Deum' ('God') and 'Deus' ('God'), whereas the Greek agapomen is usually read as indicative ('we love'), and most Greek manuscripts lack both explicit nouns.
reason: Greek agapomen has the same form in the indicative and the subjunctive, so the Greek manuscripts do not "read indicative"; that is how editors usually take it.

old: The Vulgate explicitly reads "Jesus" as the one who saved the people from Egypt, agreeing with major early Greek manuscripts, whereas the Textus Receptus and some translations read "the Lord."
new: The Vulgate explicitly reads "Jesus" as the one who saved the people from Egypt, agreeing with major early Greek manuscripts, whereas other Greek witnesses, including the Textus Receptus, read "the Lord."
reason: Removes a claim about what English translations do; the Greek comparison is kept.

old: These are the ones who separate themselves, merely natural, not having the Spirit.
new: These are the ones who separate themselves, natural, not having the Spirit.
reason: animales is simply "natural" (as for animalis elsewhere in the edition, e.g. James 3:15); "merely" has no Latin basis.

old: I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like that of a trumpet,
new: I was in spirit on the Lord's day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like that of a trumpet,
reason: fui in spiritu (lowercase in the critical text, contrast Spiritus in 2:7) is a disputed referent (John's state vs. the Holy Spirit); capital "Spirit" settles it, and the edition already has "in spirit" for the same phrase at 17:3.

old: "To the angel of the church of Ephesus write: These things says the One who holds the seven stars in His right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands:
new: "To the angel of the church of Ephesus write: This is what the One who holds the seven stars in His right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands, says:
reason: Latin "Hæc dicit" is rendered with the edition's standard formula "This is what X says".

new: Latin age poenitentiam (literally "do repentance") is the standard Vulgate idiom for repenting, paired with the verb poenitere in 2:21.
reason: Note no longer glosses pœnitentiam agere as "do penance"; the edition renders it "repent" (literal "do repentance").

old: And to the angel of the church of Smyrna write: These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives:
new: And to the angel of the church of Smyrna write: This is what the first and the last, who was dead and lives, says:

new: And to the angel of the church of Philadelphia write: This is what the Holy One and the True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens, says:

old: Look, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie; look, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you.
new: Look, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie; look, I will make them come and worship before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you.
reason: adorent is rendered "worship" throughout Revelation, including the identical construction adorare ante pedes at 19:10 and 22:8; "bow down" softens the Latin.

old: And to the angel of the church of Laodicea write: These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of the creation of God:
new: And to the angel of the church of Laodicea write: This is what the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of the creation of God, says:

old: And immediately I was in the Spirit, and look, a throne was set in heaven, and One seated upon the throne.
new: And immediately I was in spirit, and look, a throne was set in heaven, and One seated upon the throne.
reason: fui in spiritu (lowercase in the critical text) is a disputed referent; capital "Spirit" decides it. Aligned with "in spirit" for the same phrase at 17:3.

old: "Worthy are You, Lord our God, to receive glory, and honor, and power, because You created all things, and because of Your will they existed and were created."
new: "Worthy are You, Lord our God, to receive glory, and honor, and power, because You created all things, and because of Your will they were, and were created."
reason: erant is simply "they were"; "existed" interprets.

old: Latin infernus ("hell") denotes the underworld or realm of the dead (Greek Hades). Notably, the Clementine Vulgate reads "over the four parts of the earth" (quatuor partes) and singular "to him" (illi), whereas the Greek reads "over a fourth of the earth" and (in critical editions) plural "to them."
new: Latin infernus ("the underworld") denotes the realm of the dead (Greek Hades). Notably, the Clementine Vulgate reads "over the four parts of the earth" (quatuor partes) and singular "to him" (illi), whereas the Greek reads "over a fourth of the earth" and (in critical editions) plural "to them."
reason: Note gloss aligned with the edition's rendering of infernus as "the underworld"; the "hell" gloss (a claim about traditional English renderings) is removed.

old: The Vulgate reads plural "Their wrath" (irae ipsorum), referring jointly to God and the Lamb, whereas critical Greek editions read singular "His wrath."
new: The Vulgate reads plural "Their wrath" (irae ipsorum), referring jointly to Him who sits on the throne and the Lamb; some Greek manuscripts read singular "His wrath."
reason: The note wrongly says critical Greek editions read "His wrath"; the major critical editions read the plural, with the singular only in some manuscripts.

old: And all the angels were standing around the throne, and the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell on their faces in the sight of the throne and worshiped God,
new: And all the angels were standing around the throne, and the elders, and the four living beings; and they fell on their faces in the sight of the throne and worshiped God,
reason: quatuor animalia is "the four living beings" everywhere else in the edition's Revelation (4:6-9, 5:6-14, 6:1-7).

old: Latin poenitentiam agere (here and in 9:21) is the standard Vulgate idiom for 'to repent,' literally meaning 'to perform repentance/penance.'
new: Latin poenitentiam agere (here and in 9:21) is the standard Vulgate idiom for 'to repent,' literally meaning 'to perform repentance.'
reason: Note no longer glosses pœnitentiam agere as "do penance"; the edition renders it "repent" (literal "do repentance").

old: Latin dabo duobus testibus meis ("I will give to My two witnesses") preserves the elliptic biblical construction without an explicit direct object, denoting God's granting of a prophetic commission.
new: Latin dabo duobus testibus meis ("I will give to My two witnesses") preserves the elliptic biblical construction without an explicit direct object.
reason: Drops an interpretive claim that decides the speaker and the object; the note keeps only the grammatical point.

old: The Clementine Vulgate distinctly specifies hujus mundi ("of this world") and closes the acclamation with Amen, both absent from standard Greek editions.
new: The Clementine Vulgate reads hujus mundi ("of this world") where standard Greek editions have simply "of the world," and closes the acclamation with Amen, which they lack.
reason: The Greek also has "of the world"; only hujus ("this") and the closing Amen are distinctive, so the note is corrected.

old: And the dragon grew angry with the woman, and he went away to do battle with the rest of her offspring, who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus Christ.
new: And the dragon grew angry with the woman, and he went away to do battle with the rest of her seed, who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus Christ.
reason: Latin semine (offspring sense) is rendered "seed", the edition's collective singular.

old: The Vulgate uses the past tense adoraverunt ('worshiped') where the Greek has a future tense, and unambiguously links ab origine mundi ('from the beginning of the world') to the Lamb who was killed.
new: The Vulgate uses the past tense adoraverunt ('worshiped') where the Greek has a future tense.
reason: Latin word order (like the Greek) does not make the attachment of ab origine mundi unambiguous; the claim is removed.

old: And they were singing, as it were, a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders; and no one was able to recite the song except those one hundred forty-four thousand who were bought from the earth.

old: And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God sitting on the throne, saying, "Amen! Hallelujah!"
new: And the twenty-four elders and the four living beings fell down and worshiped God sitting on the throne, saying, "Amen! Hallelujah!"

old: And I heard something like the voice of a great crowd, and like the sound of many waters, and like the sound of great thunders, saying, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God, the Almighty, has begun to reign.
new: And I heard something like the voice of a great crowd, and like the sound of many waters, and like the sound of great thunders, saying, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God, the Almighty, has reigned.
reason: regnavit is a plain perfect ("has reigned"; cf. regnasti "reigned" at 11:17); "begun" has no Latin basis.

old: And he carried me up in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God,
new: And he carried me up in spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God,
